News.title: Reckless teens kill couple in horror crash after stealing SUV & speeding down wrong side of road during police chase
News.content:
A CREW of four teens have allegedly killed a couple as they smashed into a stolen car while driving the wrong way down the road in a dramatic police chase.

The teens are accused of slamming a £160k SUV into another car after trying to escape cops in an hours-long chase.



The New Jersey youths allegedly swiped the Mercedes-Benz G Wagon on Saturday morning.

They went on to crash head-on into a sedan containing Robert Barr Jr., 54, and Alice Stilwell, 67, sending their car flying and killing them both, according to prosecutors.



The alleged joyriders were first spotted by police in Longport at 3.42am, who tried to pull the vehicle over.

But the teens sped off over the JFK Memorial Bridge, cops said, pulling them into a high-stakes chase.

read more world news SEA SPLASHDOWN Shocking moment plane crashes into sea in front of stunned beach-goers

Police then tracked down the car’s owner – who was yet to even realise the luxury SUV had been taken – and told officers across the county to be on the lookout for it.

Cops said they found the Mercedes four hours later at 7.46am in Hamilton Township with a Land Rover.

Both cars allegedly fled the area.



Police gave chase to the Mercedes, but eventually lost sight of it.

Just six minutes later, the teens were allegedly speeding on the wrong side of the road when they slammed into the couple’s car.

Robert and Alice were sent careening into a petrol station by the impact.

Prosecutors said they were both killed in the crash.



Officers found the wreck seconds later and arrested four people who had allegedly tried to flee the Mercedes on foot.

The four, three juveniles and one adult, were largely unscathed after the crash, authorities said.

Nayshaun Brown, 18, and three other teens who were not named because of their ages, were charged with joyriding, conspiracy to commit aggravated assault and eluding police.

Prosecutors did not reveal who was driving at the time of the accident.

Alice was a “beloved mother and grandmother”, and Robert her long term partner, a GoFundMe revealed.



Friend of the family Nicole Wright called their deaths a “devastating loss” on the fundraising appeal.

She wrote: “This unimaginable tragedy has left their family in deep grief, and the shock of how suddenly it happened has made this painful time even harder to bear.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Her daughters and their families are now doing their best to honor their mother (grandmother) while carrying the emotional and practical burdens that come with such a devastating loss.”

She added: “Every contribution, no matter the size, will help ease some of the weight this family is carrying and show them they are not alone as they honor their mother’s memory.”

News.title: Third drone & explosives found near German airport with device ‘tied to tree’ as ‘smoking gun’ evidence of plot revealed
News.content:
A THIRD drone and more explosives have been found near a German airport following a suspected Russian attack attempt earlier this month.

The chilling discovery comes after a “smoking gun” piece of evidence linking the Kremlin to the plot was uncovered by investigators.



Chaos broke out at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4 after a rigged drone was discovered near a fleet of Ukrainian cargo planes.

Moments later, the panic escalated when a second unidentified object collided with an incoming aircraft.



Experts also warned the dramatic ordeal showed how Vladimir Putin is willing to take down a European passenger jet.

It has now been revealed that authorities discovered a third drone and more bombs just west of the airport.

Authorities made the shocking find in a field in Kabelsketal, Saxony-Anhalt, on August 14.

Around 50g of a military-grade explosive substance called hexogen was reportedly seized – sparking fears the suspected attack was meant to take place on a larger scale.



A “technical device” which may have been used to control the drone was also found in the abandoned village of Kursdorf in Saxony, also near the airport.

The hardware, alongside an antenna and other electronic devices, were strapped to a tree with tape, Bild reported.

Scorched parts of the ground and metal fragments were also found, suggesting an explosive may have detonated, reports say.



The first drone was found near a fleet of planes owned by Antonov – a major Ukrainian aerospace firm.

Antonov planes have used Leipzig/Halle Airport as an operating base since Russia‘s full-scale invasion in 2022.

After the drone was found, the southern runway of the airport, a major hub for DHL and Ukrainian jets, remained closed while bomb experts examined the device.

A bomb disposal robot was even deployed to the tarmac to handle the dramatic situation.

Several planes, including a passenger flight, were diverted overnight.



Amid the chaos while air traffic was being redirected, one cargo plane had to abort its landing.

It then reportedly hit an unknown object before landing in Hanover, where minor damage to the tail fin section was discovered.

Just last week, it was reported that evidence of Putin’s plot to hit the German airport was linked to a series of parcel bombs that targeted the UK.

Analysis of the drone found traces of DNA that matched at least one person suspected of being involved in a Kremlin-backed plan to send parcel bombs in the UK, according to the Mail on Sunday.

One package burst into flames as it was set to be loaded on a DHL flight to the UK in July 2024 at Leipzig airport.



A second caught fire just two days later in the UK. It had already reached a DHL depot near Birmingham.

In Poland, two similar parcels were discovered.

All were posted from Vilnius, Lithuania, and were thought to be part of a “practice plot” ahead of a suspected plan to sabotage flights to the US.

Investigators identified 22 suspects in Poland and Lithuania who are thought to be working for Russia‘s GRU spy service.

The same network is now thought to be behind the latest Leipzig drone attack.



German security services expert Professor Peter Neumann told the Mail: “They found DNA on the Leipzig drone and… the person that matches that DNA is a person who is suspected in Lithuania of involvement in the parcel bomb plot of 2024.”

Five men are on trial in Lithuania suspected of involvement in the 2024 parcel bomb plot.

Professor Neumann called the DNA the “smoking gun” that shows “the parcel bomb attack was basically led by the Russian GRU”.

And Lithuania’s prosecutor’s office confirmed “the drone incident at Leipzig Airport is linked to Lithuania”.

News.title: Chilling signs Putin is poised to fire nuke-powered ‘Flying Chernobyl’ super weapon as aircraft mass in Arctic
News.content:
VLADIMIR Putin is feared to be gearing up for a terrifying test of his perilous nuclear-powered “Flying Chernobyl” super weapon.

An influx of aircraft converging in the Arctic has sparked concerns the tyrant could fire the cruise missile which is fuelled by its own atomic reactor.



The Kremlin has long hailed the “invincible” Burevestnik missile which carries a nuclear warhead and reportedly boasts an “unlimited range”.

This means it could strike the UK should Putin ever decide to blitz the West, according to analysts.





Satellite images from across the past few weeks shows Moscow’s high-powered aircraft descending on the Novaya Zemlya archipelago in the Arctic.

The region has already hosted tests for the Burevestnik and was previously used by the Soviets as one of their main nuclear sites between 1955 to 1990.

This included the 1961 detonation of the largest nuclear weapon ever tested, the 50MT AN602 Tsar Bomba hydrogen bomb.

This week, two specialist Il-976 SKIP aircraft used to monitor missile trajectories and collect test data reportedly arrived at Rogachevo airbase.



Imagery from the archipelago already shows an A-50U airborne early-warning aircraft, four An-26 military transports, an An-74 and several helicopters at the base.

Civilian vessels previously involved in missile trials have also taken up positions in the Barents and Kara seas around the Pankovo test range.

The Kremlin, who have boasted about firing the Burevestnik before, are yet to confirm or deny the suspected test fears.



Norwegian defence analyst Thord Are Iversen says the satellite pictures are a telltale sign however.

He says they follow the same pattern seen during previous tests of Putin’s experimental 9M730 cruise missile.

He told Russian outlet The Insider: “It now appears that everything is ready for actual Burevestnik flight testing.”

The missile has reportedly been tested up to 14 times before but had only been successful twice – in 2022 and 2025.

Last year, the supposedly successful missile launch saw the weapon travel 14,000km for 15 hours, top Russian general Valery Gerasimov said.



Gerasimov added: “During the flight, the missile performed all the prescribed vertical and horizontal manoeuvres, demonstrating its high capabilities for evading missile and air defence systems.”

The previous test in 2022 only lasted for two minutes.

The chilling Flying Chernobyl nickname comes from the 1986 Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant disaster which caused irreversible damage across the Soviet Union.



Experts fears any future tests or actual usage of the weapon could lead to a similar radioactive disaster due its atomic-powered reactor.

Dubbed “Skyfall” by Nato, a top US State Department official Thomas Countryman described it as a “uniquely stupid weapon system”.

It comes as Putin’s war in Ukraine continues to rage on.

In overnight strikes, Ukraine disabled the Afipsky Oil Refinery in Krasnodar region, setting it ablaze and adding to Putin’s woes over petrol shortages.

Moscow reacted by unleashing a barrage of deadly strikes.



Civilians were killed in Russian strikes on Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia.

More than a dozen were injured in strikes on Mena, in Chernihiv region, including four children.

Kyiv was also blitzed, with a multi-story residential building crumbling just hours after UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham left the capital.



Burnham made his first visit to Kyiv as Prime Minister to mark Ukraine’s Independence Day alongside President Volodymyr Zelensky.

The trip came just after the PM handed over crucial blueprints to help Ukraine build their own long-range Storm Shadow missiles.

Moscow responded by accusing Britain of “participating” in the war with Ukraine.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Experts told The Sun the move could provoke a raging Putin to target Britain’s defence chiefs.

Outlining how Putin could retaliate, Brit ex-Army commander Hamish de Bretton-Gordon warned that Russia’s secret service could set its sights on EU defence bosses – including those in the UK.

News.title: Horror moment tornado tears through French village leaving dozens hurt & hundreds of homes damaged as roofs ripped off
News.content:
THIS is the terrifying moment a huge tornado sweeps through southern France injuring more than 40 people and destroying at least 300 homes.

A supercell thunderstorm sparked the wild tornado as it struck the town of Pomas with wind speeds of over 73mph uprooting trees and blowing roofs off houses.



A pregnant woman was among the injured after her house collapsed when she was inside.

She was found hiding under an overturned sofa which was buried beneath a collapsed wall, police said.



The woman was rushed to hospital with the condition of her baby unknown.

The local Aude region was under an amber alert for most of Monday evening as stormy skies descended across southern France.



Several roads were closed as heavy traffic remained late into the evening due to the dozens of fallen trees and debris.

Around 2,800 homes were left without electricity from 7.30pm until late in the towns of Fontcouverte, Camplong, Souilhe, Raissac d’Aude, Fabrezan, Montmaur, Soupex, Ricaud, Montclar and La Pomarède.

Emergency services were under intense strain as they received hundreds of calls from civilians warning of injuries and destruction.

Over 120 firefighters were mobilised along with the Red Cross and canine units hunting for any missing people.

The local prefecture said shortly after 10.30pm: “The material assessment indicates that 300 homes were affected.



“Forty one people were taken care of and had passed through the victim assembly point, including 15 people evacuated to a hospital.”

Many of the homes caught in the tornado’s path had their windows smashed and roofs blown off.

Search and rescue operations continued long into the night as the weather remained stormy.



Two shelters were opened up for displaced victims in Pomas and Limoux.

There were also major flight delays and cancellations at airports in Bordeaux, Marseille, Nice, Toulouse and north of Paris, said Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot.

High winds reached up to 73mph in the village of Arquettes-en-Val, according to France’s national weather service, Meteo-France.

France averages several dozen tornadoes each year, which vary in intensity but are typically not deadly, Météo France reports.

The wet and windy weather comes just weeks after a summer of heatwaves and wildfires.



France’s south-west region saw an area of 42,000 hectares burnt in one of the largest forest fires since World War Two.

Across the whole of the country, an estimated 224,000 people had to flee their homes due to multiple raging wildfires.

Across in Spain, a dozen “mini-tsunamis” left sunbathers fleeing waves as waterfront restaurants were left flooded.

Elsewhere in Europe, extreme rain and winds hit Poland and Italy.

A strong cyclone ravaged Forlì in Italy’s Emilia-Romagna region, with winds reaching around 75mph.



Wild footage shows extreme gusts of wind flipping over four planes at an airport as witnesses recalled the aircrafts being “thrown around like toys”.

News.title: I posed as a migrant to cross the Channel in a dinghy – French cops are giving people smugglers free lifts back to camps
News.content:
AN UNDERCOVER reporter was able to cross the Channel in a small boat while posing as a migrant – and claims French police are giving smugglers free lifts back to the camps.

Journalist Christian Drogan spent weeks posing as a British criminal who was on the run in Calais before boarding a UK-bound dinghy.



Working alongside Isabel Oakeshott from Talk TV, Drogan filmed his route back to the UK, including his interactions with the criminal gangs who have control over the route.

He says it was obvious who the smugglers behind the illegal crossings were “without a shadow of a doubt” – but French police did not arrest them.



Footage shows Drogan boarding an inflatable in shallow waters on the northern French coast along with dozens of migrants.

After setting off on relatively calm seas, footage shows a Gendarmerie patrol boat approaching the dinghy.

Officers are then heard saying in English: “The sea is very rough, here it is quiet, when you go further it’s very dangerous.

“The best way today is to go back.”



Drogan said the French police offered to take anyone back to shore if they had changed their mind about crossing.

He claims the four smugglers were the only people to accept the offer – and were dropped back on the beach to continue the work of their criminal network organising the journeys.

He says it took seven hours for his boat to reach the halfway point to Britain.



Drogan, a 35-year-old builder from Rochdale, has previously spent weeks undercover inside migrant camps in Calais.

He posed under different cover stories, including as a Kurd, an Armenian, and a small-time British criminal.

Once the dinghy had reached British waters, Drogan’s footage shows Border Force workers helping migrants onto a rescue vessel.

He says at this point it became obvious to the authorities that he was not a genuine migrant.

One worker told him: “You’re on the wrong boat”.



Drogan was then taken to Western Jet Foil in Dover where small boat migrants are processed.

He said at that point he was singled out and quizzed by counter terror cops about what he had seen.

Official Home Office statistics show that on the day the reporter crossed the Channel, August 3, one boat was picked up by Border Force carrying 35 people.

So far this year 15,897 people have arrived in the UK having crossed illegally from France – which is 43.8 per cent lower than this time last year.

It is not known if Drogan’s undercover journey has been counted in the official migrant arrival figures.



The Government claimed Drogan had been “reckless” and had “made it more difficult for law enforcement officers to stop small boat crossings and save lives in dangerous conditions”.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “Our partnership with France is stronger than ever, with a new deal signed by the Home Secretary delivering a 40% uplift in boots on the ground.

“Together, we are piling the pressure on the criminal gangs and preventing illegal and dangerous crossings.

“Over 1,100 boats or engines have been seized since the election, 48,000 crossing attempts have been prevented, and the number of small boats crossings are down.”

Last week footage released by the Home Office showed French police being attacked by migrants before they managed to successfully slash a dinghy as it was being launched.



Oakeshott said: “There is a very good reason no reporter has ever attempted such a mission before: because it is both extraordinarily difficult, and extraordinarily dangerous.

“Getting to the truth of what is really happening in the Channel simply isn’t possible from the safety of the beaches.”

Drogan said: “I rolled the dice with my life for this investigation, and its findings have only cemented my scepticism towards the establishment.

“This type of investigation is dangerous, but so are the people running our country.

“Truth is the most effective weapon in this fight, and that is why this kind of work has to be done.”



Drogan warned against anyone trying to copy his trip.

He continued: “I would say if anybody tries to have a go at this, It’s highly likely they could end up dead.

“France has changed since even only just sort of a year ago when I started going over.

“It’s highly highly hostile now. It feels in places like a war zone.”

'HORROR ATTACK' Afghan man, 24, charged with rape of girl, 17, in UK city centre during early hours

Abdul Shinwari, 24, has been charged following reports the teenager was attacked in Manchester.

The alleged rape happened on Hope Street, near Piccadilly Gardens, at around 1.30am on July 14.

Shinwari, of no fixed abode, has been charged with two counts of rape and two counts of sexual assault.

News.content:

BLADE CHAOS Man seriously injured and two hurt after brawl involving ‘bladed article’ in UK city centre – as two arrested

A MAN has been seriously injured and two others hurt after a “large” city centre brawl involving a “bladed article”.

Cops have arrested two men following the violent clash, which saw armed cops swarm to the scene.



Police said that the violence broke out on Calenick Street in Truro, Cornwall, at around 1.45pm.

The force added that one man suffered a “potentially serious injury” in the fracas.



Two others were left with minor injuries.

Police confirmed that two men, both in their 20s, have been arrested on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm with intent.



The force said those involved are believed to have known each other.

A number of witnesses told CornwallLive there was an extremely large police and ambulance presence in the area.

One person said: “[The road is] all cordoned off around Burger King, around 30 coppers, 12 police cars”.

A force spokesperson said there was “no wider threat to the public”.



They added: “Those involved are believed to be known to each other and there is no wider threat to the public.”

Officers are now appealing for witnesses and anyone with relevant footage to come forward.

Anybody with information is urged to get in touch with the force, quoting 50260226230.

News.title: Trump launches ‘Operation Economic Outcast’ on Iran as he tries to isolate regime with damaging new sanctions
News.content:
DONALD Trump has launched his crushing “Operation Economic Outcast” on Iran by threatening crippling sanctions on any country propping up the regime.

The US president last week vowed to unleash the “MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN” to strong-arm Tehran into accepting his peace terms.



Washington has now upped the ante with a new plan to slap severe sanctions on any country maintaining economic ties with the regime.

Iran has meanwhile vowed it will retaliate against any country participating in the US-led isolation campaign.



With the war dragging on to the six-month mark, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced “Operation Economic Outcast” as a “warning shot” to Iran‘s allies.

Bessent said that the US was giving them a chance to “remedy bad behaviour” but stopped short of naming specific countries or laying out a timeline.



“Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” he said.

“Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”

Bessent declined to answer whether the move would target China, which bought 80 per cent of Iran’s ship oil last year.

But he said: “We want to make clear here today that no one is above the reach of US sanctions.



“That if they facilitate transactions and are part of the ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money, into repression, they will be targeted.”

Bessent said that the US had identified countries who continued to deal with Iran and would set individual deadlines to cut off ties or face sanctions.

He added: “Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system. The clock just started ticking.”



Trump, he said, was making direct calls to world leaders to request that they “cease their interactions with the regime”.

Bessent did not elaborate on whether Trump had spoken with Xi Jinping after a successful summit in Beijing last month.

China’s embassy in Washington told reporters: “Regarding the ​Iran issue, sanctions and pressure do not help resolve the problem.

“China calls on the relevant parties to take responsible actions and resolve the issue through political and diplomatic means.”

Xi is set to meet Trump in Washington in late September, but fresh sanctions could sour prospects for extending a deal struck last November to keep Chinese rare earths flowing and cap US tariffs.



Iran brushed the sanctions off with the country’s finance minister saying it was “fully prepared” for them.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ali Madanizadeh also accused the US of wanting to “wage economic terrorism”.

“We know how to play this game. This time, they should not think our response will be purely defensive and that we will only defend ourselves.”

News.title: More than 70,000 social and affordable homes to be built across England over 10 years
News.content:
Ministers have announced where more than 70,000 social and affordable homes will be built in England over the next 10 years as part of an initial allocation of almost Â£10bn, in a bid to address the housing crisis.

Funding has been granted to Greater Manchester, the West Midlands, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, North East England, and Liverpool. An additional Â£6bn was previously announced for London.

It is the first part of a wider plan to build 300,000 social and affordable homes across the nation, under the government's Â£39bn social housebuilding programme.

Earlier this year, before he became prime minister, Andy Burnham had called for the entire 10-year Â£39bn affordable housing budget for England to be spent on homes for social rent - which means the cost of the unit is about half that of market rents, and there are strict criteria for who can apply for it.

"I would actually devote all of it to social housing," Burnham told The Social Housing Podcast in May.

But of the new homes announced on Monday, 60% would be for social rent.

Housing minister Matthew Pennycook told BBC Breakfast he did not accept Burnham had failed to meet his previous commitment, saying the government had taken a "pragmatic approach" and wants to "get money out the door".

He said the next tranche of funding would be more focused on council houses - which are usually also classed as homes for social rent.

It is understood ministers decided against giving councils more of the funding announced in the first tranche because they did not believe councils would be in a position to build the required number of social homes.

News.title: Beyond China's humanoid robots, a quieter machine revolution is unfolding
News.content:
"I take a nap and the world changes," says Chen Tianyu.

His world certainly does. The 28-year-old keeps up with the latest technology by spending his spare time in factories that are switching to automation. That way he knows what to prioritise when teaching his class about artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics.

In front of him, around 30 college students are studying code. One of them is typing furiously as his eyes dart from the screen to the robot: "The idea is it will grab that cylindrical piece and move it over there."

A line of industrial robots are waiting to be programmed, and in another part of the classroom, students are trying to develop robotic medical instruments. As he guides them, Chen declares: "If you are not needed by the world of AI and robotics, then you'll definitely be among those eliminated".

For the people in this room, this is a step - or rather a leap - towards a future that China is meticulously building: Xi Jinping's $20bn (Â£14.7bn) plan to put his country at the forefront of innovation and in direct competition with the US.

The evidence is all around them. They are in the Hangzhou Technician Institute, one of several huge, purpose-built vocational schools that want to churn out the next generation of tech-savvy engineers. The campus sits on the outskirts of Hangzhou, a former imperial capital whose futuristic skyline is just the first hint of its role as a global tech hub.

Across the country, there are more than two million robots working in China's factories - which is more than anywhere else - and they are continuing to scale up at extraordinary speed.

News.title: The grieving family who say the coroners' courts aren't working
News.content:
Sarah thought she knew what she was getting into when she attended a coroner's court in May 2024 to discuss the death of her second cousin.

Her day job as a murder detective meant she was used to courts, to judges, to legal argument. What she wasn't prepared for was a coroner's court. "I felt like I was on trial," she recalls of her first hearing, in Woking, Surrey. "I remember just feeling completely railroadedâ¦ It [was] far more hostile than I had ever expected."

Her cousin, Daniel Lindsay, died in 2023, aged 41. He had lived at a home in Surrey that specialises in caring for people with learning disabilities. Daniel also had Down's syndrome and type 1 diabetes.

As his death was unexpected, his case was referred to the coroner for an inquest.

What followed was one of the most stressful experiences of Sarah's life. She discovered new details about how her cousin lived, and his cause of death. The family initially thought Daniel died from a heart attack - but over the course of the inquest, they learnt that was wrong. She had expected the process to be emotional; what she didn't predict was just how complex and frustrating it would be, at times leaving her tearful and furious.

Coroners examine deaths that are not straightforward, like unexpected or violent deaths, or those that take place in state custody. Every year, thousands of British families rely on these courts for crucial answers. For many, an inquest provides the key interaction with the arms of the state at a time of trauma.

News.title: Organised crime arrests as police investigate A66 crash that killed two officers
News.content:
Twelve people have been arrested as part of the investigation into the A66 crash that killed seven people, including two police officers.

Nine men and three women, aged between 19 and 61, have been arrested across Teesside on suspicion of a range of offences including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group. One has since been charged.

In the early hours of Saturday, a Volkswagen Passat that had been pursued by police travelled the wrong way down the A66 near Middlesbrough and crashed into an oncoming police car - two PCs and all five Passat occupants died.

Cleveland Police said it was investigating "serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident".

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and 17-year-old Cole Robert Worthy.

Earlier, Cleveland Police released more details of its investigation into the lead-up to the crash and information about the 12 people it had arrested.

The force said:

It received several reports of two vehicles "being driven dangerously" on Saturday morning

The first vehicle, believed to be a Volvo XC60, was seen "ramming properties" in the Middlesbrough area

The second vehicle, a Passat, is believed to have been associated with this activity

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology

The Volvo has been recovered in Middlesbrough

Four of the five people in the Passat had previous convictions

Assistant Chief Constable Wayne Fox said the investigation had been "fast moving and complex".

He said: "The events of that tragic night will have a lasting and profound impact on the Cleveland area and the communities we seek to protect.

"We have a duty to respond to, and thoroughly investigate, the serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident and to bring all those responsible to justice."

News.title: HPV home-testing kits available for women in England who have missed cervical screening
News.content:
Dr Sue Mann, national clinical director for women's health, said: "Offering millions of women an alternative test they can do from the comfort of their own homes will be a game-changer â making it easier than ever for them to get tested.

"There are lots of reasons that may stop women from getting their cervical screening â embarrassment, lack of time or worries about discomfort â and these kits provide a discreet and convenient option we hope will encourage more women to take up the life-saving test."

The kits contain a swab, similar to a long cotton, bud which is used to collect a sample from the vagina.

It is then sent back to the NHS and if high-risk HPV is found, individuals will be invited to book a follow-up cervical screening appointment.

High-risk HPV increases the risk of cervical cancer, but it does not mean a woman will automatically develop it.

Trials of the self-testing in London suggest it could lead to one in 10 women to come forward for screening â boosting uptake by around 400,000 a year.

Other parts of the UK are also looking at introducing self-testing.

Women aged 24 to 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years â or more frequently if HPV is detected.

Through a combination of HPV vaccination, which is offered to teenagers, and improved screening, the NHS is hoping to eliminate cervical cancer by 2040.

The NHS says cervical screening appointments with a clinician is still the best way to prevent cancer â and even if you have missed an appointment you can still come forward for one.

News.title: Burnham refuses to rule out tax rises in autumn Budget
News.content:
Andy Burnham has refused to rule out tax rises in the upcoming autumn Budget, saying he "won't be unrealistic" about the "challenging" state of public finances.

The prime minister said he would take a "careful approach" to the economy, and defended his previously announced cost of living pledges as funded spending commitments.

Burnham became prime minister in July promising to give people breathing space and help with the cost of living, but questions remain over how major policies such as social care reforms will be funded.

Experts have previously warned that he and Chancellor John Healey will have little financial room to manoeuvre in their first Budget on 28 October.

Speaking during his first visit to Ukraine, Burnham said the policies announced so far including capping bus fares at Â£2 and cutting VAT on household electricity bills were "the first steps that I've felt able to make", and were doable because he was able to reprioritise funding from elsewhere.

"I took the decision early on that digital ID wasn't the top priority for now. And so we've reprioritised funding to other priorities," he said in an interview with ITV.

Asked if the public needed to accept some of the new policies would have to be paid for in tax rises, Burnham said they wouldn't necessarily have to accept that.

Pushed on whether he would need to raise taxes to cover spending gaps, he said: "I will always take a careful approach to things. I ran Greater Manchester for 10 years and we ran a very tight ship with rock solid finances.

"Nothing will change as I come into this role as prime minister. I won't take risks with people's jobs or their livelihoods or their family finances.

"I will try to help them in whatever way I can, I have already done some things that will help them."

Burnham previously told the BBC he accepts his earlier announcements aimed at tackling the cost of living are not enough on their own and hinted at further support.

Speaking during his first official overseas visit on Monday, he said while he would do what he could, "I won't be unrealistic and people really need to understand that.

"We are in a challenging position, whatever I do will be carefully thought through, it will be funded and there will be more to come as we go into the autumn."

Last week official figures showed the the government borrowed more than expected in July, despite a record month for income tax receipts.

Inflation also reached a four-month high of 2.9% in July and is expected to rise further due to the ongoing impact of the Iran war, which has hit energy prices and fuel costs.

Experts have warned Burnham and Healey that they need to either raise taxes or cut spending elsewhere as pressure on the public finances has left no room for extra borrowing.

Both the prime minister and chancellor have vowed to stick to the fiscal rules set by former chancellor Rachel Reeves.

The rules are designed to ensure day-to-day spending is funded through tax revenue by the end of the Parliament, and to reduce debt as a proportion of GDP.

Rain Newton-Smith, the chief executive of the Confederation of British Industry, said business owners wanted to create opportunities for young people but "the cost of employing people has gone up so much".

"The business leaders I speak to say that the cost of doing business has gone up so much that it's holding them back from creating opportunities," she told the Today programme.

She said targeted support for businesses would create "more growth and more opportunities that saves money for the government and ultimately leads to higher tax receipts".

News.title: Russian stadium says it won't host Kanye West gigs
News.content:
The Russian stadium that was scheduled to host two shows by Ye, the rapper also known as Kanye West, has said the events will no longer take place.

In a social media post, external, St Petersburg's Gazprom Arena said no rental agreement had been signed with the concert promoters. "Accordingly, the concert cannot take place on our site."

West would have been the first major Western performer to play Russia since it invaded Ukraine in 2022. The rapper is trying to rehabilitate his image after years of antisemitic remarks, for which he recently apologised.

Gazprom Arena acknowledged it had received complaints about West's planned appearance and stressed that it "was not and is not" responsible for his booking.

The stadium said in its statement that the sold-out concerts, scheduled for 10 and 11 October, had been organised by the Moscow-based Say Agency.

Posting on its Telegram channel, Say Agency said the stadium's announcement had come as a surprise.

"We learned about [it] at the same time as you did, through the media," the agency wrote. "As of now, the Ye concert has not been canceled," it added in a follow-up message.

"We are trying to contact the venue to find out the reason for the post and resolve the issue. We will keep you updated."

The BBC has contacted West's publicist for a comment on the uncertainty over his Russian shows.

In its statement, Say Agency said it announced the concerts earlier this month based "on an official letter that was approved by" Gazprom Arena.

The stadium subsequently sent a rental agreement, Say Agency claimed, and the agency acknowledged the contract had not yet been signed but said the deadline to do so did not expire until later this week.

Last week, Gazprom Arena had posted enthusiastically about the concerts on social media, calling Ye "the most influential musical artist of our time".

Fans reacted to its latest announcement with disappointment.

"This was the shortest concert of my life," responded one, under Say Agency's Telegram post. "It's a shame that the government is putting obstacles in your way," added another.

There is no indication that authorities intervened in the shows, but there has been opposition to West's booking from some Russian politicians.

Vitaly Milonov, a notorious conservative lawmaker, suggested the star should perform traditional Russian songs instead of his planned setlist, reflecting the anti-Western views of many nationalists.

"Maybe after this he'll stop his disgusting antics and become a normal person," Milonov added in a video statement.

News.title: Sir Chris Hoy: Campaigning for cancer screening should not be down to me
News.content:
Sir Chris Hoy believes the onus to encourage men to get tested for prostate cancer should not just be on high-profile individuals like him.

Hoy told BBC Scotland he felt privileged to have the public platform to spread awareness and would continue to do so even if there was a national screening system in place.

But he said: "It shouldn't just be down to high-profile individuals like Jeremy Clarkson or myself or any number of men who've been in a similar situation.

"There should be a more systematic and proactive approach to let men know about their own risk."

Sir Chris was diagnosed with stage 4 prostate cancer when was 47. He turned 50 in March.

News.title: Letting agent accused of not returning deposits to more than 100 tenants
News.content:
Raman Kaur and her family rented a house through Morgan, Payne & Knightly (MPK) until September 2025 when they bought their own home.

They are still waiting for their Â£900 deposit to be returned and have discovered the money was not put in a registered deposit scheme.

"It's not right, he shouldn't be doing that with our money," she said. "That's our sweat, our hard work.

"It's very stressful having a young family and with the financial crisis that we're all going through.

"We've saved that money, we've budgeted and we've had to tell the kids they can't have things.

"I think he should be ashamed of what he's done. It's not his money, he didn't earn it."

Kaur says the family visited the West Bromwich branch of MPK to resolve the matter, but found it had closed, leaving them to try phoning Singh and his staff every day.

The home the family rented is owned by an individual who did not want to be named in this article. We will refer to him as Vikram.

"I'm owed Â£700 and MPK are falsely saying they're registered in a deposit protection scheme, but they're not," he said.

"I've spent months trying to get hold of Tony Singh but the offices have shut down, and nobody answers the phone or emails.

"It feels like nobody can help us, so we contacted the BBC."

Our investigation has since found that individual sums that are owed range from Â£700 to Â£16,000.

Vikram reported his experience to Trading Standards.

Sandwell Council, which covers West Bromwich, said both Singh and MPK were no longer operating in the borough.

Singh and MPK continue, however, to operate elsewhere in the West Midlands, the BBC can confirm.

News.title: Briton fighting for Russia killed in Ukraine
News.content:
A British national has been killed in Ukraine while fighting for Russia.

Bradley Townsend is said to have died following an attack by a remote-controlled FPV drone in Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region. His death, on 10 June, is believed to be the first of a British citizen fighting for Russia in the conflict.

The 33-year-old left his home in Barnsley, South Yorkshire, earlier this year after telling his family he was going to Romania, according to the Yorkshire Post, external.

The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) confirmed it was aware of reports a British national had died in Ukraine, adding it was in contact with his family.

The news emerged as Andy Burnham arrived in Kyiv for his first foreign trip as UK prime minister.

The visit coincides with the 35th anniversary of the country's independence from the Soviet Union.

The government has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile - allowing Ukraine to produce the weapon domestically.

News.title: Boy, 16, arrested after four viable devices found in security alert
News.content:
A 16-year-old boy has been arrested under the Terrorism Act after a security alert in Omagh, County Tyrone.

Police carried out a planned search on Monday at an address in the Gardenville Avenue.

Police said four viable explosive devices were found and removed from the property for forensic examination.

Nearby residents who had been asked to leave their homes during the alert have since returned.

Det Insp Winters urged the public not to speculate about the incident.

"It's important to stress that, while the suspect has been arrested under the Terrorism Act, our investigation to establish a motive remains very much ongoing."

News.title: Man charged with murder after house fire
News.content:
A man has been charged with murder, attempted murder and arson following a fire in west London that left a woman dead and eight others in need of hospital treatment.

Pawel Kulpa, 34, faces one count of murder, eight counts of attempted murder and one count of arson with intent to endanger life.

The charges come after a fire at a residential address on Berkeley Avenue, Hounslow, at about 01:15 BST on Wednesday, 19 August.

A 50-year-old woman, named by the Met Police as Anna Kowalska, died in hospital while another woman, 40, remains in hospital in a life-threatening condition. Kulpa is due to appear at Willesden Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

News.title: Prince Harry steps down from African wildlife charity board
News.content:
The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of an African wildlife charity whose rangers had been found to have committed human rights abuses against indigenous people.

A spokesman for Prince Harry confirmed he was stepping down after being president for the charity, African Parks, for six years before becoming a member of its board of directors in 2023, but said he remains a "supporter of its mission".

Last year the organisation admitted human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in Congo-Brazzaville.

Prince Harry's resignation comes shortly after it was announced he was relocating with the Duchess of Sussex, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet from California to the UK.

Prince Harry's spokesman said "the Duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board.

"His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks' mission."

African Parks manages around 20 national parks and protected areas across 12 countries.

It was subject to an independent human rights investigation into allegations guards managed and paid by the charity had beaten, raped and tortured indigenous people in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park.

The charity said in 2025 it had improved its safeguarding processes both in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park and institutionally.

Announcing a "governance refresh of its board of directors", the charity thanked Prince Harry for his association, saying he had "brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa".

It added: "The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks' work."

The charity's website says Prince Harry served as part of the expert team that helped implement the first phase of the 500 Elephants project, which was "one of the largest and most significant elephant translocations in conservation history".

It saw wildlife experts move elephants from a park in Malawi to help increase population in areas where they have been heavily poached.

Prince Harry has said helping move elephants to safer homes was an "amazing" experience.

The Sussexes are back in the spotlight after the revelation last week they were returning to the UK this month after enrolling their children to start at a British school in September.

No change is expected to the official status of Prince Harry and Meghan and they will remain as private individuals.

Their pending return to the UK has raised questions on their security arrangements.

Last year, Prince Harry lost a legal challenge over the levels of security he and his family are entitled to while in the UK.

It is unclear what provisions will be made for their security once they return to the UK.

The couple's plans while they are in the UK are also unclear.

The BBC learned the Duchess of Sussex was in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, which would be her first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.

In early 2020, the Sussexes left the UK and stepped back from their royal duties before settling in California in March that year.

News.title: Snooker champion Graeme Dott guilty of child sex abuse
News.content:
Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been found guilty of child sexual abuse.

The 49-year-old denied two charges of lewd and libidinous behaviour towards a girl and a boy between 1993 and 2010.

During a trial, the High Court in Glasgow heard that Dott had exposed himself and inappropriately touched a primary school girl in the 1990s and attacked a young boy between 2006 and 2010.

Lord Harrower told Dott, who won the World Snooker Championship in 2006, he would be sentenced at a separate hearing in Edinburgh on 29 September.

Dott, from Glasgow, covered his face with his hands and shook his head while the verdict was delivered by jurors following a five-day trial.

He previously called the allegations made against him "disgusting".

News.title: Drugs dug up at Creamfields site ahead of festival
News.content:
Huge stashes of illegal drugs have been found buried underground at a festival site days before the event was due to begin.

More than 80,000 music fans will head to Creamfields Festival in Daresbury, Cheshire, from Thursday.

About 204 canisters of nitrous oxide - known as laughing gas - and large bags containing ecstasy, MDMA and ketamine tablets were dug up by police during a pre-event search of the grounds, Cheshire Police said.

Supt Andy Blizard said: "Every year, we counter a number of brazen individuals who think they can outsmart us by concealing drugs from view or burying them at the site months in advance."

"There is a zero-tolerance policy regarding drugs," he said.

News.title: Man charged with manslaughter in burglary case
News.content:
A man has been charged with manslaughter after a 75-year-old woman died following a suspected burglary in north London.

Police were called to Tollington Park in Finsbury Park on the night of 11 August after reports of a burglary.

Rose Smith was taken to hospital, where she died the following day. An 81-year-old man was also taken to hospital and was discharged the next day.

Jeffrey Dean Rose, 46, of Apsley Close, North Harrow, has been charged with manslaughter and aggravated burglary. He is due to appear at Barkingside Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

He was arrested on Friday, 21 August.

In a statement released earlier on Monday, Smith's family described her as an "outgoing woman" who loved "bingo, going to cafÃ©s with her friends and, above all, spending time with her family".

They described their loss as devastating, adding: "She was the life and soul of every party. She had a wonderful personality, a big heart and a way of bringing laughter and happiness wherever she went.

"We want people to remember Rose for the person she truly was - loving, fun, kind, sociable and full of life."

Rupert Lowe has raked in over £100,000 from posts on X since being elected in 2024, as the Restore Britain leader is set to make more from social media posts than from his MP salary.

Mr Lowe, who regularly posts anti-immigration content on Elon Musk’s platform, has made on average £931 per hour this year on X, according to the register of MPs’ financial interests.

This includes an £11,724.97 payment on June 10 for just five hours of work.

If he were to continue earning at the same rate through to the end of the year, his total takings would almost surpass his annual MP salary, which is £98,599.

open image in gallery Rupert Lowe, who regularly posts anti-immigration content on Elon Musk’s platform, has made on average £931 per hour this year on X ( AFP/Getty )

The payments were made via billionaire Elon Musk’s “creator revenue” programme.

The scheme allows premium users with more than 500 verified followers to “monetise” their accounts on the controversial site, which has grown increasingly toxic since it was taken over by the Tesla tycoon in 2022.

But Mr Lowe hit back, saying: “If I wanted to make money, I would not be in politics. I donate my entire net MP salary to local charities in my constituency – being a politician is the most expensive job I’ve ever had.”

Mr Lowe enjoys a considerable amount of engagement on his posts, which boosts revenue secured by the programme.

His five posts on August 24 alone garnered 683,000 views and over 70,000 likes on the platform.

On post, which received 20,000 likes called for foreign nationals living in social housing to be deported.

It said: “The honest truth is that if a foreign national is living in social housing and unable to financially support themselves? They don't just need to be evicted from the building. They need to be removed from the country.”

open image in gallery X has received a growing amount of criticism since Elon Musk’s takeover of the site, with the government having threatened to ban the platform over misuse of its Grok/AI feature ( AFP/Getty )

Another, which received 24,000 likes, responded to reports about his earnings on X, in which he said: “The Guardian is attacking me over receiving money from X. Trust me, if I wanted to make money, I would NOT be in politics. I donate my entire net MP salary to charity.

“This is the most expensive job I’ve ever had, comfortably!”

Mr Lowe acrimoniously left Reform UK in March 2025 amid claims of bullying and threatening behaviour, before going on to found his own party, Restore Britain. The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said Mr Lowe would face no criminal charges.

The party – which until now has largely been based in Mr Lowe’s constituency, Great Yarmouth – is further to the right than Reform on issues such as immigration and has enjoyed support from tech billionaire Elon Musk, who has publicly backed Restore Britain a number of times on his X platform.

X has received a growing amount of criticism since Elon Musk’s takeover of the site, with the government having threatened to ban the platform over misuse of its Grok/AI feature.

Several government departments have also ditched the site, including culture Secretary Lisa Nandy who announced she is leaving it because it “favours abuse and misinformation”.

Lego has posted record sales for the first half of 2026, with revenues rising by more than a fifth thanks to strong demand for its World Cup and KPop Demon Hunters ranges.

The Danish toy manufacturer recorded a 21 per cent increase in revenue to 41.9 billion Danish kroner (£4.8 billion) in the six months to 30 June. Over the same period, pre-tax profits rose by a third to reach 11.3 billion Danish kroner (£1.3 billion).

The company introduced over 330 new lines during the half, attracting fresh shoppers through enthusiasm for World Cup football and "consumer excitement" surrounding Formula 1 and the hit Netflix film KPop Demon Hunters.

Among the new releases was a replica model of the official Fifa World Cup trophy, alongside sets containing interactive bricks that have previously featured in Star Wars and Pokemon products.

Niels Christiansen, chief executive of Lego, said: “We are very pleased with our strong start to 2026 and the excitement we see for the Lego brand.

“Our portfolio of products offers something for everyone, and culturally relevant brand experiences continue to drive demand across the globe.”

World Cup and KPop Demon Hunters ranges helped toy giant Lego drive sales up in the first half of 2026 ( Lego )

It said operating profits jumped 22 per cent to 10.9 billion Danish kroner (£1.2 billion) despite spending on “strategic initiatives” such as sustainability, with the group looking to make its bricks out of more renewable and recyclable materials.

The surge in oil prices caused by the Iran war has driven up the cost of plastics Lego uses to make its bricks, and Christiansen said the company might see an impact in the second half but so far it has not been significant.

"We are impacted by higher oil prices, but because we purchase so much non-fossil-fuel-based material that is less correlated to the oil price, we've actually been able to manage relatively well," said Christiansen. Lego is in the process of shifting towards renewable and recyclable materials to make its bricks.

As it aims to produce closer to its main markets, Lego is building a factory and distribution centre in the U.S. state of Virginia, aiming to open by the middle of 2027.

Lego is also aiming to switch to paper based bags for its sets across all factories by 2027.

This restored palazzo in Umbria unites guests and locals over olive oil, spaghetti and botanical spritzes. With unrivalled views over Lake Trasimeno, it’s giving its Tuscan neighbours something to talk about

Location

At the edge of “Italy’s green heart” of Umbria, Rastrello sits in Panicale, a town with a permanent population of around 500. The hotel offers a great base from which to explore well-known Tuscan and Umbrian towns including Siena and Assisi, with the closest airport, Perugia San Francesco d’Assisi, a 45-minute drive away.

If you’re travelling from Florence or Rome (which are equidistant to Rastrello), it’s best to take an affordable regional train to Chiusi-Chianciano station – a 20-minute drive from the hotel. Car hire is advised to reach Rastrello from the station, with parking available out front.

Panicale’s best sights – the Cesare Caporali Theatre, Tulle Museum and the Renaissance frescoes in the Church of San Sebastiano – are all no more than a five-minute walk from the hotel.



The vibe

There’s an obvious star of the Rastrello story: olive oil. There are around 1,000 olive trees on its land, most over 400 years old. A farmhouse feel starts with wall art of the olive harvest, then drips onto the terracotta interiors of the restored 14th-century palazzo.

Rotating exhibitions in the intimate ground-floor lounges of the hotel highlight work by local artists, though the main exhibit is outside – a sparkling view of Trasimeno, Italy’s fourth largest lake.

open image in gallery Rastrello officially opened in 2020 ( Rastrello )

Look out of one window and you’ll see locals savouring espressos on Piazza Umberto I, as children kick a ball around the fountain. From another, cypress trees dot tumbling Umbrian hills.

Instead of in-room minibars, an early evening aperitivo is laid out to encourage conversation. So, from 4pm to 7pm, guests gather in the lounges and on the terrace of Rastrello for house wine, charcuterie and to chat over the buzz of birdsong and the last of the golden light.

Service

Staff here are local Umbrians who know Panicale like the back of their hands. Reception staff are as happy to walk you the three minutes to your town tour as they are escorting guests to the best evening aperitivo spot. Check-in is warm and welcoming, akin to a greeting from family.

Bed and bath

The hotel has 14 rooms, seven in the original building and seven in the new garden annex, following an extension in spring 2025. There are also two private apartments in the town with full kitchens and washer-dryers for those staying longer. Design-led rooms by Pelizzari Studio, from standard doubles to suites, are washed in earthy Umbrian tones. All offer lake views, and feature restored original features and windows with electric blackout blinds that you’ll want to keep open.

open image in gallery Design-led rooms were curated by interior architect Pelizzari Studio ( Rastrello )

Four-poster beds can be forgiven for creaking – the king mattresses are like clouds. I’m informed by general manager Chiara Verdacchi that the reason for the rooms being minimal and wardrobes wide, is to “allow space for wine, olive oil and shopping bags”. In-room steamers are a useful addition, as are large full-length mirrors and USB-C bedside charging ports.

Bathrooms have brick floors, marble rainfall showers, and exposed wooden beams on the ceiling, with Grown Alchemist toiletries sat on twin sinks.



Food and drink

Rastrello means “rake” in Italian, a nod to the tool used to hand-pick olives before they are turned into indulgent lashings of own-brand extra-virgin olive oil (EVOO), featured heavily on tables in the Cucina & Giardino restaurant. The cosy ground-floor farm-to-table restaurant delivers an ever-changing menu of unfussy seasonal dishes by chef Nicola Fanfano. Local Umbrian produce is championed in the dishes, from the charcuterie to the herbs grown in the hotel garden used to garnish plates, and the hotel’s house martini is made from vodka infused with the property’s liquid gold EVOO.

open image in gallery Take breakfast on the Rastrello terrace ( Rastrello )

I recommend staying over a Sunday to join the feast at one of the communal monthly spaghettata pasta dinners, curated by a beloved Panicale nonna or nonno. On my menu was a hearty bowl of rigatoni with fava bean and artichoke scafata, paired with a local white wine and a mushroom, potato toast I won’t be forgetting quickly.

But this isn’t a hotel that gate-keeps its guests. As there’s no lunch service at the hotel, you’re encouraged to head into town for truffle gnocchetti at Masolino, antipasti at Il Caffè della Piazza or tiramisu from Lillotatini.

Breakfast is a compact continental buffet offering of fresh cold cuts, cheeses, Greek yoghurt, granola, warm chocolate chip cake and your choice of eggs; taken in the lounges or on the garden terrace. Dietaries are well catered for with adapted dishes. For example, I was given a personal fruit salad to accommodate my kiwi allergy.

Facilities

Exploring Panicale is the best pastime here, but new dedicated wellness spaces opened alongside the annex in 2025. There is a meditation room for solo sound baths, a small basement spa and an outdoor dipping pool with sunbeds. I highly recommend a massage with EVOO-infused treatment oils.

open image in gallery Rastrello lays on afternoon aperitivo for guests in its lounge ( Rastrello )

The complimentary one-hour private sauna session is a standout amenity. Be sure to book this ambient sanctuary in the annex with lounge chairs, a shower and herbal detox teas.

Rastrello can also organise off-site seasonal activities for guests, from olive oil and wine tastings to pasta cooking classes, to truffle hunting, forest E-biking, and private Lake Trasimeno boat tours.

Accessibility

The hotel has two accessible rooms and two accessible public bathrooms, with adapted fire alarms for deaf guests. Lifts are spacious enough to allow wheelchair access to all rooms except those on the rooftop, which are reached by stairs; however, gravel on the lower terrace and cobbled steps connecting the sites of Panicale aren’t easy to navigate if you have mobility needs.

Pet policy

Small, well-behaved pets are welcome to stay at Rastrello on request for a flat fee of approximately €25 (£21) per visit.

Check-in/check-out

Check-in is from 4pm, check-out is 11am.

open image in gallery Rastrello sits in Panicale, a medieval hilltop village in Umbria ( Rastrello )

Family-friendly?

Yes, although the peaceful boutique hotel is better suited to adults. Extra beds can be added to junior suites or apartments for children, and a dedicated connecting family suite can be booked to include a living space for up to six guests.

At a glance

Best thing: The sense of community in Panicale that makes its social hubs feel blended with the hotel.

Perfect for: Solo travellers seeking some R&R.

Not right for: Rowdy, big group getaways.

Instagram from: The terrace – for spritz pics and Lake Trasimeno landscapes.

Address: V.le Guglielmo Marconi, 18, 06064 Panicale PG, Italy

Phone: +39 075 837246

Website: rastrello.com



Natalie was a guest of Rastrello

News.title: Transfer news LIVE: Arsenal given Alvarez hope, Man City target Liverpool winger, Watkins’ Villa exit
News.content:
Why Carlos Baleba Fixes Man United's BIGGEST Problem

Arsenal are hoping to secure the signing of Julian Alvarez to cap off a productive summer of incomings and boost their forward line as they look to defend their Premier League title. Elsewhere, Manchester City have agreed a €100m deal with Lille to buy midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi while Omar Marmoush and Nico Gonzalez were part of the squad to face Bournemouth despite interest from Spurs and Newcastle respectively. Interestingly, City are slso said to be interested in Liverpool’s Cody Gakpo though no club-to-club talks have taken place yet.

Firefighters are gaining ground on a fast-moving wildfire near Reno, Nevada, after flames destroyed more than 30 homes and forced tens of thousands of residents to evacuate or prepare to flee.

The Hawk Fire was 27% contained Monday after holding at roughly 23 square miles following a dangerous surge over the weekend, officials said.

“We are making progress,” U.S. Forest Service District Ranger Matt Zumstein said.

open image in gallery This image taken from video shows active wildfires Saturday ( AP )

Evacuation orders and warnings remained in place for about 63,000 residents, down from more than 90,000 at the height of the fire. Officials warned that shifting winds could still send flames through dry vegetation toward residential neighborhoods.

At least 32 homes have been destroyed and six damaged, though authorities expect those numbers to rise as assessment teams reach more burned areas. Seven people — three first responders and four civilians — have been injured.

Reno Mayor Hillary Schieve described the speed and intensity of the flames as unlike anything she had witnessed.

open image in gallery An old stove and teakettle next to a home that burned down during the Hawk Fire in Reno ( Reuters )

“It lit up these areas like nothing I’ve seen before,” she said. “It took your breath away, in the worst way.”

The fire began Saturday near the California border before exploding in size Sunday. Nevada's governor declared a state of emergency and deployed the National Guard to assist with aerial firefighting operations and secure evacuated neighborhoods northwest of downtown Reno.

Schools across Washoe County were closed Monday to keep roads clear for emergency crews.

open image in gallery A burned home smolders after it was destroyed by the Hawk fire ( AFP/Getty )

Some residents have grown frustrated over restrictions preventing them from returning home, but Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam warned that conditions remain dangerous.

“It just takes that little breeze and one ember,” he said.

Officials said the Hawk Fire is the third major wildfire north of Reno in two weeks. All three were caused by human activity, though authorities have not determined whether the Hawk Fire was started accidentally or deliberately.

open image in gallery Some residents have grown frustrated over restrictions preventing them from returning home ( AP )

The disaster has also complicated preparations for Burning Man, which is scheduled to begin Sunday in the Black Rock Desert. Many festivalgoers traditionally travel through Reno on their way to the event.

Burning Man organizers urged visitors not to take hotel rooms or other resources needed by people displaced by the fire.

“Treat our neighbors, first responders, hospitality workers and everyone affected by this emergency with patience and care,” organizers said.

For some residents, the devastation has been painfully familiar.

Crystal Hallock, 53, lost her home to fire for the second time in less than a decade. An electrical fire destroyed her previous home in 2018, and she moved into the rebuilt property the following year.

Hallock fled Saturday with her children, grandchildren and pets as smoke and flames approached. Her ex-husband remained behind trying to protect the property and her vintage Cadillac with a garden hose.

open image in gallery Two firefighters knock down hotspots in the charred remains of a home burned ( Reuters )

As conditions deteriorated, Hallock pleaded with him over the phone to leave.

“He was saying he can’t breathe, it’s so dark I can’t see, and I’m screaming at him, ‘Leave the car, just leave it,’” she recalled.

The call suddenly went dead.

About 30 minutes later, he called again. He had escaped — and managed to save the Cadillac.

open image in gallery A statue is left amid the remains of a home burned by the Hawk Fire ( AFP/Getty )

“I’m truly blessed because I have a place to stay with my animals and my grandkids,” Hallock said. “We were all able to get out safely.”

Others had little time to gather their possessions.

“Honestly, I thought it was like in a movie,” said Ruby Delatorre, who returned from a concert to find her neighborhood under evacuation orders.

Another resident, Jon Hanbury, was still waiting Monday to learn whether his home had survived.

“The flames were pretty close to my house, and the smoke was really thick,” he said from a temporary shelter at Reno's convention center.

Despite improving containment, the danger is not over. Warm, dry and breezy weather is expected across western Nevada, with critical fire conditions possible later this week.

The Hawk Fire comes during a punishing wildfire season across the West. More than 50,000 wildfires have been recorded nationwide this year, the highest number at this point in a decade, according to the National Interagency Fire Center.

Thunderstorm warnings have been issued across the country on Wednesday as the Met Office warns of flooding and disruption.

Yellow warnings for storms will be in place across England and Wales from 3am til 10pm on Wednesday. The west and east Midlands, north west, south east, south west and east of England will all be under yellow thunderstorm warnings, as will parts of Wales.

The Met Office warned there is a “small risk of flooding and disruption from thunderstorms on Wednesday.”

A band of heavy showers and thunderstorms is expected to move northwards on Wednesday morning, the forecaster warned, adding that an intense downpour of 20-30 mm rain could fall in less than an hour.

open image in gallery ( Met Office )

Some spots could see 40-50mm in two to three hours, leading to some surface water flooding, with the possibility of large hail and frequent lightning.

These showers and thunderstorms are expected to drift northwards and ease during the evening.

Homes and businesses could be flooded quickly, the forecaster said, with damage to some buildings from floodwater, lightning strikes or hail. Flooding and lightning could cause delays and cancellations to train and bus services.

The risk of spray and sudden flooding could also lead to road closures and difficult driving conditions, the forecaster added, with a chance of power cuts for some parts of the country.

Industrial action by members of air traffic control has led to Norwich airport cancelling all flights on Friday.

On 28 August, no flights will operate to or from the Norfolk aviation base as members of the Prospect union strike.

The 24-hour walkout over pay and working conditions is set to close the airport to air traffic.

Air traffic control members of the union voted in favour of industrial action, short of a strike, from 17 August.

Passengers due to travel on Friday have been advised to check with their airline for available flight options and the latest information.

Carriers that fly out of Norwich include KLM, Loganair, Ryanair and Tui.

Prospect members at Norwich airport are asking for a 10 per cent pay rise in line with market comparators and improved maternity and paternity leave.

Norwich airport said: “We apologise for the disruption and inconvenience this will cause to passengers.

“We remain firmly committed to resolving this dispute through constructive dialogue and will continue to engage with Prospect with the aim of reaching agreement.”

Prospect National Secretary David Avery said: “Norwich airport is only able to operate because of the goodwill of its air traffic control staff. The airport’s continuing refusal to countenance bringing pay and parental leave in line with the market means that that goodwill has evaporated.

“All members want is to be treated the same as their counterparts elsewhere in the country.

“We don’t want to take this strike action, especially at a time when it will impact people’s holidays, but we have been left with no choice. NAL can still avert this action, but they need to come back to the table with a deliverable and fair plan.”

News.title: Palmer and Rogers show promise of star double act for Chelsea
News.content:
“I am very happy for Cole,” Alonso said. “I have really enjoyed seeing him play with the dynamism and the freedom and the responsibility... when Cole feels this way we have a better team and a better Cole.”



Palmer makes it look very easy in this form, capable of switching the direction of play a beat before anyone else spots the opportunity. He and his old Manchester City academy friend Rogers came off before the end, Palmer having demonstrated some discomfort chasing a ball. Asked afterwards how ready he felt, Palmer responded in kind. “Did you not watch the game? I’m only joking, I’m ready... it was a difficult season with injuries and whatnot, but through the summer and since I’ve been back I’ve worked extra hard.”

If there was an attacker to compare with him on the other side it was King, who looks even better. The 19-year-old was way ahead of Arbeloa’s two young Real Madrid imports. García toiled away and took his chance, but César Palacios struggled for any impact in a position tucked in on the left. Oscar Bobb and King gave Fulham some edge but the concern, as ever, will be where Fulham get their goals.

Arbeloa pushed his full-backs high and encouraged Sander Berge to drop deep to get on the ball in the first passing phase. The Norwegian delayed too long in challenging João Pedro for Chelsea’s third – backing off and allowing Palmer to overlap to receive the pass.



Sánchez had not been the only concern for Chelsea. Back in the team, Levi Colwill misjudged a challenge on King in the first half and was relieved that the card was only yellow. Roméo Lavia took a wild swing at Calvin Bassey and was also booked. Moisés Caicedo was not fit to play. Enzo Fernández was on the bench and would come on in the second half to the kind of reception from opposition fans to which he will quickly become familiar.



There was a grin from the Argentine at those who berated him from the home stands when he returned at half-time. Fernández worked hard to transmit a general sense that the abuse did not land, although he will be relieved that the Chelsea fans were supportive. His future still feels very much in play.



It was Palmer’s subtle ball through that gave João Pedro the chance with 32 seconds of the game played. The ball came forward immediately from Lacroix’s firm header from defence. The Frenchman delivered a very accomplished assist for Rogers’s first-half goal. Before that King had equalised. There was an exchange with Timothy Castagne, and King looked up just inside the box and decided to have a swing at it. Sánchez was close enough to grasp the ball and somehow failed to do so.

Sánchez would later push a Castagne shot in the direction of García, who stooped and nodded the ball over the goalkeeper after Palmer had scored Chelsea’s third. This second error was unfortunate, but it is the kind of thing that happens to a goalkeeper as erratic as the one for whom Chelsea’s hierarchy seem to have such patience.

News.title: This summer’s wildfire epidemic is one of the worst in decades – so why are deaths so low?
News.content:
Wildfires in Britain and Europe this year are among the worst in decades, yet direct deaths are at some of the lowest levels, according to a Telegraph analysis.

As of early August, 505,683 hectares of land have burned across Europe, forcing the evacuation of more than 360,000 people as uncontrollable flames reach major cities, towns, and villages.

The problem is global – in the US, Nevada declared a state of emergency over the weekend after a wildfire caused more than 42,000 people to evacuate their homes.

But what sets 2026 apart isn’t just the vast areas of land burned, but how few deaths have been caused by the fires.

This summer, just 14 people are reported to have died in European wildfires, the vast majority in a single blaze in Almería, southern Spain.

By comparison, more than 130 people were killed in the summer of 2017 – a toll driven largely by the Pedrógão Grande disaster in Portugal, where more than 60 people died on a single stretch of road.

In 2018, at least 100 others died in a single afternoon in the Mati disaster near Athens, despite total hectares burned that year being roughly a third of current levels.

Since the modern phenomenon of summer wildfires exploded in Europe a decade ago, the direct death toll has broadly trended downward, as the chart below shows.

News.title: Swine flu outbreak in Delhi swamps clinics and hospitals
News.content:
India is battling a surge in H1N1 flu infections, prompting the federal health ministry to step up surveillance and hospital preparedness.

The national capital New Delhi has recorded 1,777 cases this year, almost eight times the number (229) reported during the same period in 2025.

Dr Randeep Guleria, a senior pulmonologist and director of Medanta Medical School, Gurugram, says the H1N1 cases are much higher than reported.

“It’s quite likely that the reported numbers are an underestimate because they depend on how many people are tested,” Guleria said. “If you speak to patients admitted to hospital who test positive for H1N1, you often find that other members of their family have similar symptoms, although they have not been tested.”

“There is a surge and we are seeing a lot of patients. We are testing only those who come to hospital and are more seriously ill,” Guleria said.

H1N1, commonly known as swine flu, is a subtype of influenza A. It is a contagious respiratory infection that can cause fever and cough and in severe cases it can lead to pneumonia and respiratory failure.

Officials at the Indian Council of Medical Research said the rise did not mean the emergence of a new strain of the virus.

The surge comes during India’s rainy season, when seasonal influenza and other respiratory infections typically increase.

Doctors in Delhi say they are seeing more patients with high fevers, persistent coughs and flu-like symptoms, although most cases remain mild.

The H1N1 cases have been reported beyond New Delhi. The metro cities like Mumbai, Chennai and Bangaluru have reported a high number of cases, although the pattern is not uniform across the country.

Doctors in Bangaluru have reported more influenza A infections among children, with some developing pneumonia and respiratory distress.

India’s health minister JP Nadda said there was a need for continued vigilance and robust surveillance. He has asked officials to monitor unusual increases and clusters of cases and ensure hospitals could respond quickly.

“Swine flu (H1N1) can show up through symptoms such as fever, cough, sore throat, headache, runny nose, body aches and fatigue… If you experience these symptoms, seek medical advice at your nearest healthcare centre,” the health ministry said on X.

Delhi’s health minister, Pankaj Kumar Singh, said the capital had enough beds, doctors, medicines and medical equipment to manage the increase. “Delhi is fully prepared to deal with the present health situation,” Singh said.

India has had several waves of H1N1 since the virus emerged globally in 2009.

The infection, commonly called swine flu, became a recurring seasonal respiratory illness after the 2009 pandemic rather than disappearing from circulation.

India recorded 3,320 H1N1 cases and 14 deaths in 2025, according to Ministry of Health data.
