World.title: Luke Gosling charged with breach of bail just weeks after alleged assaults
World.content:
Federal politician Luke Gosling has been charged with breaching his bail conditions, less than a month after he was arrested over allegations he assaulted the Northern Territory Administrator.

In July, the Labor MP was charged with two counts of assault over an alleged incident involving NT Administrator David Connolly at a community event held in Darwin earlier that month.

Mr Gosling is the Commonwealth's special envoy for defence and veterans' affairs, and has held the seat of Solomon — which includes Darwin and its satellite city of Palmerston — since 2016.

The administrator is the Crown's representative in the NT, a vice-regal role equivalent to a state governor.

David Connolly took on the job of Northern Territory Administrator earlier this year. (ABC News: Sam Parry)

Mr Gosling's bail conditions were varied in Darwin Local Court on July 31, with the federal MP banned from coming within 50 metres of the NT's Government House — where Mr Connolly resides.

Judge Stephen Geary also ordered Mr Gosling to give Mr Connolly's office 48 hours' notice before attending any event where both men would be in attendance.

If the two do attend the same event, Mr Gosling is required to stay 15 metres away from the administrator at all times.

Last month, Luke Gosling faced Darwin Local Court where he was granted bail. (ABC News: Matilda Colling)

In a statement released to media this afternoon, NT Police said Mr Gosling allegedly breached his bail conditions on August 14.

"Today he was served with a summons to appear in Darwin Local Court on 30 September 2026," NT Police said.

Gosling to fight assault charges

During Mr Gosling's first court appearance, the court heard the assault charges related to two separate incidents which allegedly occurred 30 minutes apart.

In discussing the reported details, Mr Gosling's lawyer Marty Aust SC told the court the first alleged incident had occurred "in a manner in which the administrator was unable to see the approach".

Luke Gosling to be prosecuted by Commonwealth DPP The Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions is set to take over the case against Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling, to avoid a perceived conflict of interest within the Northern Territory Director of Public Prosecutions.

The court heard the second charge pertained to an alleged hip-and-shoulder collision between the two men, during which Mr Gosling allegedly drew back his left elbow and struck Mr Connolly in his upper rib.

Mr Gosling has strenuously denied the assault allegations, with his lawyer previously telling media the charges would be contested in court.

The federal MP has faced pressure to step down from his political role since news broke of the alleged assault, including from Shadow Defence Minister James Paterson and NT Senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese declined previous opportunities to speculate on Mr Gosling's political future, earlier saying it would be inappropriate to comment while the legal process is underway.

Federal Opposition Leader Angus Taylor urged Mr Albanese to stand down the Solomon MP.

In a statement released after news broke of the fresh charge, Angus Taylor urged the prime minister to stand down the Solomon MP. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"When these serious charges were first laid, we said this was a test of the prime minister's leadership and Luke Gosling should be stood down from his special envoy role while the matter is dealt with," Mr Taylor said in a statement, released this afternoon.

"Now Mr Gosling has also been charged with allegedly breaching his bail, the case for the prime minister to act is even stronger.

"These allegations are matters for the courts, but Anthony Albanese has a decision to make about who serves in his government. He should stand Mr Gosling down today."

The offices for both Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Mr Gosling have been contacted for comment.

World.title: Distress beacon borrowing program proposed after teen hiker's death
World.content:
A New South Wales mayor has described Lily Hooper as an amazing woman full of spirit and adventure who was taken too soon, while promising to establish a bushwalking safety program in her honour.

The 18-year-old's body was found in bushland of the Nattai National Park, near Mittagong, last Thursday after an eight-day search.

Almost 1,000 people from multiple agencies took part in the search when she did not return from her solo hike on the Bonnen Pic Walking Trail.

The cause of her death is not yet known, but NSW Police have said her body was located a significant distance from the path.

Wollondilly Shire Council held a minute's silence at its council meeting on Tuesday afternoon.

Mayor Matt Gould said the council would collaborate with NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service to make bushwalking safety equipment more readily available.

Lily Hooper, 18, went missing while hiking in Nattai National Park. (Supplied: NSW Police)

"I've spoken with Lily's family about how our community might permanently remember her," Cr Gould said during council's ordinary meeting on Wednesday.

"Rather than creating a single physical memorial … we will establish a program in Lily's memory where council purchases personal locator beacons and makes them available for residents and bushwalkers to borrow free of charge, alongside practical bushwalking safety information.

"A personal locator beacon is something you hope nobody ever needs to activate, but if someone does find themselves in trouble in remote country, having one can make an enormous difference.

"My hope is that this becomes a living and practical legacy in Lily's name, something that helps people enjoy the bush safely."

Matt Gould says the community's response to Lily Hooper's death has been overwhelming. (ABC News)

Cr Gould also thanked emergency crews involved in the search for Ms Hooper and said there had been an enormous outpouring of community grief.

"While most of us never knew Lily personally, I think over the past two weeks, our community has come to understand just how special she was through the people who did," he said.

Purple lights, flags lowered

Tributes left in memory of Ms Hooper at Oakdale's Willis Park, south west of Sydney, have been carefully collected after the town was hit by wet weather.

With the support of her family, council staff gathered some of the cards and signs on Monday to protect them from rain.

The items have been passed on to the Hoopers, with the memorial space to remain open to the community until Friday.

An outpouring of grief has followed the death of bushwalker Lily Hooper. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Just hours after Ms Hooper's body was found, Wollondilly Performing Arts Centre was lit up purple and the council chamber's flags flown at half mast.

Ms Hooper's former school, Campelltown Performing Arts High School, posted an online tribute, describing their 2025 graduate as a kind, humorous and respectful young woman.

"[She] lit up every room with her infectious smile, positive energy and determination to live life to the full," the post read.

"This loss has had a significant impact on our students, staff and wider school community."

Meanwhile, a fundraiser organised by the Rotary Club of Wollondilly North in support of the Hooper family has raised a growing $30,000.

Dozens of community members, friends and family have flocked to Oakdale's Willis Park to pay their respects to Lily Hooper. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

State government honour

NSW Premier Chris Minns on Monday promised to work with Ms Hooper's family on a special tribute to honour her.

Her father, Jim Hooper, told 7NEWS he would like the flag on the Sydney Harbour Bridge lowered as she worked as a Bridge Climb tour guide.

"I want to talk with them and work on it together, but we'll do something special for Lily and frankly it's the least we can do," Mr Minns said.

" It's a terrible life lost and it's a lovely family. "

NSW Deputy Premier Prue Car said on Sunday the government was open to reviewing safety signage in national parks to prevent deaths like Ms Hooper's.

"We are open to ideas on that. We are constantly saying to people, 'Try and get your kids off their phones and into nature,' but we have to make sure we are making that are safe as possible," she said.

Lily Hooper went missing is in rugged terrain south of Sydney. (Supplied: NSW National Parks)

The comments come just days after Mr Minns vowed to apologise in person to Ms Hooper's family after he told parliament their daughter was found alive.

"I'm also absolutely devastated and profoundly sorry that anything I said may have added to the grief that that family has gone through," Mr Minns said on Friday.

Emergency services are examining whether a miscommunication about a police code may have led to Ms Hooper being incorrectly identified as alive.

A coronial investigation is also underway.

World.title: SA wildlife park to vaccinate 100 birds against deadly H5 bird flu
World.content:
About 100 captive native birds at Cleland Wildlife Park will be vaccinated against H5N1 bird flu.

They include critically endangered orange-bellied parrots and, regent honeyeaters, endangered red-tailed black cockatoos and vulnerable regent parrots, in addition to 26 other bird species at the park.

Primary Industries and Regional Development Clare Scriven said Cleland would be the first South Australian wildlife park to gain approval to administer the H5N1 vaccine to its captive birds.

It recently received federal funding to upgrade several aviaries in anticipation of the arrival of bird flu in Australia.

Cleland Wildlife Park general manager Kelly Bramhill said biosecurity measures have restricted public access to three other aviaries not subject to the upgrades.

"Vaccination for us really is that last line of defence," she said.

Vaccine not a 'silver bullet'

Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said Australia currently had around 1,500 vaccine vials available.

The vaccines are not fully protective against the disease, and would require two shots to maximise immunity.

Native Australian species are receiving the vaccine for the first time, and will be monitored before undergoing the final dose.

Ms Scriven said the vaccine was "not a silver bullet".

"We are not 100 per cent sure of the effectiveness of the vaccines on particular species," she said.

Cleland Wildlife Park general manager Kelly Bramhill said vaccines are the last stage of efforts to protect the sanctuary's native birds. (ABC News)

Ms Scriven said logistical difficulties capturing, vaccinating and monitoring wild birds meant captive and endangered species were the government's current priority.

SA's chief veterinary officer Dr Skye Fruean said Zoos SA, which operates the Adelaide Zoo and Monarto Safari Park, was the only other organisation working through a vaccine approval process with the Department for Primary Industries and Regions.

"We’re working with them to make sure that it can meet all the regulatory requirements and can be done safely … we’ve been discussions with them for a little while and will meet them again this week," Dr Fruean said.

A vaccination program for Phillip Island's little penguin colony is also underway.

World.title: Brumby cull on hold after advocate launches last minute court action
World.content:
The National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) has temporarily suspended aerial culls and trapping operations in a northern NSW national park following an urgent injunction from an advocate, claiming the killing of brumbies there is unlawful.

The five-day aerial culling operation of feral horses, pigs, foxes and deer was scheduled to take place from Monday in Yuraygir National Park, north of Coffs Harbour, but has been postponed for at least two weeks to allow for court proceedings.

Anti-brumby culling advocate Carmen Jackson filed an urgent injunction to the Land and Environment Court about 1am on Monday, with the matter adjourned to later that morning.

Carmen Jackson (right) says she filed the injunction at 1am on Monday, concerned National Parks and Wildlife did not have the authority to conduct brumby culls in Yuraygir National Park. (Supplied: Carmen Jackson)

Justice Rachel Pepper today adjourned the matter, telling the court final hearings would be heard on September 9 to allow both parties to gather their evidence.

She told the court there was "urgency involved".

"The undertaking has been given in good faith by the department, again at short notice and I do think the matter needs to be dealt with quickly for your sake, the animals in question and the department," Justice Pepper said.

Speaking on behalf of the NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water, the department's principal legal officer Nicholas Sandstrom told the court they would "suspend trappings and all operations until that date".

In a statement, a spokesperson for the NSW NPWS said they acknowledge the proceedings and will comply with any directions from the court, confirming all aerial, ground shooting and trapping operations in the National Park and State Conservation Area would be suspended.

Aerial culls of wild horses, foxes, deer and pigs in the national park were due to commence on Monday. (ABC South East NSW: Adriane Reardon)

"Animal welfare is a high priority, and all operations are conducted under strict procedures," the statement read.

"As the matter is before the court, it would be inappropriate to comment further."

Brumby debate re-ignited

Ms Jackson said she was concerned NPWS did not have the statutory authority to perform the culls.

She said she does not support brumby control measures, with the court proceedings sparking renewed debate over their handling.

"Our brumbies are our Australian heritage; they're also sentient beings on Country," she said.

"I believe all animals have the right to be on Country. How do we signify that a brumby is less significant than a native animal on Country, considering they've been here 200 years."

State member for Clarence and Nationals MP Richie Williamson welcomed news this week's operation had been put on hold.

Richie Williamson has voiced opposition to the operation in Yuraygir National Park. (Supplied: Richie Williamson)

Community members also gathered at Halfway Creek on Saturday ahead of the planned culls, calling for the operation's end and arguing the north coast brumby population was small.

Professor David Watson, from Charles Sturt University, said brumbies were incredibly destructive for the habitat of other native animals, which were forced to compete for food and resources.

"Four or five animals aren't going to have a huge impact on a huge national park, but they breed … the right number is no horses," he said.

David Watson says feral horses are incredibly destructive and do not belong in national parks. (Supplied: David Watson)

" Our ecosystems have had no evolutionary history of dealing with a large hoofed animal like this, so they really do wreck the place. "

He said while he understands concerns, brumbies were as destructive to the Australian environment and wildlife as other feral pests.

"I get it … I love horses, they are special animals and humans have had a connection with horses for a long time."

"[But] from an ecological point of view that goes out the window."

World.title: Two Victoria Police officers cleared of manslaughter over man's death
World.content:
Manslaughter charges against two Victoria Police officers have been thrown out by a magistrate who contrasted the case with the death of George Floyd.

Luke Briggs, 35, died eight days after he was arrested in a convenience store car park at Hoppers Crossing, in Melbourne's south west, in July 2024.

Constable Alexander Papanastassis, 30, and Sergeant James Fitzgerald, 46, were each charged with negligent manslaughter over his death, but they fought the charges at a committal hearing.

Luke Briggs, 35, died eight days after he was arrested by two officers. (Supplied: Robinson Gill Laywers)

Melbourne magistrate Patrick Southey on Tuesday determined there was insufficient evidence for the case to go to trial and dismissed the charges.

"The evidence is so weak that the prospect of a conviction is minimal," Mr Southey said.

"It may be the manner in which Mr Briggs was restrained was the substantial and operative cause of death, but we'll never know."

Mr Briggs allegedly became unresponsive during the arrest, and the officers performed CPR before calling for medical assistance.

The 35-year-old died in a Melbourne hospital intensive care unit on July 23, surrounded by family.

Photos at the time showed bruising on his arms as he lay in a hospital bed.

Mr Briggs's family suing the state

In delivering his ruling, Mr Southey referred to the high-profile case of African American man George Floyd in the United States.

Mr Floyd was murdered by a white police officer who was arresting him in May 2020.

His dying words of "I can't breathe" were also said by Mr Briggs, the magistrate noted.

"It seems to me the parallels end there," Mr Southey said.

"There is no comparison to this case where … the police were doing the best they could.

"It was not a perfect job but the best they could do in all the circumstances."

The magistrate noted Mr Briggs was a large, powerful man whose behaviour had been irrational due to methamphetamine use.

"It was an unfortunate, tragic chain of events but in my view, it does not amount to criminal negligence," Mr Southey said.

He awarded costs to Constable Papanastassis and Sergeant Fitzgerald, who have both been suspended from duties since the incident.

Members of Mr Briggs's family were visibly upset as the decision was handed down on Tuesday afternoon.

The family is separately suing the state, accusing the officers of breaching their duty of care and Victoria Police of failing to "properly supervise, control or train their employees, officers and/or agents".

Mr Southey indicated his ruling had no basis on any civil proceedings and the prosecution could still choose to directly indict the two officers on fresh criminal charges.

The Police Association Victoria said it stood by its members throughout the whole process and would continue to support them.

"That night they did what any of their colleagues would have done," secretary Wayne Gatt said.

"They pulled over a suspicious vehicle and attempted to speak to the driver.

"When the situation escalated into a physical confrontation, they tried to manage it peacefully, but they were not afforded that opportunity."

Mr Gatt said the officers' actions "did not amount to criminal negligence, nor did their conduct warrant the intervention of the criminal law" and acknowledged the sometimes dangerous work officers did in the field.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Chinese factory workers accidentally caught on camera glasses
World.content:
Factory workers who helped make a Chinese-brand of camera glasses appear to have been unknowingly filmed by the devices in accidental videos.

7.30 bought a pair of budget glasses made by Shenzhen-based company Oho Sunshine online and found footage already on the device, which appears to be from inside the factory.

The collection of four short videos, dated last year, shows a number of workers sitting at their desks inspecting the glasses, while listening to jaunty electronic music.

Video appears to have been filmed inside a factory while the glasses were being made. (ABC News)

One video clearly identifies a worker lifting a pair and shaking them vigorously.

Another three videos, up to 10 minutes long and dated this year, show only black with atmospheric audio, suggesting the glasses were activated while inside a case or box.

The shoot button on the side of the frames is sensitive and easily switched on.

The workers appear to be filmed unknowingly by the glasses. (ABC News)

7.30 approached Oho Sunshine, with questions about the apparent privacy breach but received no response.

Oho Sunshine was founded in 2009 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen in Guandong province, north of Hong Kong, as a smart wearable technologies manufacturer, according to the company's website.

The accidental leak perhaps proves not even the workers who make camera glasses are safe from being filmed and provides a rare insight into the globalised production chain.

Do you know more about this story? Contact Jason Om at Om.Jason@abc.net.au.

Rise of camera glasses

7.30 reporter Jason Om wearing the Oho Sunshine camera glasses that already had footage on them. (ABC News: Craig Hansen)

Camera glasses are enjoying a surge in popularity as cheap brands flood the market. Oho is just one of numerous companies manufacturing similar devices.

They look like ordinary glasses and allow you to record video and audio, largely without people knowing.

While some models have a built-in light to indicate filming, there are now services that remove the indicator cheaply.

A pair of Ray-Ban Meta glasses. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

The glasses can play music and make calls, with more high-tech versions allowing users to live-stream or swipe through messages on a display in the lenses.

Meta's fashionable Ray-Ban smart glasses can cost up to $700 a pair, but basic versions can be bought online for as little as $40.

Kmart Australia's $89 Anko brand of camera glasses recently sold out, prompting an online petition to stop their sale amid concerns about privacy and their use by male content creators recording women without their knowledge and uploading the videos to potentially millions of followers.

While filming in public places is generally legal, the devices have raised new concerns around privacy.

Filmed without consent on 'rizz cam'

Beth Knight was filmed with camera glasses at a train station and later found the video of herself online. (ABC News: Daniel Ioh)

Beth Knight, 18, found herself the subject of lurid commentary from online users after a man filmed her with camera glasses and uploaded it to social media without her knowledge.

At the time of the incident late last year, she was 17 and by herself at London's busy Waterloo station.

"I'd missed my train, so I had 40 minutes to wait in the station," Ms Knight told 7.30.

"Then pretty much immediately a man approached me and opened with, 'I've seen you, I found you attractive,' and I immediately shut him down, and I said I had a boyfriend."

She discovered that their conversation had been turned into content after she heard about other cases.

"I started looking up buzzwords. I was looking up, "picking up girls", "Meta Glasses", "Waterloo", all of those into the TikTok search bar, and that's when I found his page."

She saw a video of her interaction titled, "POV: You approach her instead of walking by".

Beth Knight says she asked the content creator to remove the video of her and he blocked her. (Instagram)

"It was framed as a successful pick-up, like a win, when I know in the moment I was incredibly uncomfortable … because it was a strange man refusing to accept my soft hint of a no," she said.

"He had very much framed it as, 'Look, I've picked her up, I got her Instagram, I've won here,' and over the top of the video he was instructing men watching that when girls say they have a boyfriend they're lying."

Ms Knight was not lying and thought the man would get the message and leave.

The man is a content creator who touts himself as a pick-up artist and advertises male coaching on his social media account.

Digital extremism researcher Milica Stilinovic, from Sydney University, said such content was known as "rizz cam" — rizz being slang for charisma — where women are sometimes filmed without their consent.

"I would find it horrendous to be treated that way and then subjected to a global audience," she told 7.30.

Ms Stilinovic led a study that reviewed more than 350 Instagram videos filmed with camera glasses.

Milica Stilinovic is concerned about the use of camera glasses. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

"Pick-up artists are adjacent to the manosphere, or part of the manosphere, and they have a dual purpose to exist," she said.

"One is to build the self-confidence of men, supposedly through the subjugation of women, and the second part is to sell male coaching, which is basically like a multi-level marketing scheme.

"Some of the worst examples included underage girls. Some of [the filmers] approached women who were inebriated. Some of them approached women who were semi-nude at beaches."

Ms Knight said her experience left her feeling angry.

"It's weird to watch it back," she said.

"But the anger definitely came from the fact that it was spun so heavily to look good on his part.

" I went home and sobbed to my parents. "

She said she asked the content creator to take the video down, but he blocked her.

7.30 has contacted the creator for comment, but he did not respond.

Is it legal?

According to Australia's Privacy Commissioner, Carly Kind, the use of camera glasses in public is largely legal, with laws varying across states.

"Wearing smart glasses in public to capture images of things that happen in public is generally not illegal under Australian law," Ms Kind told 7.30.

"[But] when you are in a private premises or a private space, and that might include a private home, a vehicle, or potentially a semi-private space like a gym or a workplace, for example, then you're likely going to run up against laws that do prohibit the use of surveillance devices."

Carly Kind is worried about the use of camera glasses in workplaces and around "vulnerable groups". (ABC News: Scott Kyle)

In Victoria, where filming inside a private business is generally allowed, one content creator known as "The Latte Bloke" uses camera glasses to review coffee around Melbourne.

He is not a pick-up artist, but his videos feature staff and customers.

"The Latte Bloke" uses camera glasses as he reviews coffee around Melbourne. (Instagram)

One 19-year-old cafe worker said she did not consent to being filmed while serving him.

Her aunt, Tara Venn, told 7.30 her niece was upset after seeing herself in a video online.

She was new in the job.

"It was a bit affronting [for her]," Ms Venn said.

She said content creators should consider the ethics of filming someone.

This cafe worker says she did not give consent to be filmed by The Latte Bloke. (Instagram)

"Common sense says you are polite and you ask if you are going to invade a person's privacy by filming them without them knowing," Ms Venn said.

"I just want people to think and to actually use good manners and decency."

The content creator declined to be interviewed but told 7.30:

"Latte Bloke is all about filming the latte experience and having a bit of fun reviewing the coffee. The focus has never been on the staff or customers, and I'd never intentionally want to make anyone feel uncomfortable."

Potential real-world consequences

Attorney-General Michelle Rowland has asked Australia's Privacy Commissioner to make recommendations about camera glasses in Australia.

Ms Kind says she was already worried about them.

The Albanese government has asked the Privacy Commissioner to make recommendations about camera glasses. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

"If you think about their use in workplaces, there's a high likelihood that corporate espionage could be permitted through these kinds of glasses without proper control," Ms Kind said.

"I think the theft of personal information through the use of the glasses is also a potential offence that we could see spiralling out here, and [there are] obviously real risks around vulnerable groups, women and children."

In New South Wales it is illegal to create or share sexually explicit videos or audio of someone without their consent.

Last year, new federal privacy laws made serious invasions of privacy an offence; however, the commissioner told 7.30 there was a high bar to prove it was intentional and caused harm.

In the UK, some pubs and restaurants have reportedly banned the devices, while in Germany, rights advocacy group HateAid has lodged a complaint to German prosecutors against Meta and other companies, claiming such devices breach the country's covert recording laws.

Ms Stilinovic wants camera glasses temporarily banned in Australia.

"I would suggest that we stop the rollout of smart glasses until regulation and policymakers have caught up to keep societies safe," she said.

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays at 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: 'Significant' fencing safety issues at pool where toddler drowned, inquest hears
World.content:
It is likely a backyard swimming pool where a toddler drowned was never required to be subject to an application for an approval, a coronial inquest has heard.

South Australia Deputy State Coroner Emma Roper is investigating the death of a 19-month-old boy after he drowned in the pool at his family's rented home in Salisbury, in Adelaide's north in November 2022.

Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.

In his opening address, counsel assisting the coroner Darren Evans said on the day of the drowning, the boy — whose name has been suppressed — was with his mother, as well as his four siblings who he had been asking to go outside with him.

Mr Evans said it was about 5:20pm when the boy's siblings noticed he was missing.

"The family looked for him … his sister then found him floating in the swimming pool outside," he said.

Mr Evans said the girl found her brother near the pool's steps, before she "grabbed him by the hands and pulled him out".

"Their mother came and turned [the boy] upside down to drain water from his mouth," Mr Evans said.

"Neighbours heard a commotion and came over to assist, calling triple zero, and then commencing CPR with advice over the phone."

The pool gate was kept shut with a bicycle lock. (Supplied: SA Coroners Court)

The court heard when paramedics arrived, the boy had been moved onto the living room floor, and that after about 30 minutes "a return of spontaneous circulation was achieved".

He was taken to the Women's and Children's Hospital, but died seven days later, as a result of a severe hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy injury post cardiac arrest.

"There was no further treatment that could reverse the brain injury … it was identified that his condition was not compatible with life," Mr Evans told the court.

Ms Roper said the circumstances of the boy's death were "likely to have had and will continue to have a profound impact upon his siblings".

"It may be that it remains unknown who opened the pool gate on the day of his death, but it appears to be open at the time he's retrieved from the water," she said.

Faulty pool gate

The court heard when police attended the family's home, the boy's mother told officers the pool gate was "usually closed" and that she did not know how it came to be open or how her son got in.

It heard the top hinge on the pool gate was missing at the time, and there was a bicycle lock that had been put around it to keep it shut.

"[The boy's] father says that he noticed this was broken but did not raise it with the landlords, as he thought it was simple enough to fix himself with a new hinge," Mr Evans said.

Police commissioned a review of the pool by Salisbury Council pool inspector Jeff Shillabeer, who gave evidence that he found a number of "significant" issues with the safety of the fencing.

An inspector found several safety issues with the pool fencing. (Supplied: SA Coroners Court)

Mr Shillabeer said the "most notable" of those were the fact the gate did not close by itself, there was a gap greater than 10cm under the fence, and that there were climbable objects around the pool including a rabbit hutch and brick barbecue.

The court heard when he attended the property for a re-inspection in January 2023, all safety issues had been rectified by the property owners.

'Grand-fathered' safety compliance

The deputy coroner will consider whether improvements could be made to the regulation of older pools — particularly where the home is rented out — including whether the state government should implement a regular inspection regime, which is already in place in other states.

The court heard the pool was "likely" constructed prior to 1972, and therefore never required to be subject to an application for an approval or be entered onto the council's records.

Mr Evans said the requirement of pool fencing was only enforced under law after that time.

"The legislative regime continues to allow for grand-fathered safety compliance for pools installed in previous decades," Mr Evans said.

Mr Shillabeer said councils were only required to inspect a pool when a new one was built, and that there was no legislative requirement for an inspection after a transfer of sale.

He also told the court that, in his role as an inspector, he had carried out checks of pools following the death of a child at least five times.

The inquest continues.

World.title: Bulldogs tie down Preston as Martin and Panthers pause talks on new deal
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Bulldogs tie down Preston as Martin and Panthers pause talks on new deal Dan Walsh Updated August 25, 2026 — 6:44pm ,first published 2:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Canterbury have landed a significant retention blow, with rising star Jacob Preston to remain at the club on a new four-year deal as Liam Martin and the Panthers pause talks on a potential contract extension. The Bulldogs on Tuesday night confirmed Preston and the club had agreed to an upgraded, long-term deal after months of protracted negotiations. Jacob Preston is set to stay at the Bulldogs long-term. NRL Photos Preston’s management had recently publicly raised the prospect of taking the 24-year-old to market on November 1. But sources have indicated an improved offer worth around $800,000 a year was enough to keep Preston at Belmore until the end of 2031. Penrith officials, meanwhile, met with Martin’s manager Allan Gainey on Tuesday, and agreed to hold fire on further negotiations until after the conclusion of the Panthers’ season – ideally with a fifth premiership in six years.



Martin, 29, is seeking a three-year deal that would tie him to Penrith until the end of 2030. Sources speaking on the condition of anonymity given the confidential nature of the matter have indicated the Panthers are open to that length of deal for Martin, while a two-year deal was also discussed. Panthers back-rower Liam Martin. Getty Images However, the dollar amount of any potential offer is still in flux given superstar halfback Nathan Cleary is yet to begin any meaningful extension talks of his own. Fellow co-captain Isaah Yeo is closing in on a deal beyond 2027 which, as revealed by this masthead, is a good chance of being locked in before the finals kick off in a fortnight.



The Panthers won’t employ a hard-and-fast shutdown on contract negotiations once the post-season starts, but will prioritise their premiership tilt over the next six weeks. “Talks were productive,” Gainey said of Tuesday’s meeting with Panthers general manager Shane Elford and chief executive Matt Cameron. Nathan Cleary is no closer to sorting out his future. Getty Images “Both parties are mindful of the timing and potential distractions around upcoming finals. “We are confident we can get to a mutually beneficial position once Panthers have finished their commitments for 2026.”



The Panthers have had several retention wins recently despite losing star winger Brian To’o (PNG Chiefs) and Liam Henry, Scott Sorensen and Jack Cole (Perth Bears) to the NRL’s incoming clubs. Back-rower Isaiah Papali’i has recommitted on a yet-to-be-announced two-year extension, while centre Paul Alamoti has also re-signed until the end of 2029. Rising NSW Origin star Casey McLean was also extended until the end of 2030 last week. Cleary said last week he is not ready to address his future, and is yet to confirm privately or publicly whether he wants to re-sign before the November 1 free agency date or test his value on the open market. Sources close to the champion No.7 have indicated the lack of clarity does not necessarily point to an exit from Penrith, despite the Chiefs making Cleary their halfback priority if he comes off-contract.

World.title: The tone-deaf Tigers have provided a lesson for all footballers
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion The tone-deaf Tigers have provided a lesson for all footballers Michael Gleeson Sports columnist August 25, 2026 — 6:36pm

August 25, 2026 — 6:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Of all the moments to make yourself the story, this wasn’t it. Sure, the Richmond players celebrating the end of their season didn’t think they were making themselves the story, but no one does until they are on the front page. Right now, in the post-Pullman environment, this was the time for footballers to know not to put themselves and their club at risk of becoming the story. So keep your shirt on, your belt buckled and your pants up (advice for the ages). Richmond players outside the venue in Garfield. MEDIA-MODE.COM A week ago – before the events at the Pullman – Richmond players being filmed behaving as they were, shirtless in the cold, play-acting whipping each other’s backsides with belts, would be schoolboyish and boorish but little more.



Post-Pullman, the off-field behaviour of all footballers is viewed through a different, less forgiving lens – noting that police are still investigating the incident, with no arrests or charges laid. What may have been seen as innocent tomfoolery a fortnight ago is doubtfully appropriate now. Maybe it’s a correction football needed to have. Loading The Richmond players thought they had done all the right, careful things and gone out of their way to avoid trouble. They hired a bus to take them as a group to country Victoria. They hired out the pub in Garfield from 11am to 6pm and requested no female staff be working out of a sense of due caution. They had chaperones with them to keep an eye on them, like teachers on a school trip. They thought that secreted away in Garfield, population 2114, in west Gippsland, they were at risk of offending no one except each other and the cows over the beer garden fence.



They didn’t dress up in try-hard costumes that utterly misunderstood the line between humour and just offensive, like GWS and Geelong. They didn’t book topless waitresses or strippers (and certainly not to the team hotel at 4am). Nor did they hire people with dwarfism to throw and accidentally set on fire (see St Kilda a few years ago). The pub manager said the Richmond players were nothing but fun and well-behaved. Related Article Updated

AFL off-field behaviour Embarrassed Tigers say Mad Monday antics did not reference Swans scandal Apparently, one young player walked out of the bathroom still fixing his pants with his belt and another player quickly saw the untethered belt and ripped it out, lassoing it about. One player dropped his pants for reasons he is surely still wondering about today and was whipped lightly on the backside with it. It was camp but not intended, as has been assumed and feared, to be about the Swans or the women who have made complaints against them. Were the Richmond players mocking that situation? They say not. In fact, they are indignant and are shocked at the very idea people would think so. After the week we have had, they shouldn’t be surprised that people would add two plus two and get Sydney Swans.



You would hope the pictures without words told a misleading story and it was nothing to do with the Swans. You would hope so, because to think otherwise is an appalling idea. The point of this story, whether you consider it an outrage or a beat-up, and the lesson for all players on Mad Mondays, Whacky Wednesdays, Thickhead Thursdays and F---wit Fridays is that they have to know: whatever players do as a group off the field is viewed through a different, less forgiving lens now than it was before. Behaviour lightly regarded as fun last week is a comment on toxic, blokey football culture this week. For many the response to that is “about time”. Max Gawn said on radio on Tuesday: “As an industry, we have a lot of people telling us that stuff is going on within our four walls. It’s our time to start listening. Is this one of these cases? I’m not sure. But it’s a great chance for us to reflect on lots of people giving the AFL feedback on culture. It’s another thing to listen to, so we should.”



News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

World.title: Federal Darwin MP charged with breaching bail after alleged assault on King’s representative
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsFederalCourts Federal Darwin MP charged with breaching bail after alleged assault on King’s representative Rob Harris August 25, 2026 — 6:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling has been charged with breaching bail in relation to the ongoing allegations he assaulted Northern Territory Administrator David Connolly. NT Police said on Tuesday they allege Gosling breached his bail conditions on Friday, August 14, and served him with a summons to appear in Darwin Local Court on September 30. Police did not specify what is alleged to have occurred. Federal MP Luke Gosling, centre, at the TIO Stadium in Darwin on August 14. Facebook/Luke Gosling MP Gosling posted a picture to Facebook at the Test match in Darwin between Australian and Bangladesh on the date of the alleged breach. It was reported by the NT News that Connolly was at the venue but it was unclear if that is where the alleged offence occurred.



The MP, who is the Albanese government’s special envoy for defence, veterans’ affairs and Northern Australia, was arrested at his home last month and charged with two counts of assaulting Connolly with the offences carrying a maximum penalty of 14 years’ imprisonment. He appeared in Darwin Local Court on July 31, successfully applying to vary his bail conditions so he could attend the same public events as Connolly, provided he stayed at least 15 metres away and gave Connolly’s office 48 hours’ notice. He was also banned from coming within 50m of the NT’s Government House, where Connolly resides. The administrator is the Crown’s representative in the NT, a vice-regal role equivalent to a state governor. Related Article Crime Courts hears details of Labor MP’s alleged assault of NT administrator Prosecutors had opposed the variation, telling the court Connolly had cancelled public engagements because of concerns about encountering Gosling and arguing the restrictions were needed for the administrator’s “safety and well-being”.



The alleged assaults occurred at the Darwin Thai Grand Festival on July 18. It is alleged Gosling approached Connolly from behind in the first incident and, in the second, collided with him before drawing back his left elbow and striking him in the upper right rib area. Gosling denies the allegations. His lawyer, Marty Aust, has described the prosecution case as “incredibly weak” and accused police of politicising the matter. Gosling has also disputed the police account of events leading to his arrest, saying he was first contacted while working in Queensland and that his office had been trying to arrange a meeting with detectives. Police Commissioner Martin Dole said detectives had made multiple attempts to contact him before the arrest.



The Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions is preparing to take over the assault case from the NT DPP, which cited a perceived conflict of interest. It was reported by ABC Darwin the conflict relates to concerns about how the acting NT DPP’s handling of the case could be perceived given the prospect of a permanent appointment to the role. Under section 44 of the Constitution, a federal MP convicted and sentenced for an offence punishable by at least one year’s imprisonment can be disqualified from parliament, meaning any conviction could trigger a byelection. He has held the seat of Solomon — which includes Darwin and its satellite city of Palmerston — since 2016. He held off a threat from the Country Liberals by just 1500 votes in May last year. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has refused to stand down Gosling from his role as an envoy for veterans over the assault charges, despite calls from the Coalition.



His office has declined to comment, citing an ongoing legal process. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: One Nation’s idea of Australian culture is obsolete
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The claim by Pauline Hanson and One Nation supporters that immigration is altering Australia’s culture “too much” relies on a static, outdated view of identity (“Immigration motivates One Nation devotees”, August 25). Culture is not an artifact preserved in stone but something that naturally evolves as society grows. To conflate monoculture with social harmony is to misunderstand modern Australia. What binds us together is not a uniform ethnicity, religion or heritage but our commitment to shared democratic values like parliamentary democracy, the rule of law, gender equality and a fair go for all. Embracing our evolving cultural landscape does not weaken Australian identity, it reflects a mature, confident nation grounded in principles that unite us. John Bailey, Canterbury Polling shows more than half of those who say they will vote for Pauline Hanson’s One Nation will not change their mind. Alex Ellinghausen With the conflicting migration numbers we’re being fed by One Nation and the Coalition, it’s time for the real stakeholders to stand up. Each of the alternative governing parties are trying to outbid each other to get to the lowest number and are confusing themselves and voters in the process. It’s time for business bodies to stand up and tell us how many new Australians they need to sustain or grow their businesses. They need to provide some real numbers to the argument so that this ridiculous bidding war ends and reality is forced on these politicians. Ian Ferrier, Long Jetty Wow, tell us something we don’t know. Hanson’s message has always been one of exclusion and grievance: “We’re being swamped by Asians … Indigenous Australians get privileged treatment … there’s no such thing as a good Muslim”. So it’s no surprise her most devoted followers are focused not on the solution to problems like the cost of living but on finding someone to blame. Like the populist US president, Hanson makes a fine living off the system by fuelling discontent among those who feel they’ve been left behind. She has no answers, but that’s never been her goal. Phil Bradshaw, Naremburn It’s not surprising that One Nation voters are anti-immigration, given the survey’s findings that Pauline Hanson’s voters represent a higher proportion of tradies and lower-income workers, sectors where many immigrants are deployed. However, we do need immigration as the country develops. The problem is how to find appropriate jobs and work locations for immigrants on arrival. We are notoriously slack in efficiently placing skilled people and others who come to Australia. By contrast, Canada and Germany have set up comprehensive systems to assess skills and find industries and locations for arriving workers. Certainly there may be a case for more or less immigration but the real issue is how do we ensure immigrants reach their full occupational and social potential in their new country? David Catchlove, Newport The survey results are no surprise, given Pauline Hanson’s well-known antipathy to a range of migrants – Asians generally and Muslims particularly. However, it’s still far from clear which immigration policy One Nation fans favour. Is it the member for Farrer David Farley’s figure, which seems about the same as Labor’s target, or the much lower total nominated by the party’s director, James Ashby? There is an important difference between these two men: the former was recently elected by the people; the latter was simply appointed but is a dab hand at putting on stunts with a mop. Nick Franklin, Katoomba



Unwanted twist The poll of One Nation voters showing support for Ben Roberts-Smith tells us how shifts in opinion in Australia can fly under the radar (“Hanson isn’t only hero for those who want her to lead”, August 25). These voters are at the conventional end of a spectrum that extends all the way to the wacko sovereign citizen brigade. They sound a clear warning as that case wends its tortuous way through the courts – the danger that he could be claimed as some kind of martyr and galvanise attacks on Andrew Hastie in particular. BRS serving as a lightning rod for disaffection is a twist in the political landscape that Australia really doesn’t need. Margaret Johnston, Paddington Ben Roberts-Smith is a hero among One Nation voters. Getty Images Win for the West Shane Wright explores the $23 billion the GST deal favouring WA currently costs Australia, the $60 billion it is expected to blow out to, and the $6 billion it will cost to support other states if WA improves its iron ore royalty income (“PM backs GST deal, leaves future taxpayers on the hook for billions”, August 25). What he fails to mention is that Labor holds more than 70 per cent of WA’s federal seats and our PM intends to keep them all. It’s a pity he doesn’t realise how many eastern Australian seats he’s about to lose as a result. Brian Barrett, Padstow Anthony Albanese has predictably assured West Australians there will be no change to the GST deal while he remains PM. He is no doubt demonstrating political nous in doing so; however, a stronger leader might have pointed out to them that their good fortune is at the expense of every other tax-paying Australian, and that we’re better off being united rather than divided. We’re also better off removing rather than adding pressure to the nation’s debt, to consider our future generations. Bruce McKinnon, Mosman



Mindless devotion Peter Hartcher paints a grim picture of the trashing of American prestige under Donald Trump’s presidency (“How Trump is weakening America”, August 25). But as baffling as the ineptitude in his economic, military and diplomatic behaviours is the mindless devotion he continues to attract from devoted acolytes, media cheer squad and wider support base. No other political identity in American history has achieved the mass hypnosis Trump has managed, and it’s hard to see how the nightmare of such mindless adulation will end, if it ever does. I suspect that his influence on US politics and policy will far outlive him, perpetuated by the zealots already in his thrall. Adrian Connelly, Springwood From the catastrophic failure of his war in Iran to his non-stop abuse of US allies while federal debt passes 120 per cent of GDP, Trump has damaged America’s reputation in ways no one could have imagined. But the greatest damage he has inflicted upon America is his deep lack of moral integrity. This is why Democratic presidential hopeful Jon Ossoff has directed his criticism of Trump as being self-seeking and corruptible. Ossoff appeals to the needs of black voters and poor working families while lambasting Trump’s military overreach in Iran as one of America’s greatest foreign policy failures. Perhaps Ossoff’s own presidential campaign could instead read MAMA: Make America Moral Again. Rev Vincent Zankin, Rivett (ACT) Correspondent Rob Phillips applauds Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney for standing up to Donald Trump’s bullying, but is silent about Anthony Albanese’s comparative meekness (Letters, August 25). Carney is fast gaining a reputation as the leader of the West for calling out Trump’s betrayal of loyal allies and forging new trade relationships. Has Australia publicly supported Carney’s coalition of middle powers or is it still hanging onto the tattered coat-tails of the USA as that nation blithely trashes its friends and cosies up to dictators and war criminals? Salvatore Sorbello, Campsie Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press via AP Closer than you think Scott Poynting is right about the threat of a nuclear attack on Canada by the US (Letters, August 25). In the ’70s, singer Randy Newman wrote Political Science, a satirical song about American foreign policy during the Cold War in which he suggests America should drop “the big one” on its detractors. Among complaints about other countries, he says that “Canada’s too cold”. Thankfully, we need not worry about nuclear threats to Australia, as he sang: “We’ll save Australia. Don’t wanna hurt no kangaroos. We’ll build an all-American amusement park there. They got surfin too.” Phew! Jim Croke, Stanmore



Thanks to Scott Poynting for making me laugh out loud with his comment about US bombers being too far away to reach us. Does the RAAF base near Katherine NT not count? US fighter-bombers rotating through Katherine and Darwin could easily reach our major population centres if America decided we needed bringing to heel. Alan Stanley, Upper Corindi I’m not sure whether Scott Poynting is being ironic, but of course we do have US bomber bases quite near us. On our soil, in fact. Given the capriciousness of the US government, indeed their anti-democratic, anti-trade actions, perhaps it’s time we asked them to take these military targets back to the USA. Colin Hesse, Nowra I have bad news for Mr Poynting. At our invitation, the US regularly operates (nuclear armed?) B52s out of RAAF Base Darwin. Be afraid, be very afraid! Clive Dye, Broulee All the US bombers would have to do is fill up in Darwin before bombing us. On the way back, they could refuel again. Oh dear, how very Milo Minderbinder. Stephen Turner, Seaforth By George I was elected to Georges River Council in 2021 by residents who wanted better consultation on planning matters (“The state wants 800 new homes in this Sydney suburb. The council is arguing for more”, August 25). Along with my fellow councillors I have worked constructively with staff, my colleagues and the community to achieve better outcomes. Since 2024, however, the state government has usurped council powers through non-consultative processes such as its Low and Mid-Rise Housing Policy and State Significant Development. That’s not local democracy, and it has pushed me to the brink of resignation. I doubt my supporters elected me simply to get footpaths and potholes fixed – they wanted me to represent their views on the decisions that shape their neighbourhoods. Peter Mahoney, Oatley On the one hand is a scheme for multiple towers up to 22 storeys high to be dumped onto one side of a busy arterial road, serviced only by a narrow, one-way lane with difficult exit points. The proposal is half-baked to the extent that it leaves the other half of King Georges Road and the rest of the precinct to its own devices. On the other hand, there is a master plan from Georges River Council encompassing the entire Beverly Hills town centre and considering community interests. It should hardly be a contest if the government allows reason and good planning processes to prevail. Doug Walker, Baulkham Hills



Nature lucks out Bravo to Cathy Wilcox for spotlighting the sickening spread of H5 bird flu in the broader context of escalating climate change (Letters, August 25). Are we letting nature die? The Albanese government allocated just $496 million to on-ground, nature-focused programs in this year’s budget. Last year BHP alone received more in diesel discounts than this entire national spend. Taxpayers actually pay $13 billion every year in diesel rebates that fuel the climate crisis and accelerate threats facing our wildlife. From a budgetary perspective, nature definitely lucks out. Our priceless, precious native species deserve better. Amy Hiller, Kew (Vic) Photo: Cathy Wilcox Bucolic musings Thank you, Michael Thomas, for your reminiscences of the quiet life in leafy Cheltenham (“Leafy locale tailor-made for families”, August 25). Similarly, when young, I compared our little town, where there were few shops but many cows, with living in a retirement village. Now, sadly, as the last of the picturesque dairy farms have been sold off, the peace and quiet of much of our area has been replaced with traffic noise, and real estate agents outnumber the cows. Gardens with beautiful, tall old trees are seen as a hindrance to further development, and the sound of mooing at night has been replaced with the perpetual murmur of the motorway. I wish the powers that be realised the importance of maintaining the greenery and beauty of our localities – for everyone’s sakes. Therese Hume, Picton Power struggles While gas will play an essential role in providing reliable power and in a number of industrial processes for some time yet, in support of Ken Enderby’s plea to reduce the use of gas in people’s homes (Letters, August 25) I would add that reticulation of gas incurs the high risk, indeed the probability, of leakage. Natural gas, methane, has a very high global warming potential, and numerous studies in other countries confirm its reticulation is a major source of fugitive emissions. Peter Lane, Margaret River (WA)

World.title: Ex-2GB host denies ‘tailoring evidence’ to assist Alan Jones
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content A former 2GB host has denied tailoring his evidence to assist Alan Jones after he told a court he did not see the then-broadcaster appearing to touch a young man under the table at a lunch in Sydney. Jason Morrison, now The Daily Telegraph’s chief of staff, returned to the witness box on Tuesday in the Downing Centre Local Court after a legal issue temporarily halted his evidence on Monday. Jason Morrison told the court on Monday that there was some joking among lunch guests. Ben Symons He said he did not see Jones at the lunch about 20 years ago with his hand under the table, seemingly in the lap of a man in his early 20s known as complainant “C”. At the time, both Jones and Morrison worked at 2GB.



Jones, 85, is standing trial on 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent spanning a 17-year period from 2003 to 2020. He denies the allegations. The trial centres on the evidence of six male complainants. “C” has told the court that Jones put his hand under the table at the lunch and touched him on the penis over his clothing. Prosecutor Georgina Wright, SC, put to Morrison on Tuesday that he did see Jones with his hand under the table, and that he reacted with “surprise and amusement at what you saw”. “I’ve just told you I didn’t see it, so no, I didn’t,” Morrison said. Wright suggested he had also seen “C” looking uncomfortable.



“I wouldn’t say uncomfortable, no,” he replied. Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Tuesday. Thomas Wielecki The court has heard the lunch was attended by guests from Jones’ professional and personal life, and they did not all know one another. Morrison told the court on Monday that there was some joking among lunch guests about Jones and “C” because the young man was “stuck” at the “least fun” end of the table next to the broadcaster. However, he said that “C” had been smiling and there was “nothing [in his demeanour] that worried me”.



Wright put to him that “the joking was about the defendant appearing to give some romantic attention to ‘C’, wasn’t it?” “Well, that was our joke,” Morrison said. “There was a time during the lunch where Alan put his arm over C’s shoulder … and we were making fun of the situation. “I certainly know I never for a second thought anything that you’ve described to me happened. It was not meant with any particular malice or ill intent.” Wright asked: “Are you suggesting that the joke was simply because Alan put his arm around ‘C’?” “Yes,” Morrison said.



Morrison said that “the joke was they looked like a couple” but “I think it’s a big step to say that we genuinely thought they were one”. He described the jokes as banter. Wright put to him that the joke was said because Jones put his hand under the table in the lap of “C”. “No. If I was aware of that … I would have raised it,” Morrison said, referring to his “forthright manner”. “I didn’t, because I didn’t see that happen.” He denied a suggestion by Wright that he was being “deliberately evasive” when answering questions about the jokes.



“There was a general joke going that ‘C’ and Alan had coupled up, wasn’t there?” Wright said. Related Article Alan Jones trial ‘Great couple’: Ex-2GB star recalls ‘banter’ about Alan Jones and young man “The joke was they looked like they’d coupled up,” Morrison replied. He agreed that it was significant enough for him to tell police about it in a statement in 2024. “You’ve tailored your evidence about there being light-hearted banter to assist the defendant, haven’t you?” Wright said.



“That’s offensive,” Morrison replied. “I’m here under oath. I find that offensive.” Wright pressed that “the jokes were about Alan appearing to give romantic attention to ‘C’.” “Not romantic, that’s [a] very different connotation,” Morrison said. “Sexual?” she said. “No,” the former 2GB host said. Morrison said he did not hear anyone say to “C” after the lunch: “You copped a feel under the table.”



The complainant has previously given evidence that words to this effect were said to him after the lunch by another guest, leaving him “deeply embarrassed”. Strike Force Bonnefin was formed by NSW Police’s sex crimes squad following a major investigation by this masthead’s chief investigative reporter, Kate McClymont, into allegations against Jones. The broadcaster was arrested in November 2024. Wright put to Morrison on Tuesday he had a “long-standing pejorative view of The Sydney Morning Herald”. “I’ve had my experiences which have allowed me to form that [view],” he said. Morrison was shown text messages he had sent between 2017 and 2020, before the reporting on the allegations against Jones in 2023, including one referring to the “pigs at the Herald”.



He disagreed that he had a generalised view that the Herald and McClymont “unfairly target” Jones. “The phrase ‘pigs in the media’ was a bit of an in-joke,” Morrison said. “Alan used the phrase often on the air.” He could not recall the context of the texts but said it probably referred to reporting at the time. The court heard he sent a text to Jones on October 14, 2018, in which he referred to McClymont as a “piece of work”. “I guess people are allowed to have views about things 10 years ago in private with each other,” Morrison said. “I obviously had a view about something that was around in the press that day.” Later on Tuesday, Wright referred to a transcript of a conversation between Morrison and McClymont in 2023. Morrison said he “did not consent to a recorded conversation with Kate, or indeed with anybody at the Herald, so I don’t know how this could be a transcript”.



This prompted extended legal argument about whether any recording was lawful and could be admitted in evidence. That argument has yet to be resolved. Wright told the court that McClymont was “a very experienced journalist, but I don’t express a view about the evidence”. The trial continues. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: How a Brisbane author’s brain tumour inspired a children’s book
World.content:
Welcome to CityChats, where Brisbane Times meets our city’s most interesting characters on our most iconic form of transport. This week, children’s book author and illustrator Sophie Beer tells us about her unlikely corporate background, how her real-life experiences with loss and grief inspire her work and why children’s literature is the backbone of society. Beer is waiting for us at North Quay ferry terminal after travelling almost an hour by boat from Bulimba for the interview. She’s dressed head-to-toe in colour and impossible to miss. Her bright personality is evident from the moment we meet. Author and graphic artist Sophie Beer. Studio Gentle/Sophie Vaughan Where do you write your best? Do you have any certain rituals or things you need in your space to set you up for success? Oh my gosh, yes. I’m one of those people that has to hyper focus, so I need a coffee, and complete quiet, just my computer and me, tapping away. Usually, I try to get an hour or so done in the mornings when my brain is fresh.



Do you have music playing or anything like that or is it silence? Oh, no, I never do. But then I was talking to an amazing writer, Jeremy Lachlan, who does kids’ books. He was like, “I write to movie soundtracks.” Which I was like, “That is so cool.” How long have you been writing children’s books and illustrating? It would have been 2016 when I got into it. It was all I ever really wanted to do, but for some reason I did a law degree before that. I was like, “you can’t make a living being an artist for kids”, but apparently you can. I just didn’t know that at the time.



Related Article City life The responsibility that comes with being ‘mum’ to an arts institution You see this creative path, but it’s like, oh no, it’s not going to happen. Yeah, totally! It’s like thinking you’re going to be a rock star or something. I worked at a law firm for a little bit – I won’t say which one. I was the person getting into trouble because I was doodling on the side of affidavits and stuff. And then one day, one of the senior legal people saw one of my doodles, and he’s like, “Sophie, you’re in the wrong profession.” I mean, I’m sure there are creative lawyers out there but for scatterbrain, rainbow-vomit me, yeah, that’s not a vibe. Do you ever run into kids that are dressed up as your characters for Book Week?



Not yet, unfortunately. One day, fingers crossed, one day it’ll happen. You mentioned before that children’s literature is so important to you. Why is it so important to you? Related Article Literature Forgot Book Week? Emergency costumes that require zero craft skills I feel like it’s the cornerstone of society. Not to be overblown, but legitimately, it is. I really want warmth and compassion and kindness to come through with the books I write. I do like to communicate a lot of social issues in my work, but at the same time, I never want to do it in, like, a preachy way. I have a five-year-old, and he’s really into books, which is great, but he only likes nonfiction books.



Like the encyclopedia? Totally. We’re reading a bug encyclopedia at the moment. But I find myself, every night, I get excited, ’cause I’m like, “I get to read about bugs tonight!” Can you tell me a little bit about your novel, Thunderhead? Ah, yes, this is my baby! It’s about this kid who learns that they have a genetic illness which is going to make them deaf, and they’re a huge music nerd. I took inspiration from my own story.



I went half-deaf from a brain tumour nine years ago. I wanted to read a book about being a huge music nerd and knowing you’re going to lose your hearing, and I couldn’t find one, so I [thought] I guess I have to write the book. And it’s been really beautiful, I’ve had so many people reach out and be like, I’m a pianist, I’m a music teacher, my daughter plays the flute, and I’ve just found out I have progressive hearing loss, or I am going deaf, or I have gone deaf. And those emails always make me cry. Has your hearing loss affected how you consume music? It has, unfortunately, yeah, ’cause I have tinnitus as well, as... it’s noise-affective, so if I hear something really loud, my ears buzz. So, I can’t put on punk music and rock around any more. But I guess that was the ethos of the novel – there’s beautiful things in life and they come and go.



Are your other books inspired by real-life experiences, too? I have quite a few that I’ve drawn from my own life. I went through IVF with my little bubba and I have two books about that. It was quite emotional. I have two picture books that deal with that. One is called Baby, You’re a Rainbow, so it’s about having a baby after losses, and things like that. But it’s not a sad book, it’s cute and like, “Oh, you’re here now! We’re going to celebrate!” Yeah, it’s very sweet. The other one is called Before We Met, which is written by a lovely lady called Gabrielle Tozer. She’s lives in Wagga in New South Wales, and I did the illustrations. So I tried to put an IVF story in the illustrations – me working through my own feelings about IVF. Loading



Yeah, I’m an IVF baby. Are you? Oh my god! Yeah. And I remember my mum just told me one day, I was a teenager, and I just couldn’t understand what it meant. I was just like, “What do you mean, like, test tube?” Test tube baby! So, I imagine having a book like that when you’re a kid, that would have been so nice.



Yeah, because [becoming a parent] can happen so many different ways. Every family is as special and gorgeous as every other, so it doesn’t matter if they come together in a slightly unorthodox way. World.title: Bulldogs tie down Preston as Martin and Panthers pause talks on new deal
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Bulldogs tie down Preston as Martin and Panthers pause talks on new deal Dan Walsh Updated August 25, 2026 — 6:44pm ,first published 2:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Canterbury have landed a significant retention blow, with rising star Jacob Preston to remain at the club on a new four-year deal as Liam Martin and the Panthers pause talks on a potential contract extension. The Bulldogs on Tuesday night confirmed Preston and the club had agreed to an upgraded, long-term deal after months of protracted negotiations. Jacob Preston is set to stay at the Bulldogs long-term. NRL Photos Preston’s management had recently publicly raised the prospect of taking the 24-year-old to market on November 1. But sources have indicated an improved offer worth around $800,000 a year was enough to keep Preston at Belmore until the end of 2031. Penrith officials, meanwhile, met with Martin’s manager Allan Gainey on Tuesday, and agreed to hold fire on further negotiations until after the conclusion of the Panthers’ season – ideally with a fifth premiership in six years.



Martin, 29, is seeking a three-year deal that would tie him to Penrith until the end of 2030. Sources speaking on the condition of anonymity given the confidential nature of the matter have indicated the Panthers are open to that length of deal for Martin, while a two-year deal was also discussed. Panthers back-rower Liam Martin. Getty Images However, the dollar amount of any potential offer is still in flux given superstar halfback Nathan Cleary is yet to begin any meaningful extension talks of his own. Fellow co-captain Isaah Yeo is closing in on a deal beyond 2027 which, as revealed by this masthead, is a good chance of being locked in before the finals kick off in a fortnight.



The Panthers won’t employ a hard-and-fast shutdown on contract negotiations once the post-season starts, but will prioritise their premiership tilt over the next six weeks. “Talks were productive,” Gainey said of Tuesday’s meeting with Panthers general manager Shane Elford and chief executive Matt Cameron. Nathan Cleary is no closer to sorting out his future. Getty Images “Both parties are mindful of the timing and potential distractions around upcoming finals. “We are confident we can get to a mutually beneficial position once Panthers have finished their commitments for 2026.”



The Panthers have had several retention wins recently despite losing star winger Brian To’o (PNG Chiefs) and Liam Henry, Scott Sorensen and Jack Cole (Perth Bears) to the NRL’s incoming clubs. Back-rower Isaiah Papali’i has recommitted on a yet-to-be-announced two-year extension, while centre Paul Alamoti has also re-signed until the end of 2029. Rising NSW Origin star Casey McLean was also extended until the end of 2030 last week. Cleary said last week he is not ready to address his future, and is yet to confirm privately or publicly whether he wants to re-sign before the November 1 free agency date or test his value on the open market. Sources close to the champion No.7 have indicated the lack of clarity does not necessarily point to an exit from Penrith, despite the Chiefs making Cleary their halfback priority if he comes off-contract.

World.title: The tone-deaf Tigers have provided a lesson for all footballers
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion The tone-deaf Tigers have provided a lesson for all footballers Michael Gleeson Sports columnist August 25, 2026 — 6:36pm

August 25, 2026 — 6:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Of all the moments to make yourself the story, this wasn’t it. Sure, the Richmond players celebrating the end of their season didn’t think they were making themselves the story, but no one does until they are on the front page. Right now, in the post-Pullman environment, this was the time for footballers to know not to put themselves and their club at risk of becoming the story. So keep your shirt on, your belt buckled and your pants up (advice for the ages). Richmond players outside the venue in Garfield. MEDIA-MODE.COM A week ago – before the events at the Pullman – Richmond players being filmed behaving as they were, shirtless in the cold, play-acting whipping each other’s backsides with belts, would be schoolboyish and boorish but little more.



Post-Pullman, the off-field behaviour of all footballers is viewed through a different, less forgiving lens – noting that police are still investigating the incident, with no arrests or charges laid. What may have been seen as innocent tomfoolery a fortnight ago is doubtfully appropriate now. Maybe it’s a correction football needed to have. Loading The Richmond players thought they had done all the right, careful things and gone out of their way to avoid trouble. They hired a bus to take them as a group to country Victoria. They hired out the pub in Garfield from 11am to 6pm and requested no female staff be working out of a sense of due caution. They had chaperones with them to keep an eye on them, like teachers on a school trip. They thought that secreted away in Garfield, population 2114, in west Gippsland, they were at risk of offending no one except each other and the cows over the beer garden fence.



They didn’t dress up in try-hard costumes that utterly misunderstood the line between humour and just offensive, like GWS and Geelong. They didn’t book topless waitresses or strippers (and certainly not to the team hotel at 4am). Nor did they hire people with dwarfism to throw and accidentally set on fire (see St Kilda a few years ago). The pub manager said the Richmond players were nothing but fun and well-behaved. Related Article Updated

AFL off-field behaviour Embarrassed Tigers say Mad Monday antics did not reference Swans scandal Apparently, one young player walked out of the bathroom still fixing his pants with his belt and another player quickly saw the untethered belt and ripped it out, lassoing it about. One player dropped his pants for reasons he is surely still wondering about today and was whipped lightly on the backside with it. It was camp but not intended, as has been assumed and feared, to be about the Swans or the women who have made complaints against them. Were the Richmond players mocking that situation? They say not. In fact, they are indignant and are shocked at the very idea people would think so. After the week we have had, they shouldn’t be surprised that people would add two plus two and get Sydney Swans.



You would hope the pictures without words told a misleading story and it was nothing to do with the Swans. You would hope so, because to think otherwise is an appalling idea. The point of this story, whether you consider it an outrage or a beat-up, and the lesson for all players on Mad Mondays, Whacky Wednesdays, Thickhead Thursdays and F---wit Fridays is that they have to know: whatever players do as a group off the field is viewed through a different, less forgiving lens now than it was before. Behaviour lightly regarded as fun last week is a comment on toxic, blokey football culture this week. For many the response to that is “about time”. Max Gawn said on radio on Tuesday: “As an industry, we have a lot of people telling us that stuff is going on within our four walls. It’s our time to start listening. Is this one of these cases? I’m not sure. But it’s a great chance for us to reflect on lots of people giving the AFL feedback on culture. It’s another thing to listen to, so we should.”
