World.title: Federal Darwin MP charged with breaching bail after alleged assault on King’s representative
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsFederalCourts Federal Darwin MP charged with breaching bail after alleged assault on King’s representative Rob Harris August 25, 2026 — 6:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling has been charged with breaching bail in relation to the ongoing allegations he assaulted Northern Territory Administrator David Connolly. NT Police said on Tuesday they allege Gosling breached his bail conditions on Friday, August 14, and served him with a summons to appear in Darwin Local Court on September 30. Police did not specify what is alleged to have occurred. Federal MP Luke Gosling, centre, at the TIO Stadium in Darwin on August 14. Facebook/Luke Gosling MP Gosling posted a picture to Facebook at the Test match in Darwin between Australian and Bangladesh on the date of the alleged breach. It was reported by the NT News that Connolly was at the venue but it was unclear if that is where the alleged offence occurred.



The MP, who is the Albanese government’s special envoy for defence, veterans’ affairs and Northern Australia, was arrested at his home last month and charged with two counts of assaulting Connolly with the offences carrying a maximum penalty of 14 years’ imprisonment. He appeared in Darwin Local Court on July 31, successfully applying to vary his bail conditions so he could attend the same public events as Connolly, provided he stayed at least 15 metres away and gave Connolly’s office 48 hours’ notice. He was also banned from coming within 50m of the NT’s Government House, where Connolly resides. The administrator is the Crown’s representative in the NT, a vice-regal role equivalent to a state governor. Related Article Crime Courts hears details of Labor MP’s alleged assault of NT administrator Prosecutors had opposed the variation, telling the court Connolly had cancelled public engagements because of concerns about encountering Gosling and arguing the restrictions were needed for the administrator’s “safety and well-being”.



The alleged assaults occurred at the Darwin Thai Grand Festival on July 18. It is alleged Gosling approached Connolly from behind in the first incident and, in the second, collided with him before drawing back his left elbow and striking him in the upper right rib area. Gosling denies the allegations. His lawyer, Marty Aust, has described the prosecution case as “incredibly weak” and accused police of politicising the matter. Gosling has also disputed the police account of events leading to his arrest, saying he was first contacted while working in Queensland and that his office had been trying to arrange a meeting with detectives. Police Commissioner Martin Dole said detectives had made multiple attempts to contact him before the arrest.



The Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions is preparing to take over the assault case from the NT DPP, which cited a perceived conflict of interest. It was reported by ABC Darwin the conflict relates to concerns about how the acting NT DPP’s handling of the case could be perceived given the prospect of a permanent appointment to the role. Under section 44 of the Constitution, a federal MP convicted and sentenced for an offence punishable by at least one year’s imprisonment can be disqualified from parliament, meaning any conviction could trigger a byelection. He has held the seat of Solomon — which includes Darwin and its satellite city of Palmerston — since 2016. He held off a threat from the Country Liberals by just 1500 votes in May last year. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has refused to stand down Gosling from his role as an envoy for veterans over the assault charges, despite calls from the Coalition.



His office has declined to comment, citing an ongoing legal process. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Ex-2GB host denies ‘tailoring evidence’ to assist Alan Jones
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content A former 2GB host has denied tailoring his evidence to assist Alan Jones after he told a court he did not see the then-broadcaster appearing to touch a young man under the table at a lunch in Sydney. Jason Morrison, now The Daily Telegraph’s chief of staff, returned to the witness box on Tuesday in the Downing Centre Local Court after a legal issue temporarily halted his evidence on Monday. Jason Morrison told the court on Monday that there was some joking among lunch guests. Ben Symons He said he did not see Jones at the lunch about 20 years ago with his hand under the table, seemingly in the lap of a man in his early 20s known as complainant “C”. At the time, both Jones and Morrison worked at 2GB.



Jones, 85, is standing trial on 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent spanning a 17-year period from 2003 to 2020. He denies the allegations. The trial centres on the evidence of six male complainants. “C” has told the court that Jones put his hand under the table at the lunch and touched him on the penis over his clothing. Prosecutor Georgina Wright, SC, put to Morrison on Tuesday that he did see Jones with his hand under the table, and that he reacted with “surprise and amusement at what you saw”. “I’ve just told you I didn’t see it, so no, I didn’t,” Morrison said. Wright suggested he had also seen “C” looking uncomfortable.



“I wouldn’t say uncomfortable, no,” he replied. Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Tuesday. Thomas Wielecki The court has heard the lunch was attended by guests from Jones’ professional and personal life, and they did not all know one another. Morrison told the court on Monday that there was some joking among lunch guests about Jones and “C” because the young man was “stuck” at the “least fun” end of the table next to the broadcaster. However, he said that “C” had been smiling and there was “nothing [in his demeanour] that worried me”.



Wright put to him that “the joking was about the defendant appearing to give some romantic attention to ‘C’, wasn’t it?” “Well, that was our joke,” Morrison said. “There was a time during the lunch where Alan put his arm over C’s shoulder … and we were making fun of the situation. “I certainly know I never for a second thought anything that you’ve described to me happened. It was not meant with any particular malice or ill intent.” Wright asked: “Are you suggesting that the joke was simply because Alan put his arm around ‘C’?” “Yes,” Morrison said.



Morrison said that “the joke was they looked like a couple” but “I think it’s a big step to say that we genuinely thought they were one”. He described the jokes as banter. Wright put to him that the joke was said because Jones put his hand under the table in the lap of “C”. “No. If I was aware of that … I would have raised it,” Morrison said, referring to his “forthright manner”. “I didn’t, because I didn’t see that happen.” He denied a suggestion by Wright that he was being “deliberately evasive” when answering questions about the jokes.



“There was a general joke going that ‘C’ and Alan had coupled up, wasn’t there?” Wright said. Related Article Alan Jones trial ‘Great couple’: Ex-2GB star recalls ‘banter’ about Alan Jones and young man “The joke was they looked like they’d coupled up,” Morrison replied. He agreed that it was significant enough for him to tell police about it in a statement in 2024. “You’ve tailored your evidence about there being light-hearted banter to assist the defendant, haven’t you?” Wright said.



“That’s offensive,” Morrison replied. “I’m here under oath. I find that offensive.” Wright pressed that “the jokes were about Alan appearing to give romantic attention to ‘C’.” “Not romantic, that’s [a] very different connotation,” Morrison said. “Sexual?” she said. “No,” the former 2GB host said. Morrison said he did not hear anyone say to “C” after the lunch: “You copped a feel under the table.”



The complainant has previously given evidence that words to this effect were said to him after the lunch by another guest, leaving him “deeply embarrassed”. Strike Force Bonnefin was formed by NSW Police’s sex crimes squad following a major investigation by this masthead’s chief investigative reporter, Kate McClymont, into allegations against Jones. The broadcaster was arrested in November 2024. Wright put to Morrison on Tuesday he had a “long-standing pejorative view of The Sydney Morning Herald”. “I’ve had my experiences which have allowed me to form that [view],” he said. Morrison was shown text messages he had sent between 2017 and 2020, before the reporting on the allegations against Jones in 2023, including one referring to the “pigs at the Herald”.



He disagreed that he had a generalised view that the Herald and McClymont “unfairly target” Jones. “The phrase ‘pigs in the media’ was a bit of an in-joke,” Morrison said. “Alan used the phrase often on the air.” He could not recall the context of the texts but said it probably referred to reporting at the time. The court heard he sent a text to Jones on October 14, 2018, in which he referred to McClymont as a “piece of work”. “I guess people are allowed to have views about things 10 years ago in private with each other,” Morrison said. “I obviously had a view about something that was around in the press that day.” Later on Tuesday, Wright referred to a transcript of a conversation between Morrison and McClymont in 2023. Morrison said he “did not consent to a recorded conversation with Kate, or indeed with anybody at the Herald, so I don’t know how this could be a transcript”.



This prompted extended legal argument about whether any recording was lawful and could be admitted in evidence. That argument has yet to be resolved. Wright told the court that McClymont was “a very experienced journalist, but I don’t express a view about the evidence”. The trial continues. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: How a Brisbane author’s brain tumour inspired a children’s book
World.content:
Welcome to CityChats, where Brisbane Times meets our city’s most interesting characters on our most iconic form of transport. This week, children’s book author and illustrator Sophie Beer tells us about her unlikely corporate background, how her real-life experiences with loss and grief inspire her work and why children’s literature is the backbone of society. Beer is waiting for us at North Quay ferry terminal after travelling almost an hour by boat from Bulimba for the interview. She’s dressed head-to-toe in colour and impossible to miss. Her bright personality is evident from the moment we meet. Author and graphic artist Sophie Beer. Studio Gentle/Sophie Vaughan Where do you write your best? Do you have any certain rituals or things you need in your space to set you up for success? Oh my gosh, yes. I’m one of those people that has to hyper focus, so I need a coffee, and complete quiet, just my computer and me, tapping away. Usually, I try to get an hour or so done in the mornings when my brain is fresh.



Do you have music playing or anything like that or is it silence? Oh, no, I never do. But then I was talking to an amazing writer, Jeremy Lachlan, who does kids’ books. He was like, “I write to movie soundtracks.” Which I was like, “That is so cool.” How long have you been writing children’s books and illustrating? It would have been 2016 when I got into it. It was all I ever really wanted to do, but for some reason I did a law degree before that. I was like, “you can’t make a living being an artist for kids”, but apparently you can. I just didn’t know that at the time.



Related Article City life The responsibility that comes with being ‘mum’ to an arts institution You see this creative path, but it’s like, oh no, it’s not going to happen. Yeah, totally! It’s like thinking you’re going to be a rock star or something. I worked at a law firm for a little bit – I won’t say which one. I was the person getting into trouble because I was doodling on the side of affidavits and stuff. And then one day, one of the senior legal people saw one of my doodles, and he’s like, “Sophie, you’re in the wrong profession.” I mean, I’m sure there are creative lawyers out there but for scatterbrain, rainbow-vomit me, yeah, that’s not a vibe. Do you ever run into kids that are dressed up as your characters for Book Week?



Not yet, unfortunately. One day, fingers crossed, one day it’ll happen. You mentioned before that children’s literature is so important to you. Why is it so important to you? Related Article Literature Forgot Book Week? Emergency costumes that require zero craft skills I feel like it’s the cornerstone of society. Not to be overblown, but legitimately, it is. I really want warmth and compassion and kindness to come through with the books I write. I do like to communicate a lot of social issues in my work, but at the same time, I never want to do it in, like, a preachy way. I have a five-year-old, and he’s really into books, which is great, but he only likes nonfiction books.



Like the encyclopedia? Totally. We’re reading a bug encyclopedia at the moment. But I find myself, every night, I get excited, ’cause I’m like, “I get to read about bugs tonight!” Can you tell me a little bit about your novel, Thunderhead? Ah, yes, this is my baby! It’s about this kid who learns that they have a genetic illness which is going to make them deaf, and they’re a huge music nerd. I took inspiration from my own story.



I went half-deaf from a brain tumour nine years ago. I wanted to read a book about being a huge music nerd and knowing you’re going to lose your hearing, and I couldn’t find one, so I [thought] I guess I have to write the book. And it’s been really beautiful, I’ve had so many people reach out and be like, I’m a pianist, I’m a music teacher, my daughter plays the flute, and I’ve just found out I have progressive hearing loss, or I am going deaf, or I have gone deaf. And those emails always make me cry. Has your hearing loss affected how you consume music? It has, unfortunately, yeah, ’cause I have tinnitus as well, as... it’s noise-affective, so if I hear something really loud, my ears buzz. So, I can’t put on punk music and rock around any more. But I guess that was the ethos of the novel – there’s beautiful things in life and they come and go.



Are your other books inspired by real-life experiences, too? I have quite a few that I’ve drawn from my own life. I went through IVF with my little bubba and I have two books about that. It was quite emotional. I have two picture books that deal with that. One is called Baby, You’re a Rainbow, so it’s about having a baby after losses, and things like that. But it’s not a sad book, it’s cute and like, “Oh, you’re here now! We’re going to celebrate!” Yeah, it’s very sweet. The other one is called Before We Met, which is written by a lovely lady called Gabrielle Tozer. She’s lives in Wagga in New South Wales, and I did the illustrations. So I tried to put an IVF story in the illustrations – me working through my own feelings about IVF. Loading



Yeah, I’m an IVF baby. Are you? Oh my god! Yeah. And I remember my mum just told me one day, I was a teenager, and I just couldn’t understand what it meant. I was just like, “What do you mean, like, test tube?” Test tube baby! So, I imagine having a book like that when you’re a kid, that would have been so nice.



Yeah, because [becoming a parent] can happen so many different ways. Every family is as special and gorgeous as every other, so it doesn’t matter if they come together in a slightly unorthodox way. World.title: Youths on proposed social media ban: Cautious approval, but questions around enforcement
World.content:
Young people question proposed social media ban Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

"How are you going to enforce this?" That's the response from young people who grew up with social media to the proposed ban for under-16s.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said social media is exposing young people to harmful content, addictive technology and pressure they aren't equipped to deal with, and the government would push ahead with the Online Safety Bill.

"We would never knowingly let our children wander into places in the real world we know to be unsafe. We put boundaries around cars, around alcohol, around gambling, because we know children aren't yet equipped for them."

So, it has been proposed that social media platforms will risk financial penalties if they don't take steps to verify the age of users.

But some Auckland 17- and 18-year-olds say they're not convinced a complete ban will work.

For some teens who jumped on to social media around 12 years old, some of what the government mentioned during their announcement resembled their experiences.

Checkpoint spoke with some Year 13 students from Auckland's Albany Senior High School.

Jeremy Ouwejan said he often saw content that came from online communities such as the manosphere.

"Andrew Tate speaking to young impressionable men about very damaging ideologies like misogyny, transphobia and homophobia, or, armchair psychology that says how to manipulate your friends and how to do certain things.

Andrew Tate. AFP / DANIEL MIHAILESCU

"Or people will say, 'I used to be a dietitian, here's what you should and shouldn't eat.' [Instagram] Reels on working out and harmful gym content saying, 'If you're not benching 100kg are you even a real person?'"

Ouwejan said he also had seen posts that were violent.

"I'll hop onto Reels and I'll be flashed with a [dead] body. It'll completely ruin the experience of just wanting to talk to a friend."

Last year, research from Te Mana Whakaatu / The Classification Office, found young people don't generally go looking for objectionable content. But it could be hard to avoid when it came up on social media, in group chats or was shown around in person.

Some examples of this included pornography and real-world violence.

Another student, Natalie Osmond, told Checkpoint coming across extreme, violent and misogynistic content every day took a toll.

"When you're giving people ranked numerical scores, especially women… it's objectification to the highest level. You can't just put a number value on someone, it's bad it comes with the podcasts.

"A lot of my feed is about Ariana Grande for example, and other female artists. The [comments] will be all about body image and they're just saying horrible things."

Ariana Grande. CHRIS DELMAS

But, she said, social media also came with its positives.

"Social media is also a good way to get informed from people. There's a fine line between getting informed and seeing all of the bad stuff.

"I do think it's a crazy time to be alive and we can see what's going on in any corner of the world."

Osmond agreed restricting some parts of social media and having consequences for creating or promoting harmful content was a good thing.

"I wish it was socially acceptable to have a Nokia brick - I know I could actually do that, but I really couldn't.

"Also, even as a child I remember being 12 years old and it would socially stunt you even if you weren't allowed social media... you're pressured to have it from a very young age."

But Osmond and the other students Checkpoint spoke to weren't convinced a ban would work, with reports from Australia of teens using loopholes to get around it.

Ouwejan said change was needed, but had to be thought through.

"I think currently there is a lot of very young people on some very damaging platforms, and it is changing them for the worse for the rest of their lives.

"However, as we have seen from Australia and what we can interpolate from other studies and other bans, banning is not the way to go - we need a controlled method, but balancing that with free speech."

Another student, Isabella Green, said she was concerned around how the government would enforce a ban.

"How are you going to track and enforce this? That doesn't feel like it's something that would respect the privacy of people."

ACT and New Zealand First will not support the bill, meaning National will need Labour's support if it's to progress.

Not enough evidence - commissioner

Doubts over whether social media ban is enforceable Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Children's Commissioner Jane Searle told Checkpoint more evidence into the effectiveness of a complete ban was needed before implementing one in Aotearoa.

"We know that [kids have told] us that they want the internet to be made safer or online harm to be reduced for them. Whether the solution is just in a complete ban, that remains to be seen, and we need to look at the evidence around that."

Children's Commissioner Jane Searle. Stephen Barker / Barker Photography via Child Matters

Searle said that a more comprehensive plan to tackle the issues around social media was needed, rather than just an outright ban.

"I think that we need good education for young people and their families to be able to make good decisions that keep them safe. But we also need to be able to hold tech companies to account and have robust obligations on them.

"Then we need to look at the regulation - do we have an independent regulator?"

She said there was also a concern over young people who may be marginalised or isolated as the result of a ban.

"We need to be very careful when we move forward, and we need to look at the evidence. We need to know, what will this ban look like in practice? How will it actually impact the way that young people are engaging with social media?"

Searle said there wasn't currently enough information to know if a ban would be successful.

"Even if you look at other countries, what they've implemented, it wasn't long ago, so we don't have that evidence to know."

She said more onus needed to be put on social media companies to manage what content they were showing to young people.

"It's about how they design the algorithms, how they engage with young people, how they put checks in places on what age and what is age appropriate."

However, she acknowledged that enforcing regulations on large tech companies would be difficult.

"I think we need to try and we need to put as much in place as possible. And then hopefully we can work with other governments around the world to actually have some influence as well."

World.title: Man found guilty of threatening to kill people at two Auckland schools
World.content:
A man has been found guilty of threatening to kill people at two Auckland schools and saying he would destroy police stations and buildings at Parliament.

A jury in the Manukau District Court today found Tiedan Huo guilty of 12 charges relating to threats against Waiuku and Rutherford colleges and other public buildings.

Huo was also convicted for unlawful possession of a firearm, unlawful possession of explosives and possession of objectionable material.

Huo denied all charges and mid-way through the trial elected to act for himself in place of the lawyers who had been acting for him.

The charges stemmed from a manifesto, in which he spoke of using 3D-printed firearms in an attack.

The jury took just under three hours to find him guilty on all charges.

In his opening address to the jury, Crown prosecutor Gareth Kayes said that on 12 March last year, staff at Waiuku College woke to a chilling email that had been sent at 1.42am.

"It was titled 'Important: Don't come to school tomorrow'. And it started with the words 'This is my manifesto'."

The email spoke of being bullied and humiliated by teachers at the school, being unfairly treated by police and being made to feel like a second-class citizen for being Chinese.

"I am going to do something about this now. I have began [sic] preparing for doing something about this since February this year and have finished now."

The email went on to set out in some detail the preparations the sender said they had made to carry out attacks on Waiuku and Rutherford colleges, as well as damaging the Pukekohe and Te Atatu police stations and buildings at Parliament.

That included making firearms using a 3D printer and creating bullets and explosives to be used in an attack.

The sender said they wanted to kill more people than the Christchurch mosque terrorist, who murdered 51 innocent people on 15 March 2019.

"Do not assume that my guns will not work or are fake because they are 3D printed, that will be very bad."

The email was purportedly sent by a female former Waiuku College student, but after she allowed police to examine her electronic devices, officers established this was not the case, and their inquiries led them to Huo.

World.title: Warriors call on debutant Luke Laulilii for Knights clash
World.content:
The ladder-leading Warriors have called up a debutant to replace their injured winger as they chase a second NRL minor premiership.

The Warriors have made three changes for Sunday's round 26 game against the Newcastle Knights including the addition of right winger Luke Laulilii who comes in for Dallin Watene-Zelezniak.

Watene-Zelezniak crossed for his 20th try of the season in Saturday's 45-26 win over South Sydney but it was later revealed he had played on for a spell after breaking his collarbone during a dive near the corner flag.

Laulilii will become the Warriors' 300th NRL player after signing from the Wests Tigers in June.

The 20-year-old scored 10 tries in 17 NRL appearances for his former club.

In six New South Wales Cup outings since joining the Warriors. he has averaged 180 metres a game, scored two tries and made 22 tackle breaks.

Halfback Te Maire Martin comes back from injury for the sold-out game at Go Media Stadium after missing the last three matches with a hamstring injury.

Te Maire Martin is one of three changes for the Warriors against the Knights. David Neilson/Photosport

He's reunited in the halves with his regular partner Chanel Harris-Tavita who filled in at halfback for 60 minutes against the Broncos and then started at No. 7 for the first time since 2021 in the Rabbitoh's game.

As well as Martin, regular right edge centre Ali Leiataua is back after missing the South Sydney encounter through illness.

The Warriors go into the contest leading the competition, one of three teams on 38 points but narrowly ahead of second-placed Penrith on points for and against.

At the business end of the season, the Warriors have qualified for the NRL playoffs 10 times in their 31-season history but have only claimed one minor premiership, in 2002, when they pipped the Knights on points differential.

World.title: National MPs 'misappropriate' time for questions in the House
World.content:
National is being accused of making a mockery of Parliament's processes by deliberately not giving itself enough time to answer questions from Opposition MPs in the House.

Leader of the House Louise Upston says National has tried to fix the system to ensure that does not happen, but not all parties agreed on proposed changes.

In the House on Tuesday, MPs took part in the Estimates debate, which scrutinises Budget spending decisions.

The debate runs for 11 hours over a number of sitting days.

Each party is given a certain amount of time to speak, spread across the course of the debate, and the party whips allocate that time between their members.

Nearing the end of the debate on Tuesday afternoon, Upston - in her capacity as Social Development Minister - refused to continue answering questions because her time allocation was up.

Chair Greg O'Connor had earlier warned members asking questions to be mindful of that.

"Her colleagues before have... let's just say, misappropriated her time," he said.

Upston answered some further questions from the Greens' Ricardo Menéndez March and Labour's Willow-Jean Prime, then stopped.

"I have no more time, I'm not speaking, all right, so I don't want to upset anyone, we've tried to improve this process and the Labour Party didn't agree," she said.

"You're speaking right now!" Menéndez March said.

O'Connor said MPs could continue to ask questions, but it was up to National how it allocated its time.

Questions continued, but Upston did not.

"Mr Chair, we have an allocation, I'm not going to take time off following ministers where there are energy, resources, health and housing (still to be debated)," said Upston.

Menéndez March asked to grant 15 seconds of his own allocated time to Upston so she could give yes or no answers, which O'Connor allowed.

"Doesn't mean I'm gonna use it," Upston said.

She answered one further question, then stayed silent.

"Crickets," Prime said.

Menéndez March later told RNZ ministers were entitled to do that, but it showed National did not take scrutiny of the executive seriously, choosing to give lengthy speeches in answer to simple questions to run down the clock.

"It makes a mockery of a process that is supposed to allow for the scrutiny of ministers, and for ministers to be accountable to decisions that they have made," he said.

"It is up to the National Party on how to manage that time, but when throughout the debate you see ministers using their time to give political speeches and throw platitudes instead of answering questions, it is no surprise that as we draw close to the end of this debate, ministers are choosing to not answer questions."

Menéndez March said he did not get adequate answers to questions about whether any beneficiaries lost payments as part of a new policy change, and about cuts to the accommodation supplement for low-income homeowners.

Upston said National had proposed trialling a change to the Estimates debate to ensure ministers would not run out of time.

"National has sought to make improvements to what we know is not a great system but these haven't been agreed to by all parties," she said.

"We agree the format doesn't work as it should."

World.title: Dads' junk food diet could have 'long-reaching effects' on offspring - study
World.content:
The effects of obesity caused by western junk food diets can be passed to children through their dad's sperm, according to new research.

The data from the University of Auckland's Liggins Institute suggests what the father is eating could - in some cases - be more influential than the mother's diet, which has long been a focus.

The study looked at the impact of high-sugar, high-fat junk food diets on breeding rats and their babies as they aged.

Fathers diet could be linked to obesity in children Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

Dr Ben Albert - a paediatrician and senior research fellow at the Liggins institute - told Checkpoint the study gave a junk food diet to various mum and dad rats, and then looked at the results.

"In our study we have very carefully controlled the diets of mum and dad rats and shown that when dads had this junk food diet, it had really long-reaching effects on the offspring, right through to adulthood.

"We've found that if the dad had the junk food, even though the offspring were all treated exactly the same and ate normal diets their whole lives, they had greater body weight, greater body fat, higher blood pressure."

The researchers found the metabolism was working abnormally in the rats that had junk food eating dads, changing the way insulin worked in their bodies and increasing their risk of diabetes and heart disease.

"What it means is that if a child is born from a dad who is carrying more weight before they conceive, then that child is already born with kind of the dice already loaded against them. They're already at increased risk of weight problems and diabetes down the line. It doesn't mean that what they do in their life won't be important, in fact, it might be exceptionally important because their risk is higher - but it means that everything is harder from the start," Albert said.

The research team had more questions to answer, including how many months before conception the diet would affect the sperm.

But Albert said it was possible it was a relative short period of time.

"Because it takes about two months for a sperm to develop from start to end. And so the hope would be that perhaps if dads could dramatically improve their health for around two months, that would actually set their babies up on a healthier path, but the study to show that hasn't been done yet."

World.title: Stored chemistry experiment in Horowhenua College science lab became potentially explosive substance, principal says
World.content:
The Defence Force were called to Horowhenua College after a stored chemistry experiment in a science lab became a potentially explosive substance, the principal says.

Emergency services were called to the school about 10.20am.

Principal Grant Congdon said a stored solution made up for a senior chemistry experiment "precipitated" over time into a potentially explosive substance in a storage cupboard at the school.

A bomb disposal robot removed the flask, he said and it was detonated by Defence Force ordinance disposal staff in the school's back field.

"A big bang and the chemical is gone," Congdon said.

Congdon said the solution, known as Tollens' reagent, which contained silver ions and ammonia, had been stored for a number of years before it was discovered by a staff member who raised the alarm.

"It had been there for such a long time that there's been a transformation within the flask to the point where a precipitate had formed and that any sort of movement, friction or heat can potentially make it explode.

"On the side of the flask, you could see it there as a black powder, that was the part of what was in the flask which was potentially dangerous," Congdon said.

Congdon said police, Fire and Emergency, ambulance and two members of the Defence Force Bomb squad equipped with protective suits and a bomb disposal robot attended.

He said about up to 130 students were evacuated.

The school did not have enough time to alert neighbours on the school's boundaries before the chemical was destroyed, he said.

"It was a big enough bang for someone several hundred metres away to feel the blast impact. So it was a fairly decent noise," Congdon said.

Congdon said the days events were "a first" in his years as an educator.

He was unable to say exactly how long the chemical had been stored in the school but it would have amounted to years.

The school would be reviewing its storage and safety procedures in response to the incident, Congdon said.

"And obviously it raises questions for us to just check and see how is our storage procedures for chemicals and gases and all those sorts of things around the college, just to check that we've got procedures in place that are fit for purpose," Congdon said.

Congdon said he was impressed with the performance of staff and emergency services responding to the discovery and he was grateful the situation had come to a safe ending.

"The oversight from FENZ, the bomb disposal guys were just so professional and the communication to everybody was on point.

"We had to be pretty flexible with looking after students and removing them from rooms as things as that chemical was being uplifted and then taken out to the back field. Staff were amazing. Everyone just worked very well together."

World.title: Auckland commuters may pay up to $7 a trip as congestion charge options revealed
World.content:
Congestion charge may cost up to $7 Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

Auckland Councillors have voted to take the next steps with three potential options for congestion charging during peak times.

The three proposed time-of-use charging schemes were predicted to reduce peak time congestion by anywhere from 2 percent to 13 percent.

One option was to charge commuters entering the city centre during rush hour, while another included city fringe suburbs like Newmarket and Newton, and possibly Ponsonby and Parnell.

A third option would also include core motorways such as from the Harbour Bridge to Point Chevalier and Mount Wellington.

Waitākere Ward councillor Shane Henderson said any charges would need to be balanced with investment in transport alternatives.

Waitākere Ward councillor Shane Henderson. Auckland City Council / Supplied

"In West Auckland that means the northwestern busway will need to be committed to by the government ... because people need proper alternatives."

Henderson said it was important to get Aucklanders feedback on the three proposals.

City Centre Cordon is described as the "fairest, simplest" and "most feasible scheme", saving four minutes of travel time. Supplied / Auckland Council

"We're putting it out to the people, and saying 'what do you think about this?' And we'll go from there."

After the options are confirmed by the Transport and Infrastructure Delivery Committee on Tuesday, initial public consultation will start in mid-November before an option is decided on in 2027.

Council documents described the city centre option as the "fairest, simplest and likely most feasible scheme," but noted it would raise limited revenue to improve public transport.

Charges for this option would be around $3-$4 in the morning peak, and $2-$3 in the afternoon.

The city-fringe option was described as "significantly improved effectiveness compared to the city centre cordon," but noted it would include Auckland Hospital.

Option 2: City Fringe Cordon would charge drivers entering via Newmarket, Newton, Parnell and Ponsonby during peak hours. Supplied / Auckland Council

Charges for this option would be in the order of $5-$6 in the morning peak, and $2-$3 in the afternoon.

The option including the core motorways was described as "providing significant net revenue to fund improved public transport alternatives" such as rapid bus transit routes next to motorways.

Charges for this option could range from $5 to $7 and would likely only apply in the peak direction.

Council documents estimated the charges could save drivers four minutes per trip for the city centre option - up to 12 minutes per trip if core motorways are included.

After an option is confirmed in 2027, it would be ratified and get ministerial approval in 2028.

Option 3: Core motorways and city centre includes the Harbour Bridge, Pt Chevalier and Mt Wellington Supplied / Auckland Council

Auckland's traffic congestion was not a new issue - as the city grew, congestion was expected to increase.

Time of use charging has been used overseas to to reduce congestion in cities, and legislation allowing its introduction here passed its final reading at Parliament in November.

Auckland Council staff told councillors at Tuesday's transport and infrastructure delivery committee meeting they had worked through a long-list of 13 potential congestion charging solutions, and whittled that down to three options which are predicted to reduce congestion by two to 13 percent at peak times.

Council's strategic transport lead Hamish Bunn said the three options put forward were chosen because they are based around the central city where there are the most options for public transport.

Bunn said the final cost would be set by a Scheme Board, to be made up of representatives of Auckland Council and the New Zealand Transport Agency, and there could be graduated across peak times and shoulder times.

Several councillors said they were concerned about the impact of the charges on low-income people.

Bunn said a focus of public engagement due to take place after the election in November would be to find out how each option would impact Aucklanders in different scenarios, and to produce deeper analysis of the social impact of the proposed schemes.

Councillors wanted to know how the money would be spent. Legislation stipulated the funds earned be spent on transport solutions in the area where it's collected, Bunn said.

Waitākere ward councillor Ken Turner put forward an amendment, proposing a fourth option for the public of "do not proceed" be added.

Bunn said doing that would diminish the depth of feedback the council would get on the specific options being considered, and the amendment was voted down.

Aucklanders will have another chance to have their say once a final proposal for one scheme is determined, and goes out for public consultation in late 2027.

In mid-2028, the Ministers of Finance and Transport would then need to approve the scheme, before it would be implemented in 2030 or 2031.

Urban design planner voices support for charges

Auckland councillors to decide on congestion charge Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Urban design advocate Patrick Reynolds from the advocacy group Greater Auckland believed charging commuters to drive in and out of Auckland's city centre via core motorways would save time and money.

Reynolds told Checkpoint people who still chose to drive would have much faster journeys.

"People who still choose to drive at that time will have much faster journeys. The decongestion benefits will be most significant, and the revenue raised that we can reinvest in better alternatives is higher," he said.

Reynolds rejected suggestions people who could least afford the charges would pay the most.

"That isn't really supported. They certainly won't be paying the most, partly because of their location. In other words, we pretty well know who drives at peak time to the city centre, and it isn't factory workers in South Auckland," he said.

"It's lawyers in Shortland Street."

Reynolds said that emergency and public transport vehicles should be exempt from the charges, but not gig workers, rideshares and taxis.

"I mean, there will be instances where those people will pay, but they'll also get a quicker journey, and if they're a tradesperson or a delivery person or a freight truck driver, they will be saving a fortune by saving 10 minutes. Also, of course, if you're a business person, this is a tax-deductible cost of business," he said.

"We have, especially freight and delivery representatives coming and telling us that congestion is piling enormous costs onto everything that we buy because they can only do fewer trips per day through the city. This is the cost of congestion. I mean, we pay one way or another."

World.title: Richmond denies players 'making light' of Swans scandal on Mad Monday
World.content:
The Richmond Football Club has denied its players were "referencing or making light of recent matters" in footage recorded during their post-season celebrations.

Tiger players were recorded during a drinking session at a Victorian country pub, with one player seen feigning shock after being spanked on his rear by a teammate.

Another teammate whips a fellow player on the back with a belt in footage captured by news outlets yesterday, leading to speculation they were referencing the ongoing Sydney Swans scandal.

The club denied that was the case.

"Richmond is aware of a video circulating from a player end-of-season gathering," a statement read.

"The club has spoken to the players who have expressed their embarrassment over their behaviour.

"The players are adamant they were in no way referencing or making light of recent matters."

Swans will not be invited to Brownlow ceremony AFL boss Andrew Dillon speaks to the media about the Sydney Swans scandal, saying "the actions of a few don't define the actions of the entire industry".

The Tigers finished second last this season with a 3-20 win-loss record.

The pub that hosted Richmond's drinks said the controversy had been blown out of proportion.

"In our view, this has been blown out of proportion," the Garfield Hotel, 80 kilometres east of Melbourne, said in a statement posted on social media.

The hotel said it "could not speak more highly" of how players behaved.

"For such a young group, they were extremely respectful and a fun group of boys to deal with," the statement read.

Nick Blakey (left) is one of the Swans suspended for breaching club standards. (AAP Image: Dean Lewins)

"They enjoyed a few quiet beers to unwind after a long season and we see nothing wrong with that.

"They had booked out the venue for the afternoon, so they were the only patrons on site.

"They enjoyed their afternoon and moved on."

The hotel noted media were waiting for the Tigers players "in the hope of capturing a misstep, which we consider disappointing".

The Richmond footage emerged hours after AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon fronted the media for the first time since the Swans scandal began.

"I have been asked a lot in recent days, what message football should be sending young people and what we should be saying to our kids," Dillon said.

"For me, the answer is straightforward: it doesn't matter who you are, it doesn't matter what you do, whether you're an AFL footballer — the way we treat women says a lot about who we are as people, as a community and as a game.

"Quite simply, respect for women is not negotiable."

Dillon said the actions of the five suspended Swans players had "fallen well short of the standards our game expects and community deserves".

"While there are players involved, we cannot lose sight of the bigger picture. More importantly, there are women who have made a report to police and they should be shown care and respect," he said.

World.title: NRL changes rules to allow Jai Arrow to 'play' 100 games for Souths
World.content:
Jai Arrow will make cameo appearances in the final two rounds of the regular season in order to reach 100 games for South Sydney.

In one of the feel-good stories of the NRL season, the forward who retired with motor neurone disease in May has been approved to start on the field in rounds 26 and 27.

Arrow will then be substituted out in the opening seconds before any active involvement in play.

Arrow, in jersey number 23, has been named co-captain with Cameron Murray, who is listed to come off the bench.

It came after the Rabbitohs made an appeal to the NRL to grant the former Queensland representative an on-field swansong while still able to walk and run.

The initiative gives Arrow two final chances to farewell an NRL career that featured a grand-final appearance in 2021 and 12 State of Origin caps.

The NRL has granted Souths special dispensation to name Arrow as an extra player on today's team list and an extra substitution in their rotation.

Arrow vows to help others fight MND Former NRL player Jai Arrow says he is determined to raise money and awareness for Motor Neurone Disease until a cure is found.

The matches, against Gold Coast and the Sydney Roosters, will bring Arrow's tally to 180 career games and 100 for the Rabbitohs.

Arrow will lead the team out on both occasions and sit on the interchange bench in Souths kit after being substituted out.

The Titans and Roosters have both approved the plan, as have the Rugby League Players Association.

"We are very grateful to Peter [V'landys] and the NRL, and Clint [Newton] at the RLPA, for supporting our proposal," Souths chief executive Blake Solly said.

"We believe this will provide great inspiration for everyone watching the game from the stadium or at home, showing that MND will not hold Jai, or anyone else, back from achieving what they want to achieve in life."

The NRL world has rallied around Arrow since his shock diagnosis and immediate retirement in May.

The league threw Arrow "the world's biggest birthday party" on the day Souths beat Newcastle in July, rolling out a birthday cake in the shape of the 31-year-old's jersey and presenting him with a commemorative jersey.

Fundraising efforts have already passed $1 million in support of Arrow, who is the father of a young daughter.

Players from all clubs have shown their support by marking tries with arrow celebrations throughout the month of July.
