World.title: McVeigh to canvass Hird return as icon urges Bombers fans to unite
World.content:
New Essendon coach Mark McVeigh says he will speak to James Hird about returning to the club in a different capacity after a second failed bid to be coach.

McVeigh was unveiled on Tuesday in a press conference that was also attended by a number of Essendon's current players.

Both he and club president Andrew Welsh indicated their desire to have Hird involved.

"I'd love to see James as a part of the club going forward. He's such a fantastic football person," Welsh said.

"I feel there's significant value James can bring, not just tokenistic, but real value to our club and our playing group.

"Certainly, part of my messaging was that Mark and I would want to catch up with him when the time is appropriate."

While Welsh said a pair of calls to Hird had gone unanswered on Monday night, McVeigh said he had shared a conversation with his former captain.

"I love James Hird, he's one of my best mates. It was difficult to go through the process against a good friend," he said.

McVeigh (right) called Hird (left) one of his "best mates" after beating him to the Essendon job. (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

"I don't fear those people [Hird's supporters], I actually embrace how they feel, and I understand it, to be fair.

"He's been a constant in my life since I was 17 years of age. We spoke this morning, and the way he spoke of how proud he was of this moment for me, it hasn't broken us, we're still together, but I understand and embrace the feelings of the people that love James Hird, because I do too."

McVeigh, Welsh and club CEO Tim Roberts called for unity at the club amid rumours of a potential board challenge from unimpressed Hird fans.

"I don't ask for your patience, I ask for your re-alignment to our club," McVeigh said.

"I sit here year after year, and we get people coming out of the shadows that want to challenge the board," added Welsh.

"I can tell you since I've been here that this club has never been more united.

"These people want to keep living in the shadows and keep on trying to destabilise our club, we don't jump at shadows.

"We're a strong club and we'll continue to make sure that we make the right decisions on behalf of our members and our teams and our staff to get this club moving forward again."

Tim Watson (pictured) has called for unity at Essendon after Mark McVeigh's signing. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

The plea for unity came as Essendon legend Tim Watson has the club's passionate supporters to "put [their] weapons down".

"There's got to be a unification of the club now," he told SEN on Tuesday morning.

"People have to put down their weapons and get behind this appointment of a former player — somebody who has been passionate about the football club.

"This is part of the healing process that needs to take place. Ultimately, it's a much bigger thing than the emotion that might be associated with it now. There is an enormous amount of work to do.

Live Moment Look back at Mark McVeigh's first press conference as Essendon's new senior coach. McVeigh says Bombers 'won't live in the past' Pretty good way to end the press conference from the new Essendon coach. He receives another round of applause from those in attendance before walking off the podium. Welsh with another clue on Hird returning I reckon it's going to be a full-court press on the Dons trying to get Hird to say yes to some kind of role within the club. "We have great people that we want to get back involved with the club in meaningful ways," Welsh says. "I look at this as a point that we can re-align that passion." McVeigh with an insight into his game plan McVeigh explains what areas he's going to try and fix on-field. "In the phases of the game, we can't focus on one. If you look at the numbers, we're the bottom of the table in a lot of areas. "I do want them to be brave, I do want them to play with flare, but we do need to fix up our defence. "They [the players] need to come back prepared physically and ready to learn. "The system we'll put in place, you need to understand, otherwise you'll get found out. "When we get all three phases going in the right direction, Essendon will fly." Show more

"Congratulations to him. He's been an Essendon man all his life. He's loved this football club, that was clear in the days that he played.

"He's had a great development profile if you look at where he's been and what he's been doing. He's been part of elite coaching departments [at GWS and Sydney]."

McVeigh has signed a three-year contract with Essendon and was the unanimous choice of the Essendon board.

World.title: Piastri searching for answers as teammate re-enters F1 title picture
World.content:
Oscar Piastri's "disappointing" end to the Dutch Grand Prix has left the Australian and his McLaren team searching for answers, while his teammate has roared back into the Formula 1 title picture.

Last weekend in Zandvoort was shaping to be a good weekend for Piastri.

The Australian was matching the pace at the front through qualifying, and after a terrific second start in the grand prix following Max Verstappen's heavy crash, Piastri was on course for a first podium finish since Miami in May.

Piastri struggles after slow pit stop, Norris wins as Verstappen crashes Reigning world champion Lando Norris has doubled his grand prix win tally in 2026, producing a pair of brilliant overtakes to win the Dutch Grand Prix.

Piastri had performed a breathtaking overtake on Mercedes driver George Russell to move into third and was not far off the pace set by leaders Kimi Antonelli and teammate Lando Norris, despite being on a harder compound tyre.

But a slow first pit stop knocked Piastri back behind Russell and out of third place, and it only got worse from there.

Piastri, who won the Dutch Grand Prix in 2025, fell right off the pace and finished a distant sixth as Norris surged to victory.

Piastri was running third until a slow pit stop knocked him out of the podium position at Zandvoort. (Reuters: Benoit Tessier)

The sudden pace drop-off has left Piastri with plenty of questions that he and the team will want answers to.

"The first stint felt reasonable, but from the second stint onwards, the pace was simply not there, and it became a real struggle," he said.

"We will review the entire weekend and analyse to understand why we experienced such a significant performance drop-off.

"A slow pit stop didn't help, but the fundamental issue was the lack of pace, which is something we'll work on ahead of Monza.

"That's the priority now, to dig into the data with the team to find the root cause and ensure we can move forward in a more positive direction for the upcoming races."

Piastri's situation is a far cry from where he was at the conclusion of last year's Dutch Grand Prix, when he claimed his seventh grand prix win of the season and was the championship leader.

But while Piastri is seeking answers to get back to the front of the grid, Norris is threatening to stay there.

'The fight's still on': Norris re-enters the F1 title picture

McLaren entered the 2026 season having won the previous two constructors' championships, and with Lando Norris as reigning drivers' champion.

Reigning Formula 1 drivers' champion Lando Norris has won the past two grands prix. (Reuters: Benoit Tessier)

But with a new era of regulations, McLaren's 2026 season started poorly.

Piastri crashed on his way to the grid in Melbourne and he and Norris did not start in Shanghai due to car issues.

Norris then had back-to-back retirements in Montreal and Monaco, meaning he failed to finish three of the opening six grands prix.

But the reigning world champion has returned to winning ways, triumphing in Hungary before the mid-year break and then again last weekend in the Netherlands.

With back-to-back wins and growing confidence in his season, Norris has re-emerged as a drivers' championship contender.

F1 drivers' championship standings after Dutch Grand Prix 242 — Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes

183 — George Russell, Mercedes

183 — Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari

159 — Lando Norris, McLaren

155 — Charles Leclerc, Ferrari

With 10 or 11 rounds remaining this season, depending on conflict in the Middle East, Norris is sitting fourth in the standings, 83 points behind leader Kimi Antonelli.

It is a huge gap, but recent history shows it is not an impossible feat.

At the conclusion of last year's Dutch Grand Prix, Max Verstappen was 104 points behind then-leader Piastri with nine rounds remaining.

Verstappen surged towards the end of the season while Piastri slumped. Verstappen fell two points shy of Norris in the standings, but finished a stunning 11 points ahead of Piastri.

Having seen what is possible, Norris has made this year's title fight a four-way race with Antonelli, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton.

Norris's message to his team over the radio after taking the chequered flag on Sunday certainly sounded like the Briton believed his championship hopes are far from over.

"Let's keep pushing. Thank you for the hard work. Let's keep bringing upgrades, let's keep bringing performance, please," he said.

"The fight's still on."

Out of the car, Norris was quick to point out that there is a long season still ahead of the drivers and that he was not getting ahead of himself with an 83-point deficit.

"One race at a time. A lot of people say it now, but it is the truth of it. There's no point in thinking that far ahead," he said after winning on Sunday.

"There are plenty of things we can do better, and we need to do better if we want to fight for a championship.

"We have to keep working hard. There's still plenty of races, plenty of opportunity for everyone."

Norris's deficit to Antonelli was 101 points prior to the weekend in Hungary, but the McLaren champion has reduced that by 18 with two tremendous weekends.

However, the 83-point gap is significant and Antonelli has extended his overall championship lead.

Entering the Dutch Grand Prix weekend, the young Italian's lead over Hamilton was 50 points, and 59 over Russell.

After the weekend, his lead is 59 points over both Hamilton and Russell.

F1 heads to Monza for the Italian Grand Prix in two weeks, one of the fastest tracks on the calendar and vastly different to the tight and twisting circuits in Hungary and the Netherlands where Norris has won this year.

World.title: 'A dangerous individual': Ex-snooker champ convicted of child sex abuse
World.content:
Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been convicted of sexually abusing two primary school children in Scotland in the 1990s and early 2000s.

Dott, 49, was found guilty of abusing a girl from 1993-96 and a boy from 2006-10 after a five-day trial at the High Court in Glasgow. The judge ordered Dott to be held in custody ahead of his sentencing on September 29.

The woman, now in her 40s, testified that Dott sexually abused her on multiple occasions, "caressing" her bottom over her clothing, exposing himself and touching her with parts of his body, including his penis.

The man, now in his late 20s, said he was abused on multiple occasions, with Dott touching him inappropriately, kissing him and performing sexual acts.

Dott with his wife Elaine after winning the snooker world championship in 2006. (Getty Images: Rui Vieira)

"Dott is a dangerous individual, and I hope this conviction provides some measure of comfort to those impacted by his crimes," Detective Inspector Gary Smillie from Police Scotland said.

Snooker's governing body suspended Dott in April 2025 after he was charged in the case. The Scot was ranked number 56 in the world at the time and dropped from the rankings after the season.

On Monday, the World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association revoked Dott's membership following an emergency board meeting. The WPBSA also said it wrote to the World Snooker Tour to request his immediate removal from the WST Hall of Fame.

Dott won the World Snooker Championship in 2006 and was a runner-up twice.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Zak Butters trade rumours dominate Port Adelaide's turbulent season
World.content:
It's been a tumultuous year for Port Adelaide.

Its newly-appointed coach Josh Carr had to navigate a new system with an injury riddled list; using 39 of its 44-listed players and finishing the season with 15 unavailable.

He also had to build chemistry and belief despite a contract decision overshadowing his campaign.

Its vice-captain and dual All-Australian Zak Butters has dominated headlines all season as one of the biggest free-agents available this off-season; and has now confirmed the worst-kept secret in football that he has requested a trade to Victoria.

"I've made a decision to head home. It's obviously been one that I've wrestled with for a while now. It's been a tough decision and one that I haven't taken lightly," Butters said on Monday.

"Although I've loved my time in Adelaide … I'm probably at a stage in my life where I'd like to get back around some family and friends and enjoy some more time with them."

Butters denied reports in June that he had begun telling those close to him he was eager to move east after a trip back home during the round 12 bye; another chapter in a compendium of updates on the dual Showdown medallist's future.

So why was the club so protective of Butters when he had a foot out the door?

There are two key foundations of any negotiation in any industry. Value and relationships.

Growing speculation

As the weeks progressed and the speculation grew, the four-horse race between Richmond, Geelong, Collingwood and the Western Bulldogs intensified as the coverage evolved into a public bidding war; increasing Butters' contract terms and giving the Power fuel for higher trade demands.

Every story has a source … and every source has an agenda.

Zak Butters to leave Port Adelaide Star Port Adelaide midfielder Zak Butters has informed the Power he wants to return to Victoria.

Player agents are looking to maximise demand and clubs want their outgoing stars to leave at a high price.

Relationships between the two parties are also incredibly important in future dealings. Clubs are constantly trying to find the balance between fair compensation and long-term favours.

For Port Adelaide this was the case two years ago when Dan Houston was desperate to move to Collingwood but the Magpies didn't have the capital for a reasonable return.

The Power settled for Picks 13, 29 and 36 plus forwards Jack Lukosius and Joe Richards in exchange for its dual All-Australian defender and a future first round pick.

It was a move that was widely panned at the time but hasn't done much damage given rising key forward Jack Whitlock was taken at 29 and Joe Richards is developing into a handy midfield option.

But Dan Houston and Zak Butters are different cases.

The Power is hoping to maximise its draft haul in moving its triple best-and-fairest winner given it has rarely had early selections in recent years leading to a gulf in young talent depth.

It also has a litany of upcoming academy and father-son draftees it will need to match bids on, such as expected number one pick Dougie Cochrane and Zemes Pilot.

Matthew Richardson spoke about the Butters trade rumous in May. (ABC News: Marco Catalano)

Back in May, Port chief executive Matthew Richardson flagged on ABC Sport that the club would match any bid on Butters to force a trade given the star is a restricted free agent.

"There will be offers that we can match and we will match. It does give the club a fair bit of control in what happens," he said.

The issue is Butters current suitors have a diverse availability of picks at their disposal and the Power's best option Richmond doesn't quite align with the values Butters claimed he was eyeing when I asked him back in March what would dictate his decision.

"I think you're stupid if you don't want to win premierships," he said.

"I want to win. Family is important as well … but you can't look too far ahead."

THE CONTENDERS (As of current ladder position, all four clubs have all future picks available) Geelong: 17, 35, 53, 71

Western Bulldogs: 10, 28, 46

Collingwood: 16, 34, 63, 66, 70

Richmond: 2, 20, 38, 56

While Port navigates its way through the 20 out-of-contract players it has held fire on due to the Butters decision, there will be time for Josh Carr to reflect on his inaugural season at the helm.

Season highlights

Despite double ups with four sides who missed finals; the Power managed seven wins in 2026 and had a clear narrative throughout; it could match it with the best but could rarely beat them.

Its campaign ended with an equal league record five losses by five-points or less and eight by as much as 14-points.

A Showdown win over Adelaide in June was the highlight, plus its April upset over Geelong; but its only road wins were against fellow bottom four sides West Coast and Richmond.

It finished 16th for ball movement from D50 to F50 but defensively was a powerhouse until the final month where 10-goal losses to the Lions, Swans and Demons blew out the team's average points against to 89, dropping it down from a Top 4 side into 10th.

The other positive was its clearance work. Despite missing Connor Rozee for the majority of the campaign, and Zak Butters for the final month, the side finished second for clearance differential, blooding future stars in Jase Burgoyne, Joe Richards and Miles Bergman on ball.

Port Adelaide won seven games in the 2026 season. (ABC Riverland: Catherine Heuzenroeder)

From a list perspective it was the only side not to have a player named in the AFL's 22-under-22 squad and some of the long-term signings from the Hinkley era like Todd Marshall and Brandon Zerk-Thatcher barely featured.

Former Port midfielder and four times Showdown medallist Josh Francou believes 2026 was a free hit for Josh Carr.

"It has been a difficult campaign … the way they're defending the ground is a real plus for them but they struggle to move the ball," he said.

"Next year things start to ramp up on Josh Carr and he's got to get it right."

Despite all the adversities, it feels like Josh Carr has laid the foundation for success but a critical off-season awaits as he looks to reshape the list and keep his stars healthy for the 2027 campaign.

World.title: Cyclists run for cover as hailstorm forces La Vuelta stage cancellation
World.content:
A torrential hailstorm in the French Pyrenees forced the abandonment of the third stage of the Vuelta a España on Monday.

With 15 kilometres remaining of the 174-km route from Gruissan to Font-Romeu, the skies darkened as the peloton neared the top of the Col de Mont-Louis and huge hailstones began bouncing off the tarmac and pelting the riders.

Mats Wenzel (Kern Pharma) and Lorenzo Fortunato (XDS Astana) were 25 seconds ahead of the peloton when the elements intervened, as race leader and favourite Tadej Pogacar was seen indicating to the peloton to pull off the course.

Bedraggled riders were then seen getting off their bikes and shuffling into a hotel for shelter.

Shortly afterwards, race organisers, ASO, announced the stage would not resume, leaving fans frustrated at the finish where thick layers of hail blanketed the road.

Slovenia's Pogacar (UAE Emirates-XRG) retained his overall lead of nine seconds from Belgium's Wout van Aert (Dutch Visma-Lease a Bike) with Britain's Matt Brennan 10 seconds back.

Earlier it had been warm and sunny on the flat approaches to the mountainous finish with no sign of the chaos to come as a five-man breakaway group stayed out ahead.

Pogacar, bidding to complete his Grand Tour collection by winning the Vuelta for the first time, was always near the front of the pack with his team setting the pace.

Sadly, his expected challenge for the stage victory fell foul of the weather in an anticlimactic finish.

He will get his chance to underline his superiority again on Tuesday, though with stage four featuring three first-category climbs as the race starts and finishes in Andorra la Vella.

Reuters

World.title: From almost drowning as a child to the pinnacle of surf lifesaving
World.content:
Under an expansive blue sky and bathed in the type of sunshine that typifies Queensland's mocking parody of winter, the ocean at Surfers Paradise is made to look incredibly inviting, even on a Thursday morning in August.

But the crashing of waves into the hard-packed sand offers a reminder that beyond the beauty of the scene, the power of the ocean remains a potent force.

Australian Iron Series athlete Tiarnee Massie knows about this more than most.

The 24-year-old is a third-generation surf lifesaver at Maroochydore Surf Life Saving Club on Queensland's Sunshine Coast.

Not only that, but she is the reigning and defending Iron Series champion and will wear the yellow number 1 seed bib when the series gets underway in October with the Coolangatta Gold.

Tiarnee Massie will look to once again win the overall title when the series finishes at Surfers Paradise early next year. (Getty Images: Iron Series/Chris Hyde)

Her story could have been very different, though.

"I think I was nine months old," Massie tells ABC Sport on the Gold Coast.

"I was at home and my older sister was playing in the pool with her friends.

"Someone left the pool gate open and I found myself in the pool and drowning at the bottom of the pool."

The scenario is one that is all too painfully familiar for far too many Australian families.

The 2025 National Drowning Report, published by Royal Life Saving Australia and Surf Life Saving Australia, identified 15 fatalities of children aged four or younger, eight of which occurred in a swimming pool.

In total, the report noted that there were 357 drowning deaths over the past 12 months, a 27 per cent increase on the 10-year average.

Tiarnee Massie is aware she could have become a statistic for Australia's downing deaths. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

"My mum was actually on the phone and she had this gut instinct that something was wrong, so she hung up and she came out and she found me in the water," Massie says, knowing how fortunate she is to not be a contributing statistic to the nation's drowning tally.

"She started doing resuscitation and she saved my life that day."

That near-death experience didn't seem to do Massie any long-term harm.

Even in the short term it seems the young Massie was relatively unperturbed by the experience — she tells ABC Sport she was back in the water the very next day.

"It didn't affect me at all," Massie says.

"But it certainly affected my mum," she adds with an infectious and earnestly cheeky grin.

"Still now, when she's watching me in the ocean, she just can't watch. She's actually fainted a few times.

"She's got demons there, but she knows that I'm capable and she knows that I love it.

"I have the best family who support me. They are always coming to all of my competitions, we stay together and to be able to share these incredible experiences and moments with them, it's a dream come true."

Tiarnee Massie says her mum sometimes struggles watching her race. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

That day sparked something in Massie's mother too, who has gone on to become a CPR trainer at the Maroochydore Surf Club, joining a club that her uncle, Ashley Massie, competed for in surf lifesaving competitions.

"She never was involved [in surf lifesaving] to the extent of being a trainer until the moment that I drowned in the pool," Massie says.

"You don't know if you are someone that deals well in those situations until you're literally in the situation.

"You know, you can do all the training, but unless you actually are in that situation, you don't know whether you can do it. And my mum did it."

And incredibly, that ability to remain calm under the intolerable pressure of a life or death situation, clearly passed on to her daughter.

"I was 15, I was on a family holiday in Thailand and we were out surfing with my friends and I actually noticed that this man was struggling in the water," Massie says.

"My mum signalled me from the beach saying he's in trouble and my friend and I went over and helped him and we saved his life that day."

Competing is serious for Tiarnee Massie, but so too is the bigger picture of saving lives. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

The magnitude of that moment may have passed the then-teenage Massie by somewhat: "I was so young that I actually didn't understand the importance of what I did, I was just doing what I was trained to do," Massie says.

"I was doing what I knew how to do, I was in the ocean, I understand the ocean and I didn't understand that he couldn't."

The enormity soon struck home when the man she saved wrote her a letter.

"Later on he wrote a letter to myself and my friend, Grace, saying how grateful he was for us saving his life and that we have changed his life forever and all of this incredible stuff," she says.

"It was from that moment on that I realised how important the work that we were doing is.

"You know, I may be training to be the best ironwoman in the ocean, but most importantly, I'm training to be the best person to save a life on the beach.

"I think that is so rare in sport and that is such a special gift that we have as surf lifesavers. We are literally training to save someone's life."

Tiarnee Massie (right) will lock horns with number two seed Lily O'Sullivan (left) in the Iron Series. (Supplied)

Massie will start the defence of her title at the Coolangatta Gold, an event she came into as favourite last year, only to suffer the heartache of a broken paddle on the ski leg.

Despite that disappointment, Massey was still able to claim the series title.

Now she looks forward to honouring that yellow jersey over the course of the Iron Series, with events taking place in Coolangatta, Thirroul, Newcastle and the season final at Surfers Paradise on February 7.

"I feel so honoured to be wearing the yellow jersey this season," Massie says.

"I have looked up to every woman and man before me who has worn this jersey and to be actually in those yellow togs with the number one on them is such an honour.

"I'm just so grateful, I did all the hard yards as a young girl and stuck it out through the highs and lows of sport and all the triumphs and failures and I finally got to achieve my dream of becoming the Iron Series champion."

Tech.title: Lenovo confirms Legion Go issues after gamers report bricked devices
Tech.content:
Lenovo is aware that some Legion Go devices may experience a blank screen during installation of BIOS version V42. BIOS V42 was not distributed through Windows Update or Legion Space, and Lenovo has removed the update from its support website while we continue our validation work. Users who have successfully completed the V42 update should not need to take further action at this time.

If a device encounters a blank screen during V42 installation, users may try pressing and holding the power button for approximately 10 seconds, waiting approximately one minute, and then powering the device on again. If the device does not resume normal operation, customers should contact Lenovo Support for further assistance.

Lenovo continues to evaluate and validate future BIOS updates for Legion Go.

Tech.title: The cat-and-mouse game over 3D-printed guns has begun
Tech.content:
The creator of the world’s first 3D-printed gun claims he’s developed a way to thwart government-mandated software meant to block 3D printers from making firearms. It’s an opening volley in what’s shaping up to be an evolving battle between regulators trying to stem the tide of ghost guns and individuals trying to create workarounds.

Cody Wilson, who claims to have made the detection-defying tool, is calling it “Hochulization” as a direct jab at New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, who pushed through the nation’s first law mandating gun file detection software on new printers earlier this year. “New York is trying to reach into the internet and police how open-source 3D printing is done,” Wilson, who’s based out of Austin, Texas, told The Verge. “I think of it as a self-defense measure.”

The tool is designed to break a relatively simple approach to a 3D-printed gun ban. Wilson’s company, Defense Distributed, runs DEFCAD, the world’s largest 3D gun file repository, which he says hosts over 200,000 files of gun designs and components, such as suppressors. Each of those files can be identified by a hash, a unique string of numbers that’s created by running the file through an algorithm. In theory, a gun file detection system that uses a hashing-based identification method would look for those exact hashes to determine whether a file is a potential gun, flag it, and prevent it from printing.

Hochulization mucks up that process by automatically changing those hashes. It adds a series of bytes to each file that changes the hash without altering the function of the end product. A 3D-printed suppressor or gun, in other words, would still work as intended. “Hochulizaiton is a de minimis policy to change the hash of every file that gets created and downloaded to where there is never going to be a complete library of hashes,” Wilson says.

Wilson says he wants to apply the Hochulization treatment to all files hosted on DEFCAD by default as a means of “self-defense” against growing calls for gun detection software, which he describes as invasive digital surveillance. Wilson says he will make the tool available to DEFCAD users, though he says he also intends to make it open source, which would let an individual user with a gun file apply the tool to scramble the hash and potentially sidestep detection.

Image: Cody Wilson

“I think all the files in the repository, the 3D files anyway, should be Hochulized,” he adds. “And so that is what we’ll do.” He claims he has begun this process.

Wilson’s approach is an early indicator of the resistance to 3D-print-blocking tech. In this case, the momentum is coming from a Second Amendment advocate, but that might not always be the case. Groups of makers, digital rights experts, and members of the entertainment industry who aren’t focused on guns have all spoken out against the tech, expressing fears that requiring file scanning on printers introduces a new level of digital surveillance into the process that could limit what everyone can create.

3D-printed firearms are growing in number but remain an evolving public threat. In 2021, the New York Police Department confiscated just one 3D-printed gun. That jumped to 109 in 2024. Prominent gun policy group Everytown found similar upticks across 20 other cities. Still, when compared with the percentage of conventional firearms confiscated around the country, 3D-printed models remain comparatively small. The total number of firearms in the US has been estimated to outnumber people.

Policymakers and gun control advocates argue cases like this demonstrate a glaring gap in the legal system. People with prior felony convictions and others who aren’t legally allowed to own guns can do so anyway with the help of a 3D printer. And while many states regulate the making and selling of so-called “ghost guns,” actually enforcing those laws is notoriously difficult. This new approach, which requires 3D printers to install mandatory file-blocking software, attempts to close that gap by stopping a print before it ever starts. Industry experts are still debating whether that’s technically feasible at scale. Gov. Hochul, who pushed through the country’s first law mandating print-blocking software on new printers as part of the state’s FY 2027 budget, says it’s necessary to close what she calls a black-market “plastic pipeline.”

Hochul’s office did not respond to our request for comment regarding Wilson’s Hochulization workaround.

New York isn’t alone. A similar bill in California, AB 2047, is gaining momentum and is advancing to the Senate floor for a vote. Like in New York, this bill would require new printers manufactured or sold in the state to be equipped with print-blocking software. The state Department of Justice would publish a roster of compliant printer models, and those not on the list would be banned from sale or transfer in the state starting in December 2029.

A spokesperson for California Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, who introduced and coauthored AB 2047, declined to comment when asked about Wilson’s project.

Neither of these efforts explicitly details what print-blocking software should look like. That’s being left up to groups of industry experts with backgrounds in manufacturing technology, artificial intelligence, firearms regulation, and other relevant fields. A purely hash-matching approach would limit the number of non-guns mistakenly identified as guns, but as Wilson’s project shows, it may be trivially easy to bypass. More expansive approaches that use AI to analyze a file’s geometry and predict whether it’s a gun would almost certainly prevent more guns from being printed, but they also risk introducing more false positives.

Wilson’s hoping his tool will make its way into those working group conversations. By showing just how simple it is to complicate a purely hashing-based approach, he’s essentially trying to force policymakers’ hands into choosing between a more aggressive scanning scheme or the status quo of nothing.

“You are going to have to do more than create a database of known files and check against hashes because that’s too easy to defeat,” Wilson says.

Dartmouth College associate professor of engineering Solomon Diamond told The Verge Hochulization would likely work on a technical level to bypass a hash-based detection model. Still, he said that doesn’t necessarily make the approach useless as a policy path. In reality, it’s not clear that every 3D printer user would go the extra step to change a hash. Downloading gun files from DEFCAD also requires setting up an account and linking an email address, which is another barrier to entry. The hashing approach, in other words, is better than nothing and might stop the casual, less motivated user from downloading a gun.

Moving beyond hash matching, Wilson says his team found other ways to bypass more sophisticated detection using “adversarial noise.” To do this, his team first created their own AI detection model designed to classify guns and gun parts, trained partly on both public and non-public files from DEFCAD’s database. They based their model on claims made by other companies, such as the Spain-based Print&Go, which is working with lawmakers in New York and California.

Wilson claims he was able to get files past their own system using techniques like re-saving the same gun part as a slightly different mesh (a digital representation of the object’s surface) or adding “a small extra lump of unused geometry.” Overall, Wilson says their gun detection system, even when trained on high-quality data, still had a 30 percent false positive rate. He says that false positives speak to issues inherent to more prediction-based systems.

Wilson approaches the scanning debate as a self-described crypto-anarchist and an aggressive Second Amendment advocate. He’s a leading voice in arguing that gun files should be considered constitutionally protected speech under the First Amendment. He also created the platform Hatreon as an alternative to Patreon to thwart its speech policies, a platform that attracted extremists, white supremacists, and neo-Nazis until it was shut down in 2018.

But concerns over this proposed change to the way 3D printing works aren’t limited to gun owners. Makers and hobbyists previously told The Verge they fear this new paradigm will falsely label non-guns, like this e-reader case, as dangerous weapons and limit their freedom of expression in the process. Others are concerned a process that earnestly starts with gun file increments could be expanded by corporations looking to enforce IP and copyright protections.

Wilson isn’t new when it comes to picking fights over 3D-printed gun laws. After posting the first Liberator files online, the State Department ordered him to remove them and threatened him with jail time for allegedly violating ITAR export-control rules. Wilson and Defense Distributed sued the agency, claiming they attempted to stop him from publishing computer code, which he says is constitutionally protected under the First Amendment. That set in motion a complex web of legal fights over the broad claim that the gun file codes aren’t constitutionally protected speech, an issue that’s still being debated in courts.

Tech.title: Zillow and Redfin settle FTC antitrust case over their rental listings partnership
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The FTC and Zillow have announced a settlement that ends the case alleging that a 2025 “partnership” between Zillow and Redfin violated antitrust laws. The FTC had alleged Zillow agreed to pay Redfin to syndicate its listings, while Redfin would end its own advertising contracts and promise not to compete with Zillow for multifamily listings.

The FTC’s settlement proposal allows Redfin to continue syndicating rental listings from Zillow “unencumbered by the anticompetitive restraints” in the original deal, but also requires Redfin to restart its own rental listings advertising business, which it wound down as part of the partnership.

Daniel Guarnera, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Competition, said the deal “delivers better, quicker, more certain results for both renters and property management companies than we would have been able to achieve after prevailing at trial.” The state attorneys general of Arizona, Connecticut, New York, Virginia and Washington also agreed to the proposed settlement.

This ending also follows other recent settlements from the Trump administration in high-profile cases of companies behaving badly, like the Live Nation-Ticketmaster case, and its case against Realpage.

Tech.title: Robotaxis are real now — so is the pushback
Tech.content:
Robotaxis are expanding. So is the fight over the rules governing them.

In New York, Gov. Kathy Hochul withdrew a proposal earlier this year that would have opened the door to driverless robotaxis outside New York City after taxi drivers, unions, and state lawmakers opposed it. Six months later, commercial driverless service remains illegal in the state, and legalization efforts are stalled.

In DC, labor unions are fighting legislation that would legalize commercial robotaxis, while lawmakers are weighing a 200-vehicle cap and a 15-cent-per-mile fee that would fund Metro upgrades and aid workers displaced by autonomous vehicles. A July City Council hearing on the proposal stretched for a grueling 10 hours.

In San Francisco, Mayor Daniel Lurie, a vocal supporter of robotaxis, is now calling for tougher robotaxi regulations after Waymos repeatedly snarled traffic during emergencies and major events. And as of July, California police can now formally cite autonomous-vehicle manufacturers when their driverless cars break traffic laws.

And while Congress has yet to pass comprehensive robotaxi legislation, federal regulators have stepped up their scrutiny. The Trump administration’s National Highway Traffic Safety Administration recently warned autonomous-vehicle companies that vehicles unable to safely interact with police, firefighters, and other first responders pose a danger to the public.

Even in states that have broadly welcomed autonomous vehicles, governments are grappling with how to oversee them. Texas this year began enforcing new permitting requirements for commercial AV operators, while cities in Florida have complained that state preemption laws leave them with little power to respond to problems on their own streets.

Even in states that have broadly welcomed autonomous vehicles, governments are grappling with how to oversee them

Taxi drivers, labor unions, and safety advocates have fought autonomous vehicles for years. What’s changing is the scale and immediacy of the fight. Now that robotaxis have burst free from the pages of science fiction and onto actual city streets, policymakers are confronting a messier reality filled with questions about safety, regulation, growth, and jobs. They’re having to decide how quickly fleets should be allowed to expand, what companies must prove before they do, and how much control cities and states should have over their operations.

Waymo, the market leader, is currently operating more than 3,500 vehicles publicly in 11 US cities. Zoox — a purpose-built robotaxi without a steering wheel that bears a striking resemblance to a toaster — just began offering paid rides in Las Vegas and continues to offer free trips to users of its Explorer program in San Francisco as it collects feedback. It’s testing in a total of 10 cities and plans to extend the Explorer program to Austin and Miami later this year. Tesla, which began its Robotaxi rollout with a safety monitor aboard more than a year ago, appears to finally be growing its unsupervised fleet ahead of launching its purpose-built robotaxi, the Cybercab, later this month.

Still, for all the political attention, robotaxis remain a tiny share of the US ridehailing market. While Waymo now provides more than 500,000 paid rides a week, Uber handles about 40 million trips a day globally. At that scale, robotaxis haven’t yet displaced many driving jobs or fundamentally changed how cities move. But their visibility vastly exceeds their market share, especially when a driverless car stops in the wrong place during a blackout or interferes with an emergency response.

And the consequences could look very different as autonomous fleets grow from thousands of vehicles to hundreds of thousands. That’s why the battles taking shape across the country are increasingly about the terms of expansion: what companies have to prove before they grow, what they owe cities and workers, and how much control cities and states should have over their operations.

Photo by Michael Kappeler / picture alliance via Getty Images

What the critics want

In many places, the robotaxi rollout has outpaced the rules governing it.

“Robotaxis are popping up all over the place,” said Shua Sanchez, national campaign director of SAVE-US, a nonprofit advocating for stricter state AV legislation in the absence of federal rules. “The state legislatures don’t have experience with this technology, and there aren’t good laws on the books to regulate them.”

SAVE-US is working with lawmakers in New Jersey and New York on a three-pronged approach. It wants multi-stage testing and commercial-deployment permits, under which companies would have to demonstrate their vehicles can operate safely with a small fleet before adding more cars, while continuing to share safety data after commercial service begins. It also wants autonomous vehicles to use multiple kinds of sensors, rather than relying on cameras alone (as Tesla does), and is calling for restrictions on marketing terms like “Autopilot” or “Full Self-Driving” for consumer driver-assist features when the systems still require human oversight.

The group isn’t opposed to autonomous vehicles, Sanchez said, but is “pro the safe development of technology.” He added that AV safety isn’t a settled question, and that even a strong record today doesn’t guarantee the same after a software or hardware change.

Sen. Ed Markey (D-MA), who has pushed for greater federal oversight of AVs, makes a similar argument about transparency.

“Autonomous vehicle companies are making huge claims about how their technology is going to save lives,” Markey told The Verge in a statement. “But right now, our regulatory structure amounts to this: we hope they’re telling the truth.”

Markey has investigated AV companies’ use of remote human operators and introduced legislation that would require them to regularly report safety data.

“Right now, our regulatory structure amounts to this: we hope they’re telling the truth.” — Sen. Ed Markey

“Communities deserve transparency and consistent oversight before we let Big Tech invade their public roads,” he said.

But safety is only part of the fight. For labor groups, the stakes are also economic.

Peter Finn, Teamsters international vice president at large, called autonomous vehicles an “existential threat” to the work his members do. He pointed to the enormous number of jobs potentially affected by autonomous driving beyond rideshare drivers, including truckers, delivery drivers, and other commercial drivers.

Like other groups in the robotaxi debate, the Teamsters insist they aren’t opposed to new technology in principle. But that still leaves them staking out positions that would sharply constrain how autonomous vehicles are deployed.

That includes requiring heavy-duty autonomous vehicles like semitrucks to have a trained human operator aboard — legislation the Teamsters have twice pushed in California, only to see Gov. Gavin Newsom veto it. Finn said the Teamsters plan to pursue the issue again.

“If the technology is solely designed to automate and eliminate labor costs, the only entity benefiting from that is corporations,” Finn said.

The Teamsters’ immediate legislative priority isn’t robotaxis themselves so much as what it sees coming next.

To Finn, Waymo and Zoox are precursors to a much larger fight over autonomous driving. He pointed specifically to Zoox’s ownership by Amazon, arguing that similar technology could eventually be applied to package delivery.

Zoox and Waymo both said their current focus remains their robotaxi services.

Taken together, the objections go beyond any one safety rule or labor concern. AV resistance has become part of a broader backlash to Big Tech’s growing physical footprint, from data centers to Flock cameras. Companies are pouring enormous sums into new infrastructure, and many residents are still asking what, exactly, they get in return for having it in their communities.

Tesla Cybercabs are lined up on a lot at Tesla Giga Texas in Austin, Wednesday, April 8th. Photo by Jay Janner / The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images

Even robotaxi companies want rules

Robotaxi companies, meanwhile, are trying to get ahead of the backlash — and sidestep a patchwork of confusing state and local laws — by helping shape the rules themselves. That includes supporting certain regulations while pushing back on others they see as too restrictive.

“I want to unequivocally say we agree with the administrator and the administration and the regulatory agency. We need to be regulated,” Zoox CEO Aicha Evans recently said on Fox Business in response to NHTSA’s warnings about unsafe interactions with emergency vehicles.

Zoox said it is also trying to head off conflicts before entering new markets. Ron Thaniel, the company’s senior director of policy and regulatory affairs, said Zoox establishes lines of communication with local and state officials and conducts hands-on engagement with first responders before launching in a city. As the industry expands, he said, Zoox sees “an opportunity at the federal level to more uniformly regulate autonomous vehicles.”

Waymo told The Verge much the same thing.

“I think there definitely needs to be some regulation,” Waymo global head of public policy Justin Kintz said. “They’re powered by incredible technology that makes the world a safer place, but it still needs oversight from the federal government, from states, and from cities in the same way that they manage human drivers today.”

“I want to unequivocally say we agree with the administrator and the administration and the regulatory agency. We need to be regulated.” — Zoox CEO Aicha Evans

Zoox and Waymo are hardly alone in wanting clearer rules. The Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association, which counts both companies as members, has said only about half of US states have passed laws that allow vehicles to operate without humans. The industry group believes states should establish a legal framework for AVs, require first-responder interaction plans, and set minimum requirements before vehicles can operate without a human driver. (The association didn’t respond to requests for more specifics.)

Waymo said it has long advocated for a national AV safety standard covering minimum testing requirements, vehicle design, and data sharing. Under its preferred system, the federal government would continue setting vehicle safety standards, while states would govern road rules and cities would handle local concerns like curb space, law enforcement, and emergency response.

The disagreements emerge in the details.

In Washington, DC, Waymo said it broadly supports Councilmember Charles Allen’s effort to establish a regulatory framework allowing commercial robotaxi service, including its goals of funding transit and helping workers transition as transportation becomes more automated. But it objects to parts of the current proposal.

Waymo said a 200-vehicle limit would probably be too small for a city the size of Washington. It could accept starting small, but wants regulators to let fleets grow as companies demonstrate safe performance rather than putting a permanent ceiling into law.

“I don’t think legislation needs to set a hard cap on that,” Kintz said, “or it’s going to lead to preventing important groups from being able to access the service when they need it.”

The company has been more receptive to the proposed 15-cent fee for every mile an autonomous vehicle travels. Kintz said Waymo supports “the fundamental principle of raising revenue” for transit and affected workers, though it raised concerns that a per-mile charge could become prohibitively expensive, particularly for smaller AV operators. An annual fee, it suggested, is one possible alternative.

Emergency response is another area where Waymo says it supports regulation, even as it argues that some of the work is already underway. After NHTSA called for stronger coordination between AV companies and first responders, Waymo said it immediately asked to participate in the agency’s discussions. The company said it already maintains dedicated first responder training programs and 24/7 priority lines for dispatchers and officers, while Kintz acknowledged that “we haven’t always got it right.”

“We haven’t always got it right.” — Waymo global head of public policy Justin Kintz

Waymo is also trying to make the case that robotaxis can complement, rather than undermine, public transit. In a Streetsblog piece this month, Waymo policy development and research manager Arielle Fleisher argued the company has “common cause” with urbanists trying to reduce dependence on private cars. Waymo told The Verge that in San Francisco more than a third of its riders use the service to connect with public transportation. But research has also suggested that robotaxis could replace some trips that otherwise would have been taken on public transit, potentially undermining ridership rather than complementing it.

On labor, Waymo argues that automation will eliminate some tasks while creating others.

“These cars don’t clean, charge, fix themselves, code themselves,” Kintz said, pointing to jobs including fleet technicians, mechanics, remote support workers, and operations managers. Of course, simply taking the driver out of the driver’s seat could have huge economic implications. Earlier this month, Uber said that 10.2 million drivers and couriers earned money on its platform during the second quarter.

An Amazon-owned Zoox driverless robotaxi drives down a street on August 3rd in San Francisco. The National Highway Traffic Safety ‌Administration cleared Amazon-owned Zoox robotaxis to charge customers for robotaxi rides. Photo by Heather Diehl / Getty Images

Kintz acknowledged that autonomous vehicles could eventually displace drivers and said Waymo was “eyes open” about that possibility. But he argued the change would happen over time and that unions could help build retraining and reskilling programs for affected workers.

Asked whether autonomous driving would ultimately create more jobs than it eliminated, Kintz said it was “too soon to tell.”

Notably Waymo has continued to expand as these fights play out. The California Public Utilities Commission this month cleared the company to expand driverless passenger service across parts of 18 counties, including Sacramento and San Diego and more of the Los Angeles and Bay Area regions.

For now, robotaxis are helping a very small number of Americans get around. The fights underway today are about what happens if they don’t stay that way.

Tech.title: The Witcher 4 developers target a 2028 release
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

CD Projekt Red is aiming to launch The Witcher 4 sometime in 2028, joint CEO Michał Nowakowski says in a new video. CD Projekt Red has been working on its next mainline Witcher title for years and has shown videos of it, but now the studio is providing a target release window for when the game might actually come out.

There’s more new Witcher to come before The Witcher 4, though. At this week’s Gamescom event, CD Projekt Red will be showing off its upcoming Witcher 3 expansion, Songs of the Past, which is scheduled to release sometime in 2027. Songs of the Past is also set to be part of Gamescom’s Opening Night Live event hosted by Geoff Keighley, which kicks off at 2PM ET on Tuesday.

CD Projekt Red is also working on a multiplayer spinoff set in the universe of The Witcher that’s codenamed Project Siris. Earlier in August, the company confirmed that it laid off staff working on the game.

Tech.title: ESPN streaming plans are getting more expensive
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Streaming keeps getting more expensive: all the latest price hikes

ESPN is hiking the price of its subscription on September 17th, a change that will also impact its bundles with Disney Plus. In a support page spotted earlier by Sports Media Watch, ESPN says its ad-supported Select membership will cost $13.99 instead of $12.99 / month, while its Unlimited plan will rise to $31.99 from $29.99 / month.

The annual ESPN Select plan is also going to $139.99 from $129.99 / year, and the annual Unlimited tier is increasing to $319.99 from $299.99 / year. Meanwhile, Disney Plus bundles with ESPN Select are going up in price as well. Here’s a rundown of the changes:

Disney Plus (with ads), Hulu (with ads), and ESPN Select: $21.99 / month, up from $19.99 / month.

Disney Plus (ad-free), Hulu (ad-free), ESPN Select : $32.99 / month, up from $29.99.

Legacy Disney Plus (ad-free), Hulu (ad-free), and ESPN Select: $27.99 / month, up from $24.99 / month.

Disney Plus bundles with ESPN Unlimited aren’t affected. Last week, Axios reported that about 80 percent of Unlimited subscribers signed up through the bundle with Disney Plus and Hulu.

Though Disney last raised prices across its bundles last year, this is the first increase for ESPN, which rolled out its standalone streaming subscription last August. As part of the launch, ESPN updated its mobile app with a TikTok-like feed of videos and a personalized version of SportsCenter. ESPN also launched multiview in its app on major smart TV platforms.

Tech.title: Raspberry Pi shares its official tutorial for making a cyberdeck
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Raspberry Pi’s head of social, Ashley Whittaker, acknowledged the cyberdeck trend today, saying “we haven’t been able to get away from cyberdecks this year.” Tiny portable computers made out of things like purses, jewelry boxes, and other thrifted or recycled parts have gone viral on TikTok and other social media platforms over the past year, and Raspberry Pi now has its own guide to building one of the homemade computers.

Raspberry Pi has also increased its prices multiple times this year due to rising costs for RAM and other components, which could be another reason to support this growing market of active and would-be hobbyists. The 16GB version of the Raspberry Pi 5 included in the company’s official cyberdeck guide got a $100 price hike in April, nearly as much as the board’s original $120 price.

Raspberry Pi’s cyberdeck includes a Pi 5 board, Raspberry Pi flash drive, and a LiPo battery hidden under a Bluetooth keyboard. Image: Raspberry Pi

Raspberry Pi’s cyberdeck guide includes a parts list and detailed assembly instructions, but sticks to a fairly simple design using a plain black Pelican-style case. As content creators are proving, though, you can make a cyberdeck out of just about anything. Annike Tan, whose cyberdecks have attracted millions of views on TikTok, continues to upgrade her “mermaid” purse cyberdeck with new design details and even added a USB hub.

Tech.title: India’s Airbound bags $37M to take on trucks with rocket-like drones
Tech.content:
Airbound, an Indian startup building autonomous drones, has raised $37 million in fresh capital as it pushes to make moving goods through the air as cheap as trucking them by road.

The Series A round, led by Greenoaks with participation from DoorDash, Lachy Groom, Lightspeed, and Humba Ventures, comes less than a year after Airbound raised an $8.65 million seed round. With this funding, the three-year-old startup has raised nearly $50 million.

Airbound, and other startups in this nascent sector, argue that drones can move certain goods faster and cheaper than vehicles on the road. And while there have been successful deployments, drone delivery is still far from matching the scale and versatility of trucking.

Airbound is trying to close that gap by redesigning the aircraft to make it more competitive with ground transportation.

Conventional aircraft spend a lot of energy carrying their own weight rather than the payload, making flight expensive, particularly for moving smaller loads. Airbound’s answer is to build vertical-flight drones designed to weigh less than the cargo they carry, founder and CEO Naman Pushp said in an interview.

Airbound’s current drone, called TRT, weighs about 3.3 pounds and can carry around 2.2 pounds of payload. Its next version, currently under development, is expected to weigh about 6.6 pounds and be able to carry up to 11 pounds, Pushp told TechCrunch.

The startup uses a rocket-like, tail-sitter design for its drones, which takes off and lands vertically in an upright position before transitioning to horizontal flight. Pushp said Airbound intends to retain vertical takeoff and landing even as it develops larger aircraft to avoid dependence on runways.

“We want to build towards a world where everything has cost parity with trucking,” he said.

Founded in 2023, Airbound has completed more than 13,000 autonomous flights across the southern Indian cities of Bengaluru and Guntur, Pushp said. That includes more than 1,000 flights with the Indian hospital network Narayana Health, where its drones transport diagnostic samples between healthcare facilities.

The startup uses a single active drone on the Narayana route, flying diagnostic samples about 2.5 miles in around seven minutes. The same samples can take three to five hours to be transported by two-wheelers when factoring in the time spent waiting for enough samples to be bundled for road transport, according to Pushp.

That partnership is expanding to include Narayana’s new Banashankari hospital in Bengaluru, which was designed without an on-site diagnostic lab or blood bank and will instead rely on Airbound’s drones to connect with centralized facilities.

Three-city drone network

Airbound has set its sights on a far larger ambition to create a drone delivery network that connects three cities in the state of Andhra Pradesh. The startup has sign an agreement with the state government with an eventual target of 10,000 flights a day for retail, e-commerce, and healthcare deliveries. That daily flight target will require between 250 and 1,000 aircraft, depending on route lengths, though Pushp expects the number to be closer to 250.

The agreement does not involve a government contract or subsidy, Pushp said, adding that the Andhra Pradesh government is working with Airbound on the regulatory framework needed to enable the network. The startup expects to generate business from companies using it for deliveries.

Indian startups including Skye Air Mobility and TSAW Drones are already building aerial logistics businesses, while other Indian drone makers such as Garuda Aerospace have also explored delivery use cases. Nonetheless, Pushp argues that Airbound wants to build the aircraft that other logistics networks could eventually use rather than just trying to become the largest delivery operator.

“That’s the Boeing role — the aircraft airlines everywhere rely on, not the airline itself,” he said.

Airbound designs and manufactures its aircraft in a 43,000-square-foot facility in Bengaluru, where it keeps work on the airframe and other core systems in-house. While Pushp declined to disclose its production capacity or how many aircraft the startup has built so far, he said manufacturing would not be the bottleneck as Airbound scales.

The bigger bottleneck, Pushp noted, is regulation, particularly securing approvals for beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) operations, a certification that allows drones to fly beyond the direct sight of an operator and is critical to operating delivery networks at scale.

Those regulatory constraints have also limited Airbound’s ability to turn its flights into meaningful commercial revenue. Moreover, the startup remains broadly pre-revenue despite having a team of more than 150 employees.

“The goal is to be a giant in a few decades, not to make revenue as soon as we can,” Pushp said.

Tech.title: Situational Awareness, star AI hedge fund that nearly imploded, now being probed by the SEC
Tech.content:
In Brief

Situational Awareness, the AI focused hedge fund that was Wall Street’s fleeting obsession, is having a very bad month.

The company, led by twentysomething OpenAI alum Leopold Aschenbrenner, went all-in on a variety of AI investments and, for a period, enjoyed phenomenal growth. Then, at the end of July, a downturn in AI stocks erased billions of dollars in value at the firm. Now, federal regulators are reportedly probing the company as well.

The New York Times reports that the Securities and Exchange Commission has been subpoenaing banks that did business with the hedge fund. The subpoenas focus on the banks that supervised the fund’s trading and that channeled funding to support it, the outlet says.

The government reportedly warned the banks to “preserve any information” about the hedge fund, though it noted that Situational Awareness has not been accused of any wrongdoing.

Situational Awareness did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment but told the Times that scrutiny of high-profile funds is to be expected, and that it would “cooperate to the fullest extent with any regulatory request.”

The company, which very publicly hitched its wagon to AI’s star, may serve as a cautionary tale about the industry’s supposedly unstoppable trajectory.

Tech.title: Oura is reportedly eyeing a September IPO that could value it at more than $16B
Tech.content:
Oura, the smart ring maker, with offices in San Francisco and Finland, is reportedly planning to raise up to $3 billion as soon as next month in a U.S. IPO that values the more than 900-person company at [spits out coffee] north of $16 billion, according to Bloomberg. The outlet adds that investors are expected to sell a major chunk of stock in the offering.

A $16 billion valuation would mark an enormous jump from the $10.9 billion valuation Oura was assigned last September, when it closed an $875 million Series E round backed by Fidelity, ICONIQ, Whale Rock, and Atreides, joining earlier backers like Dexcom, The Chernin Group, Forerunner Ventures, Coatue, and Temasek.

The wearables space has gotten crowded fast.

Samsung launched its own ring, the Galaxy Ring, two years ago. But Oura’s most direct rival may be the fitness band maker Whoop, which has undergone its own reinvention. Once a performance tool for elite athletes and young men, Whoop has spent the past year courting a much broader audience, layering in hormone tracking and blood-panel testing for perimenopause and thyroid health. The move drove its own valuation up to $10 billion back in March. Oura has followed a similar path, evolving from its starting niche of biohacking CEOs into a more mainstream sleep-and-recovery brand.

Oura announced in May that it had filed confidentially for an IPO.

The company has said that it generated $500 million in revenue in 2024, roughly $1 billion in 2025, and that it expected to generate close to $2 billion in revenue in 2026, though we’ll learn much more once its S-1 filing becomes publicly available.

Not all of Oura’s recent attention has been positive. A proposed class action lawsuit filed last week in San Francisco is accusing Oura of misleading consumers about the accuracy of its sleep tracking features. Among other complaints in the filing, Oura is accused of not just claiming “to measure a heartbeat or a temperature, but the exact stage of sleep the wearer is in—which in reality requires electrodes in the scalp and sensors on the eyes, as only a hospital or other clinical setting can do.”

In a statement to TechCrunch sent over the weekend, a spokesperson pushed back against claims in that suit, saying the company plans to “defend against them in the appropriate legal forum” and that “[w]hile Oura Ring is not a medical device or a substitute for a clinical sleep study, Oura’s sleep staging has been validated and compared favorably in multiple studies against polysomnography, the gold standard.” The statement continued on to say that “[m]ultiple third-party, independent studies support our claims of accuracy and we have transparently reported on the mechanisms and measures that inform Oura’s sleep staging.”

Tech.title: Trump bought SpaceX shares two weeks after blockbuster IPO
Tech.content:
In Brief

President Donald Trump bought as much as $50,000 worth of SpaceX shares on June 23, according to a financial disclosure first reported by Reuters, two weeks after the record-setting IPO of Elon Musk’s company.

It’s not clear what price Trump paid for the shares, but by that point they had fallen from their highs of over $200. SpaceX shares were trading in the mid-$150 range on June 23. At the end of trading on Monday, shares closed at the IPO price of $135, possibly putting the president’s stake underwater.

Trump and Musk are close, despite a brief falling out last summer that involved the businessman accusing the president of withholding the Department of Justice’s files on Jeffrey Epstein because of how often Trump’s name appears in them. SpaceX has been hoovering up an increasing amount of government contracts and benefiting from the Trump administration’s deregulatory stance, according to a recent Wall Street Journal analysis.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Reuters that the president’s stock portfolio is managed by third-party financial institutions and replicate “recognized indexes, such as the Schwab ​1000.” SpaceX lobbied popular indexes to change their rules to allow for faster inclusion ahead of its IPO, which means many people likely own some of the company’s stock even if they don’t know it.

Tech.title: Zillow and Redfin settle FTC antitrust case
Tech.content:
Zillow and Redfin have reached a settlement with the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and five states, ending a legal fight over a 2025 partnership that the FTC claimed hurt competition in the rental-listing market. The settlement was announced on Monday, just as the case was scheduled to head toward trial this morning.

The case stems from a deal announced last year in which Redfin agreed to display Zillow’s rental listings on its websites rather than compete directly with Zillow for rental advertisers. The arrangement could have kept Redfin out of the rental advertising business for as long as nine years. Redfin owns Rent.com and ApartmentGuide.com, two major rental-listing platforms.

According to the FTC and attorneys general from Arizona, Connecticut, New York, Virginia, and Washington, Zillow agreed to pay Redfin $100 million to keep Redfin from competing with Zillow.

The companies defended the partnership as a way to give renters access to a larger pool of listings. The FTC, however, argued that Zillow was paying one of its largest competitors to stop competing, potentially allowing the company to charge higher prices and provide less favorable terms to property managers. It could have also reduced the quality of rental listings available to consumers.

Under the proposed settlement, Redfin will be required to reenter the rental advertising business. The order also removes restrictions that previously limited Redfin’s ability to compete independently for property-management customers.

The settlement doesn’t completely end the relationship between the two companies. Redfin can continue displaying Zillow’s rental listings, but it will once again be able to compete for its own customers. Redfin will be able to sell advertising, display listings from its own clients, and pursue new rental customers without being required to share sensitive business information with Zillow.

The Zillow-Redfin case comes just months after the DOJ’s settlement with Ticketmaster, another antitrust case involving allegations that a dominant company used its power to suppress competition. However, 26 of the 30 state attorneys general who initially sued Live Nation alongside the DOJ chose to continue pursuing the case and won their lawsuit in April.
